senses.d: Same as Tabor.
A slightly built or temporary habitation; especially, a tent.
q: Dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob.
Orange trees planted in the ground, and secured in winter with a wooden tabernacle and stoves.

senses.d: A portable structure of wooden framework covered with curtains, which was carried through the wilderness in the Israelitish exodus, as a place of sacrifice and worship.
Hence, the Jewish temple; sometimes, any other place for worship.
Figuratively: The human body, as the temporary abode of the soul.
q: Shortly I must put off this my tabernacle.

senses.d: Any small cell, or like place, in which some holy or precious things was deposited or kept.
The ornamental receptacle for the pyx, or for the consecrated elements, whether a part of a building or movable.
A niche for the image of a saint, or for any sacred painting or sculpture.
Hence, a work of art of sacred subject, having a partially architectural character, as a solid frame resting on a bracket, or the like.
A tryptich for sacred imagery.
A seat or stall in a choir, with its canopy.
A boxlike step for a mast with the after side open, so that the mast can be lowered to pass under bridges, etc.

Tabernacle.etym: [F., fr. L. tabernaculum, dim. of taberna nut. See Tabern.]

senses.d: To dwell or reside for a time; to be temporary housed.
q: He assumed our nature, and tabernacled among us in the flesh.

senses.d: A smooth, flat surface, like the side of a board; a thin, flat, smooth piece of anything; a slab.
q: A bagnio paved with fair tables of marble.

senses.d: A thin, flat piece of wood, stone, metal, or other material, on which anything is cut, traced, written, or painted; a tablet
q: And the Lord said unto Moses, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first, and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest.
And stand there with your tables to glean The golden sentences.

senses.d: Any smooth, flat surface upon which an inscription, a drawing, or the like, may be produced.
q: The opposite walls are painted by Rubens, which, with that other of the Infanta taking leave of Don Philip, is a most incomparable table.
St. Antony has a table that hangs up to him from a poor peasant.

senses.d: Hence, in a great variety of applications: A condensed statement which may be comprehended by the eye in a single view; a methodical or systematic synopsis; the presentation of many items or particulars in one group; a scheme; a schedule.
A view of the contents of a work; a statement of the principal topics discussed; an index; a syllabus; a synopsis; as, a table of contents.
A list of substances and their properties; especially, a list of the elementary substances with their atomic weights, densities, symbols, etc.

Any collection and arrangement in a condensed form of many particulars or values, for ready reference, as of weights, measures, currency, specific gravities, etc.; also, a series of numbers following some law, and expressing particular values corresponding to certain other numbers on which they depend, and by means of which they are taken out for use in computations; as, tables of logarithms, sines, tangents, squares, cubes, etc.; annuity tables; interest tables; astronomical tables, etc.
The arrangement or disposition of the lines which appear on the inside of the hand.
q: Mistress of a fairer table Hath not history for fable.

senses.d: An article of furniture, consisting of a flat slab, board, or the like, having a smooth surface, fixed horizontally on legs, and used for a great variety of purposes, as in eating, writing, or working.
q: We may again Give to our tables meat.
The nymph the table spread.

senses.d: Hence, food placed on a table to be partaken of; fare; entertainment; as, to set a good table.
The company assembled round a table.
q: I drink the general joy of the whole table.

senses.d: One of the two, external and internal, layers of compact bone, separated by diploë, in the walls of the cranium.

Table.etym: [F., fr. L. tabula a board, tablet, a painting. Cf. Tabular, Taffrail, Tavern.]

senses.d: To form into a table or catalogue; to tabulate; as, to table fines.
To delineate, as on a table; to represent, as in a picture.
q: Tabled and pictured in the chambers of meditation.

senses.d: To supply with food; to feed.
To insert, as one piece of timber into another, by alternate scores or projections from the middle, to prevent slipping; to scarf.
To lay or place on a table, as money.
In parliamentary usage, to lay on the table; to postpone, by a formal vote, the consideration of (a bill, motion, or the like) till called for, or indefinitely.
To enter upon the docket; as, to table charges against some one.
To make board hems in the skirts and bottoms of (sails) in order to strengthen them in the part attached to the boltrope.
To live at the table of another; to board; to eat.
A small table or flat surface.
A flat piece of any material on which to write, paint, draw, or engrave; also, such a piece containing an inscription or a picture.
Hence, a small picture; a miniature.
A kind of pocket memorandum book.
A flattish cake or piece; as, tablets of arsenic were formerly worn as a preservative against the plague.

A solid kind of electuary or confection, commonly made of dry ingredients with sugar, and usually formed into little flat squares; — called also lozenge, and troche, especially when of a round or rounded form.

Tablet.etym: [F. tablette, dim. of table. See Table.]

senses.d: A small drum used as an accompaniment to a pipe or fife, both being played by the same person.

Tabor.etym: [OF. tabor, tabour, F. tambour; cf. Pr. tabor, tanbor, Sp. & Pg. tambor, atambor, It. tamburo; all fr. Ar. & Per. tamb�r a kind of lute, or giutar, or Per. tabīr a drum. Cf. Tabouret, Tambour.]

senses.d: To play on a tabor, or little drum.
To strike lightly and frequently.
To make (a sound) with a tabor.
A taboret.
Something used for taking hold or holding; a catch; a loop; a button.
A spot, stain, or blemish.
Apparatus for raising or lowering heavy weights, consisting of a rope and pulley blocks; sometimes, the rope and attachments, as distinct from the block.
Any instruments of action; an apparatus by which an object is moved or operated; gear; as, fishing tackle, hunting tackle; formerly, specifically, weapons.
The rigging and apparatus of a ship; also, any purchase where more than one block is used.

Tackle.etym: [OE. takel, akin to LG. & D. takel, Dan. takkel, Sw. tackel; perhaps akin to E. taw, v.t., or to take.]

senses.d: To supply with tackle.
To fasten or attach, as with a tackle; to harness; as, to tackle a horse into a coach or wagon.
To seize; to lay hold of; to grapple; as, a wrestler tackles his antagonist; a dog tackles the game.
q: The greatest poetess of our day has wasted her time and strength in tackling windmills under conditions the most fitted to insure her defeat.

Tackle.etym: [Cf. LG. takeln to equip. See Tackle, n.]

senses.d: Furniture of the masts and yards of a vessel, as cordage, sails, etc.
Instruments of action; as, fishing tackling.
The straps and fixures adjusted to an animal, by which he draws a carriage, or the like; harness.
The African rufous-necked weaver bird (Hyphantornis texor).
Limitation; abridgment.

Tail.etym: [F. taille a cutting. See Entail, Tally.]

senses.d: Limited; abridged; reduced; curtailed; as, estate tail.
The terminal, and usually flexible, posterior appendage of an animal.
Any long, flexible terminal appendage; whatever resembles, in shape or position, the tail of an animal, as a catkin.
q: Doretus writes a great praise of the distilled waters of those tails that hang on willow trees.

senses.d: Hence, the back, last, lower, or inferior part of anything, — as opposed to the head, or the superior part.
q: The Lord will make thee the head, and not the tail.

senses.d: A train or company of attendants; a retinue.
q: “Ah,” said he, “if you saw but the chief with his tail on.”

senses.d: The side of a coin opposite to that which bears the head, effigy, or date; the reverse; — rarely used except in the expression “heads or tails,” employed when a coin is thrown up for the purpose of deciding some point by its fall.
The distal tendon of a muscle.
A downy or feathery appendage to certain achens. It is formed of the permanent elongated style.
A portion of an incision, at its beginning or end, which does not go through the whole thickness of the skin, and is more painful than a complete incision; — called also tailing.
A rope spliced to the strap of a block, by which it may be lashed to anything.
The part of a note which runs perpendicularly upward or downward from the head; the stem.
Same as Tailing, 4.
The bottom or lower portion of a member or part, as a slate or tile.
q: Would she turn tail to the heron, and fly quite out another way; but all was to return in a higher pitch.

Tail.etym: [AS. tægel, tægl; akin to G. zagel, Icel. tagl, Sw. tagel, Goth. tagl hair. √59.]

senses.d: To follow or hang to, like a tail; to be attached closely to, as that which can not be evaded.
q: Nevertheless his bond of two thousand pounds, wherewith he was tailed, continued uncanceled, and was called on the next Parliament.

senses.d: To pull or draw by the tail.
To hold by the end; — said of a timber when it rests upon a wall or other support; — with in or into.
To swing with the stern in a certain direction; — said of a vessel at anchor; as, this vessel tails down stream.
In some forms of rope-laying machine, pieces of rope attached to the iron bar passing through the grooven wooden top containing the strands, for wrapping around the rope to be laid.
A tailed coat; a tail coat.
In flying machines, a plane or group of planes used at the rear to confer stability.
Taken.
In an active sense; To lay hold of; to seize with the hands, or otherwise; to grasp; to get into one's hold or possession; to procure; to seize and carry away; to convey.

To obtain possession of by force or artifice; to get the custody or control of; to reduce into subjection to one's power or will; to capture; to seize; to make prisoner; as, to take am army, a city, or a ship; also, to come upon or befall; to fasten on; to attack; to seize; — said of a disease, misfortune, or the like.
q: This man was taken of the Jews.
Men in their loose, unguarded hours they take; Not that themselves are wise, but others weak.
They that come abroad after these showers are commonly taken with sickness.
There he blasts the tree and takes the cattle And makes milch kine yield blood.

senses.d: To gain or secure the interest or affection of; to captivate; to engage; to interest; to charm.
q: Neither let her take thee with her eyelids.
Cleombroutus was so taken with this prospect, that he had no patience.

I know not why, but there was a something in those half-seen features, — a charm in the very shadow that hung over their imagined beauty, — which took me more than all the outshining loveliness of her companions.

senses.d: To make selection of; to choose; also, to turn to; to have recourse to; as, to take the road to the right.
q: Saul said, Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son. And Jonathan was taken.
The violence of storming is the course which God is forced to take for the destroying . . . of sinners.

senses.d: To employ; to use; to occupy; hence, to demand; to require; as, it takes so much cloth to make a coat.
q: This man always takes time . . . before he passes his judgments.

senses.d: To form a likeness of; to copy; to delineate; to picture; as, to take picture of a person.
q: Beauty alone could beauty take so right.

senses.d: To draw; to deduce; to derive.
q: The firm belief of a future judgment is the most forcible motive to a good life, because taken from this consideration of the most lasting happiness and misery.

senses.d: To assume; to adopt; to acquire, as shape; to permit to one's self; to indulge or engage in; to yield to; to have or feel; to enjoy or experience, as rest, revenge, delight, shame; to form and adopt, as a resolution; — used in general senses, limited by a following complement, in many idiomatic phrases; as, to take a resolution; I take the liberty to say.
To lead; to conduct; as, to take a child to church.
To carry; to convey; to deliver to another; to hand over; as, he took the book to the bindery.
q: He took me certain gold, I wot it well.

senses.d: To remove; to withdraw; to deduct; — with from; as, to take the breath from one; to take two from four.
In a somewhat passive sense, to receive; to bear; to endure; to acknowledge; to accept.

Take.etym: [Icel. taka; akin to Sw. taga, Dan. tage, Goth. tēkan to touch; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To take hold; to fix upon anything; to have the natural or intended effect; to accomplish a purpose; as, he was inoculated, but the virus did not take.
q: When flame taketh and openeth, it giveth a noise.
In impressions from mind to mind, the impression taketh, but is overcome . . . before it work any manifest effect.

senses.d: To please; to gain reception; to succeed.
q: Each wit may praise it for his own dear sake, And hint he writ it, if the thing should take.

senses.d: To move or direct the course; to resort; to betake one's self; to proceed; to go; — usually with to; as, the fox, being hard pressed, took to the hedge.
To admit of being pictured, as in a photograph; as, his face does not take well.
That which is taken; especially, the quantity of fish captured at one haul or catch.
The quantity or copy given to a compositor at one time.
To make a picture, photograph, or the like, of; as, to take a group or a scene.
To give or deliver (a blow to); to strike; hit; as, he took me in the face; he took me a blow on the head.
One who takes or receives; one who catches or apprehended.
Apt to take; alluring; attracting.
q: Subtile in making his temptations most taking.

senses.d: Infectious; contageous.
The act of gaining possession; a seizing; seizure; apprehension.
Agitation; excitement; distress of mind.
q: What a taking was he in, when your husband asked who was in the basket!

senses.d: Malign influence; infection.
That which is told; an oral relation or recital; any rehearsal of what has occured; narrative; discourse; statement; history; story.
q: We spend our years as a tale that is told.

senses.d: A number told or counted off; a reckoning by count; an enumeration; a count, in distinction from measure or weight; a number reckoned or stated.
q: The ignorant, . . . who measure by tale, and not by weight.
And every shepherd tells his tale, Under the hawthorn in the dale.
In packing, they keep a just tale of the number.

senses.d: A count or declaration.
q: Therefore little tale hath he told Of any dream, so holy was his heart.

Tale.syn: Anecdote; story; fable; incident; memoir; relation; account; legend; narrative.
Tale.etym: [AS. talu number, speech, narrative; akin to D. taal speech, language, G. zahl number, OHG. zala, Icel. tal, tala, number, speech, Sw. tal, Dan. tal number, tale speech, Goth. talzjan to instruct. Cf. Tell, v. t., Toll a tax, also Talk, v. i.]

senses.d: To tell stories.
One who officiously tells tales; one who impertinently or maliciously communicates intelligence, scandal, etc., and makes mischief.
q: Spies and talebearers, encouraged by her father, did their best to inflame her resentment.

senses.d: Among the ancient Greeks, a weight and a denomination of money equal to 60 minæ or 6,000 drachmæ. The Attic talent, as a weight, was about 57 lbs. avoirdupois; as a denomination of silver money, its value was £243 15s. sterling, or about $1,180.
q: Rowing vessel whose burden does not exceed five hundred talents.

senses.d: Among the Hebrews, a weight and denomination of money. For silver it was equivalent to 3,000 shekels, and in weight was equal to about 93� lbs. avoirdupois; as a denomination of silver, it has been variously estimated at from £340 to £396 sterling, or about $1,645 to $1,916. For gold it was equal to 10,000 gold shekels.
Inclination; will; disposition; desire.
q: They rather counseled you to your talent than to your profit.

senses.d: Intellectual ability, natural or acquired; mental endowment or capacity; skill in accomplishing; a special gift, particularly in business, art, or the like; faculty; a use of the word probably originating in the Scripture parable of the talents (Matt. xxv. 14-30).
q: He is chiefly to be considered in his three different talents, as a critic, a satirist, and a writer of odes.
His talents, his accomplishments, his graceful manners, made him generally popular.

Talent.syn: Ability; faculty; gift; endowment. See Genius.
Talent.etym: [F., fr. L. talentum a talent (in sense 1), Gr. ταλαντον a balance, anything weighed, a definite weight, a talent; akin to τλη̑ναι to bear, endure, τολμα̑ν, L. tolerare, tollere, to lift up, sustain, endure. See Thole, v. t., Tolerate.]

senses.d: Persons added to a jury, commonly from those in or about the courthouse, to make up any deficiency in the number of jurors regularly summoned, being like, or such as, the latter.
The writ by which such persons are summoned.
To utter words; esp., to converse familiarly; to speak, as in familiar discourse, when two or more persons interchange thoughts.
q: I will buy with you, sell with you, talk with you, walk with you, and so following, but I will not eat with you.

senses.d: To confer; to reason; to consult.
q: Let me talk with thee of thy judgments.

senses.d: To prate; to speak impertinently.

Talk.etym: [Cf. LG. talk talk, gabble, Prov. G. talken to speak indistinctly; or OD. tolken to interpret, MHG. tolkan to interpret, to tell, to speak indistinctly, Dan. tolke to interpret, Sw. tolka, Icel. t�lka to interpret, t�lkr an interpreter, Lith. tulkas an interpreter, tulkanti, tulkōti, to interpret, R

senses.d: To speak freely; to use for conversing or communicating; as, to talk French.
To deliver in talking; to speak; to utter; to make a subject of conversation; as, to talk nonsense; to talk politics.
To consume or spend in talking; — often followed by away; as, to talk away an evening.
To cause to be or become by talking.
The act of talking; especially, familiar converse; mutual discourse; that which is uttered, especially in familiar conversation, or the mutual converse of two or more.
q: In various talk the instructive hours they passed.
Their talk, when it was not made up of nautical phrases, was too commonly made up of oaths and curses.

senses.d: Report; rumor; as, to hear talk of war.
q: I hear a talk up and down of raising our money.

senses.d: Subject of discourse; as, his achievment is the talk of the town.

Talk.syn: Conversation; colloquy; discourse; chat; dialogue; conference; communication. See Conversation.

senses.d: One who talks; especially, one who is noted for his power of conversing readily or agreeably; a conversationist.
q: There probably were never four talkers more admirable in four different ways than Johnson, Burke, Beauclerk, and Garrick.

senses.d: A loquacious person, male or female; a prattler; a babbler; also, a boaster; a braggart; — used in contempt or reproach.
That talks; able to utter words; as, a talking parrot.
Given to talk; loquacious.
q: The hawthorn bush, with seats beneath the shade, For talking age and whispering lovers made.

senses.d: High in stature; having a considerable, or an unusual, extension upward; long and comparatively slender; having the diameter or lateral extent small in proportion to the height; as, a tall person, tree, or mast.
q: Two of far nobler shape, erect and tall.

senses.d: Brave; bold; courageous.
q: As tall a trencherman As e'er demolished a pye fortification.
His companions, being almost in despair of victory, were suddenly recomforted by Sir William Stanley, which came to succors with three thousand tall men.

senses.d: Fine; splendid; excellent; also, extravagant; excessive.

Tall.etym: [OE. tal seemly, elegant, docile (?); of uncertain origin; cf. AS. un-tala, un-tale, bad, Goth. untals indocile, disobedient, uninstructed, or W. & Corn. tal high, Ir. talla meet, fit, proper, just.]

senses.d: To broach or enter upon; to taste, as a liquor; to divide; to distribute; to deal out.
q: In the time of famine he is the Joseph of the country, and keeps the poor from starving. Then he tameth his stacks of corn, which not his covetousness, but providence, hath reserved for time of need.

Tame.etym: [Cf. F. entamer to cut into, to broach.]

senses.d: Reduced from a state of native wildness and shyness; accustomed to man; domesticated; domestic; as, a tame deer, a tame bird.
Crushed; subdued; depressed; spiritless.
q: Tame slaves of the laborious plow.

senses.d: Deficient in spirit or animation; spiritless; dull; flat; insipid; as, a tame poem; tame scenery.

Tame.etym: [AS. tam; akin to D. tam, G. zahm, OHG. zam, Dan. & Sw. tam, Icel. tamr, L. domare to tame, Gr. �, Skr. dam to be tame, to tame, and perhaps to E. beteem. √61. Cf. Adamant, Diamond, Dame, Daunt, Indomitable.]

senses.d: To reduce from a wild to a domestic state; to make gentle and familiar; to reclaim; to domesticate; as, to tame a wild beast.
q: They had not been tamed into submission, but baited into savegeness and stubbornness.

senses.d: To subdue; to conquer; to repress; as, to tame the pride or passions of youth.

Tame.etym: [AS. tamian, temian, akin to D. tammen, temmen, G. zähmen, OHG. zemmen, Icel. temja, Goth. gatamjan. See Tame, a.]

senses.d: The bark of the oak, and some other trees, bruised and broken by a mill, for tanning hides; — so called both before and after it has been used. Called also tan bark.
A yellowish-brown color, like that of tan.
A brown color imparted to the skin by exposure to the sun; as, hands covered with tan.

Tan.etym: [F. tan, perhaps fr. Armor. tann an oak, oak bar; or of Teutonic origin; cf. G. tanne a fir, OHG. tanna a fir, oak, MHG. tan a forest. Cf. Tawny.]

senses.d: Of the color of tan; yellowish-brown.

To convert (the skin of an animal) into leather, as by the usual process of steeping it in an infusion of oak or some other bark, whereby it is impregnated with tannin, or tannic acid (which exists in several species of bark), and is thus rendered firm, durable, and in some degree impervious to water.
To make brown; to imbrown, as by exposure to the rays of the sun; as, to tan the skin.

Tan.etym: [F. tanner, LL. tannare. See Tan, n.]

senses.d: To get or become tanned.
To thrash or beat; to flog; to switch.
One whose occupation is to tan hides, or convert them into leather by the use of tan.
A sixpence.

A fabric, usually of worsted, worked upon a warp of linen or other thread by hand, the designs being usually more or less pictorial and the stuff employed for wall hangings and the like. The term is also applied to different kinds of embroidery.

Tapestry.etym: [F. tapissere, fr. tapisser to carpet, to hang, or cover with tapestry, fr. tapis a carpet, carpeting, LL. tapecius, fr. L. tapete carpet, tapestry, Gr. �, �. Cf. Tapis, Tippet.]

senses.d: To adorn with tapestry, or as with tapestry.
q: The Trosachs wound, as now, between gigantic walls of rock tapestried with broom and wild roses.

senses.d: A sailor; a seaman.
A thick, black, viscous liquid obtained by the distillation of wood, coal, etc., and having a varied composition according to the temperature and material employed in obtaining it.

Tar.etym: [OE. terre, tarre, AS. teru, teoru; akin to D. teer, G. teer, theer, Icel. tjara, Sw. tjära, Dan. tiære, and to E. tree. √63. See Tree.]

senses.d: To smear with tar, or as with tar; as, to tar ropes; to tar cloth.
Tore.
A weed that grows among wheat and other grain; — alleged by modern naturalists to be the Lolium temulentum, or darnel.
q: Didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? From whence then hath it tares?
The “darnel” is said to be the tares of Scripture, and is the only deleterious species belonging to the whole order.

senses.d: A name of several climbing or diffuse leguminous herbs of the genus Vicia; especially, the V. sativa, sometimes grown for fodder.

Tare.etym: [Cf. Prov. E. tare brisk, eager, OE. tarefitch the wild vetch.]

senses.d: Deficientcy in the weight or quantity of goods by reason of the weight of the cask, bag, or whatever contains the commodity, and is weighed with it; hence, the allowance or abatement of a certain weight or quantity which the seller makes to the buyer on account of the weight of such cask, bag, etc.

Tare.etym: [F. tare; cf. Pr., Sp., Pg., & It. tara; all fr. Ar. tarah thrown away, removed, fr. taraha to reject, remove.]

senses.d: To ascertain or mark the tare of (goods).
A kind of small shield or buckler, used as a defensive weapon in war.
A butt or mark to shoot at, as for practice, or to test the accuracy of a firearm, or the force of a projectile.
The sliding crosspiece, or vane, on a leveling staff.
A conspicuous disk attached to a switch lever to show its position, or for use as a signal.

Target.etym: [OF. targette, dim. of OF. & F. targe, of Teutonic origin; cf. AS. targe, OD. targie, G. zarge a frame, case, border, OHG. zarga, Icel. targa shield.]

senses.d: A thin cut; a slice; specif., of lamb, a piece consisting of the neck and breast joints.
A tassel or pendent; also, a shred; tatter.
Consisting of, or covered with, tar; like tar.
To stay or remain behind; to wait.
q: Tarry ye for us, until we come again.

senses.d: To delay; to put off going or coming; to loiter.
q: Come down unto me, tarry not.
One tarried here, there hurried one.

senses.d: To stay; to abide; to continue; to lodge.
q: Tarry all night, and wash your feet.

Tarry.syn: To abide; continue; lodge; await; loiter.
Tarry.etym: [OE. tarien to irritate (see Tarre); but with a change of sense probably due to confusion with OE. targen to delay, OF. targier, fr. (assumed) LL. tardicare, fr. L. tardare to make slow, to tarry, fr. tardus slow. Cf. Tardy.]

senses.d: To delay; to defer; to put off.
q: Tarry us here no longer than to-morrow.

senses.d: To wait for; to stay or stop for.
q: He that will have a cake out of the wheat must needs tarry the grinding.
He plodded on, . . . tarrying no further question.

senses.d: Stay; stop; delay.
The ankle; the bones or cartilages of the part of the foot between the metatarsus and the leg, consisting in man of seven short bones.
The foot of an insect or a crustacean. It usually consists of form two to five joints.

Tarsus.etym: [NL., fr. Gr. � the flat of the foot, the edge of the eyelid. Cf. 2d Tarse.]

senses.d: Woolen cloth, checkered or crossbarred with narrow bands of various colors, much worn in the Highlands of Scotland; hence, any pattern of tartan; also, other material of a similar pattern.
q: MacCullummore's heart will be as cold as death can make it, when it does not warm to the tartan.
The sight of the tartan inflamed the populace of London with hatred.

Tartan.etym: [F. tiretane linsey-woolsey, akin to Sp. tiritaña a sort of thin silk; cf. Sp. tiritar to shiver or shake with cold.]

senses.d: A small coasting vessel, used in the Mediterranean, having one mast carrying large leteen sail, and a bowsprit with staysail or jib.

Tartan.etym: [F. tartane, or Sp., Pg., or It. tartana; all perhaps of Arabic origin.]

senses.d: Labor or study imposed by another, often in a definite quantity or amount.
q: Ma task of servile toil.
Each morning sees some task begin, Each evening sees it close.

senses.d: Business; employment; undertaking; labor.
q: His mental powers were equal to greater tasks.

Task.syn: Work; labor; employment; business; toil; drudgery; study; lesson; stint.
Task.etym: [OE. taske, OF. tasque, F. tâche, for tasche, LL. tasca, taxa, fr. L. taxare to rate, appraise, estimate. See Tax, n. & v.]

senses.d: To impose a task upon; to assign a definite amount of business, labor, or duty to.
q: There task thy maids, and exercise the loom.

senses.d: To oppress with severe or excessive burdens; to tax.
To charge; to tax; as with a fault.
q: Too impudent to task me with those errors.

senses.d: One who imposes a task, or burdens another with labor; one whose duty is to assign tasks; an overseer.
q: All is, if I have grace to use it so, As ever in my great Taskmaster's eye.

senses.d: To try by the touch; to handle; as, to taste a bow.
q: Taste it well and stone thou shalt it find.

senses.d: To try by the touch of the tongue; to perceive the relish or flavor of (anything) by taking a small quantity into a mouth. Also used figuratively.
q: When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine.
When Commodus had once tasted human blood, he became incapable of pity or remorse.

senses.d: To try by eating a little; to eat a small quantity of.
q: I tasted a little of this honey.

senses.d: To become acquainted with by actual trial; to essay; to experience; to undergo.
q: He . . . should taste death for every man.

senses.d: To partake of; to participate in; — usually with an implied sense of relish or pleasure.
q: Thou . . . wilt taste No pleasure, though in pleasure, solitary.

Taste.etym: [OE. tasten to feel, to taste, OF. taster, F. tater to feel, to try by the touch, to try, to taste, (assumed) LL. taxitare, fr. L. taxare to touch sharply, to estimate. See Tax, v. t.]

senses.d: To try food with the mouth; to eat or drink a little only; to try the flavor of anything; as, to taste of each kind of wine.

To have a smack; to excite a particular sensation, by which the specific quality or flavor is distinguished; to have a particular quality or character; as, this water tastes brackish; the milk tastes of garlic.
q: Yea, every idle, nice, and wanton reason Shall to the king taste of this action.

senses.d: To take sparingly.
q: For age but tastes of pleasures, youth devours.

senses.d: To have perception, experience, or enjoyment; to partake; as, to taste of nature's bounty.
q: The valiant never taste of death but once.

senses.d: The act of tasting; gustation.

A particular sensation excited by the application of a substance to the tongue; the quality or savor of any substance as perceived by means of the tongue; flavor; as, the taste of an orange or an apple; a bitter taste; an acid taste; a sweet taste.
The one of the five senses by which certain properties of bodies (called their taste, savor, flavor) are ascertained by contact with the organs of taste.
Intellectual relish; liking; fondness; — formerly with of, now with for; as, he had no taste for study.
q: I have no taste Of popular applause.

senses.d: The power of perceiving and relishing excellence in human performances; the faculty of discerning beauty, order, congruity, proportion, symmetry, or whatever constitutes excellence, particularly in the fine arts and belles-letters; critical judgment; discernment.
Manner, with respect to what is pleasing, refined, or in accordance with good usage; style; as, music composed in good taste; an epitaph in bad taste.
Essay; trial; experience; experiment.
A small portion given as a specimen; a little piece tastted of eaten; a bit.
A kind of narrow and thin silk ribbon.
q: What, then, is taste, but those internal powers, Active and strong, and feelingly alive To each fine impulse? a discerning sense Of decent and sublime, with quick disgust From things deformed, or disarranged, or gross In species? This, nor gems, nor stores of gold, Nor purple state, nor culture, can bestow, But God alone, when first his active hand Imprints the secret bias of the soul.

senses.d: One who tattles; an idle talker; one who tells tales.
Any one of several species of large, long-legged sandpipers belonging to the genus Totanus.
Very high or tall; as, a ship with taunt masts.

Taunt.etym: [Cf. OF. tant so great, F. tant so much, L. tantus of such size, so great, so much.]

senses.d: To reproach with severe or insulting words; to revile; to upbraid; to jeer at; to flout.
q: When I had at my pleasure taunted her.

Taunt.syn: To deride; ridicule; mock; jeer; flout; revile. See Deride.
Taunt.etym: [Earlier, to tease; probably fr. OF. tanter to tempt, to try, for tenter. See Tempt.]

senses.d: Upbraiding language; bitter or sarcastic reproach; insulting invective.
q: With scoffs, and scorns, and contemelious taunts.
With sacrilegious taunt and impious jest.

senses.d: A public house where travelers and other transient guests are accomodated with rooms and meals; an inn; a hotel; especially, in modern times, a public house licensed to sell liquor in small quantities.

Tavern.etym: [OE. taverne, F. taverne, from L. taberna a hut, booth, tavern. Cf. Table, Tabernacle.]

senses.d: A charge, especially a pecuniary burden which is imposed by authority.
A charge or burden laid upon persons or property for the support of a government.
q: A farmer of taxes is, of all creditors, proverbially the most rapacious.

senses.d: Especially, the sum laid upon specific things, as upon polls, lands, houses, income, etc.; as, a land tax; a window tax; a tax on carriages, and the like.
A sum imposed or levied upon the members of a society to defray its expenses.
A task exacted from one who is under control; a contribution or service, the rendering of which is imposed upon a subject.
A disagreeable or burdensome duty or charge; as, a heavy tax on time or health.
Charge; censure.
A lesson to be learned; a task.

Tax.syn: Impost; tribute; contribution; duty; toll; rate; assessment; exaction; custom; demand.
Tax.etym: [F. taxe, fr. taxer to tax, L. taxare to touch, sharply, to feel, handle, to censure, value, estimate, fr. tangere, tactum, to touch. See Tangent, and cf. Task, Taste.]

senses.d: To subject to the payment of a tax or taxes; to impose a tax upon; to lay a burden upon; especially, to exact money from for the support of government.
q: We are more heavily taxed by our idleness, pride, and folly than we are taxed by government.

senses.d: To assess, fix, or determine judicially, the amount of; as, to tax the cost of an action in court.
To charge; to accuse; also, to censure; — often followed by with, rarely by of before an indirect object; as, to tax a man with pride.
q: I tax you, you elements, with unkindness.
Men's virtues I have commended as freely as I have taxed their crimes.
Fear not now that men should tax thine honor.

senses.d: The act of laying a tax, or of imposing taxes, as on the subjects of a state, by government, or on the members of a corporation or company, by the proper authority; the raising of revenue; also, a system of raising revenue.
The act of taxing, or assessing a bill of cost.
Tax; sum imposed.
Charge; accusation.

Taxation.etym: [F. taxation, L. taxatio a valuing, estimation, from L. taxare. See Tax.]

senses.d: To impart the knowledge of; to give intelligence concerning; to impart, as knowledge before unknown, or rules for practice; to inculcate as true or important; to exhibit impressively; as, to teach arithmetic, dancing, music, or the like; to teach morals.
q: If some men teach wicked things, it must be that others should practice them.

senses.d: To direct, as an instructor; to manage, as a preceptor; to guide the studies of; to instruct; to inform; to conduct through a course of studies; as, to teach a child or a class.
q: The village master taught his little school.

senses.d: To accustom; to guide; to show; to admonish.
q: I shall myself to herbs teach you.
They have taught their tongue to speak lies.

Teach.syn: To instruct; inform; inculcate; tell; guide; counsel; admonish. See the Note under Learn.
Teach.etym: [OE. techen, imp. taughte, tahte, AS. t�cean, imp. t�hte, to show, teach, akin to tācn token. See Token.]

senses.d: To give instruction; to follow the business, or to perform the duties, of a preceptor.
q: And gladly would he learn, and gladly teach.
The priests thereof teach for hire.

senses.d: One of the series of boilers in which the cane juice is treated in making sugar; especially, the last boiler of the series.

Teache.etym: [Cf. Ir. teaghaim, Gael. teasaich, to heat.]

senses.d: Any, esp. the last, of the series of boilers or evaporating pans.
One who teaches or instructs; one whose business or occupation is to instruct others; an instructor; a tutor.
One who instructs others in religion; a preacher; a minister of the gospel; sometimes, one who preaches without regular ordination.
q: The teachers in all the churches assembled.

senses.d: The act or business of instructing; also, that which is taught; instruction.

A drop of the limpid, saline fluid secreted, normally in small amount, by the lachrymal gland, and diffused between the eye and the eyelids to moisten the parts and facilitate their motion. Ordinarily the secretion passes through the lachrymal duct into the nose, but when it is increased by emotion or other causes, it overflows the lids.
q: And yet for thee ne wept she never a tear.

senses.d: Something in the form of a transparent drop of fluid matter; also, a solid, transparent, tear-shaped drop, as of some balsams or resins.
q: Let Araby extol her happy coast, Her fragrant flowers, her trees with precious tears.

senses.d: That which causes or accompanies tears; a lament; a dirge.

Tear.etym: [AS. teár; akin to G. zärhe, OHG. zahar, OFries. & Icel. tār, Sw. tår, Dan. taare, Goth. tagr, OIr. dēr, W. dagr, OW. dacr, L. lacrima, lacruma, for older dacruma, Gr. �, �, �. √59. Cf. Lachrymose.]

senses.d: To separate by violence; to pull apart by force; to rend; to lacerate; as, to tear cloth; to tear a garment; to tear the skin or flesh.
q: Tear him to pieces; he's a conspirator.

senses.d: Hence, to divide by violent measures; to disrupt; to rend; as, a party or government torn by factions.
To rend away; to force away; to remove by force; to sunder; as, a child torn from its home.
q: The hand of fate Hath torn thee from me.

senses.d: To pull with violence; as, to tear the hair.
To move violently; to agitate.

Tear.etym: [OE. teren, AS. teran; akin to OS. farterian to destroy, D. teren to consume, G. zerren to pull, to tear, zehren to consume, Icel. tæra, Goth. gataíran to destroy, Lith. dirti to flay, Russ. drate to pull, to tear, Gr. � to flay, Skr. dar to burst. √63. Cf. Darn, Epidermis, Tarre, Tirade.]

senses.d: To divide or separate on being pulled; to be rent; as, this cloth tears easily.
To move and act with turbulent violence; to rush with violence; hence, to rage; to rave.
The act of tearing, or the state of being torn; a rent; a fissure.
A partially vitrified bit of clay in glass.
The protuberance through which milk is drawn from the udder or breast of a mammal; a nipple; a pap; a mammilla; a dug; a tit.
A small protuberance or nozzle resembling the teat of an animal.

Teat.etym: [OE. tete, titte, AS. tit, titt; akin to LG. & OD. titte, D. tet, G. zitze: cf. F. tette, probably of Teutonic origin.]

senses.d: The tenth month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of December with a part of January.
Involving tedium; tiresome from continuance, prolixity, slowness, or the like; wearisome.
q: I see a man's life is a tedious one.
I would not be tedious to the court.

senses.d: The mark aimed at in curling and in quoits.
The nodule of earth from which the ball is struck in golf.
A short piece of pipe having a lateral outlet, used to connect a line of pipe with a pipe at a right angle with the line; — so called because it resembles the letter T in shape.
The letter T, t; also, something shaped like, or resembling in form, the letter T.
To place (the ball) on a tee.
To breed, or grow, teeth.
The lime tree, or linden; — called also teil tree.
To mention one by one, or piece by piece; to recount; to enumerate; to reckon; to number; to count; as, to tell money.
q: He telleth the number of the stars.
Tell the joints of the body.

senses.d: To utter or recite in detail; to give an account of; to narrate.
q: Of which I shall tell all the array.
And not a man appears to tell their fate.

senses.d: To make known; to publish; to disclose; to divulge.
q: Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?

senses.d: To give instruction to; to make report to; to acquaint; to teach; to inform.
q: A secret pilgrimage, That you to-day promised to tell me of?

senses.d: To order; to request; to command.
q: He told her not to be frightened.

senses.d: To discern so as to report; to ascertain by observing; to find out; to discover; as, I can not tell where one color ends and the other begins.
To make account of; to regard; to reckon; to value; to estimate.
q: I ne told no dainity of her love.

Tell.syn: To communicate; impart; reveal; disclose; inform; acquaint; report; repeat; rehearse; recite.
Tell.etym: [AS. tellan, from talu tale, number, speech; akin to D. tellen to count, G. zählen, OHG. zellen to count, tell, say, Icel. telja, Dan. tale to speak, tælle to count. See Tale that which is told.]

senses.d: To give an account; to make report.
q: That I may publish with the voice of thankgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.

senses.d: To take effect; to produce a marked effect; as, every shot tells; every expression tells.
q: Lest they should tell on us, saying, So did David.

senses.d: That which is told; tale; account.
q: I am at the end of my tell.

senses.d: A hill or mound.
Operating with great effect; effective; as, a telling speech.
To mingle in due proportion; to prepare by combining; to modify, as by adding some new element; to qualify, as by an ingredient; hence, to soften; to mollify; to assuage; to soothe; to calm.
q: Puritan austerity was so tempered by Dutch indifference, that mercy itself could not have dictated a milder system.
Woman! lovely woman! nature made thee To temper man: we had been brutes without you.
But thy fire Shall be more tempered, and thy hope far higher.
She threw darkness and clouds about her, that tempered the light into a thousand beautiful shades and colors.

senses.d: To fit together; to adjust; to accomodate.
q: Thy sustenance . . . serving to the appetite of the eater, tempered itself to every man's liking.

senses.d: To bring to a proper degree of hardness; as, to temper iron or steel.
q: The tempered metals clash, and yield a silver sound.

senses.d: To govern; to manage.
q: With which the damned ghosts he governeth, And furies rules, and Tartare tempereth.

senses.d: To moisten to a proper consistency and stir thoroughly, as clay for making brick, loam for molding, etc.
To adjust, as the mathematical scale to the actual scale, or to that in actual use.

Temper.syn: To soften; mollify; assuage; soothe; calm.
Temper.etym: [AS. temprian or OF. temper, F. tempérer, and (in sense 3) temper, L. temperare, akin to tempus time. Cf. Temporal, Distemper, Tamper.]

senses.d: The state of any compound substance which results from the mixture of various ingredients; due mixture of different qualities; just combination; as, the temper of mortar.
Constitution of body; temperament; in old writers, the mixture or relative proportion of the four humors, blood, choler, phlegm, and melancholy.
q: The exquisiteness of his bodily temper increased the exquisiteness of his torment.

senses.d: Disposition of mind; the constitution of the mind, particularly with regard to the passions and affections; as, a calm temper; a hasty temper; a fretful temper.
q: Remember with what mild And gracious temper he both heared and judged.
The consequents of a certain ethical temper.

senses.d: Calmness of mind; moderation; equanimity; composure; as, to keep one's temper.
q: To fall with dignity, with temper rise.
Restore yourselves to your tempers, fathers.

senses.d: Heat of mind or passion; irritation; proneness to anger; — in a reproachful sense.
The state of a metal or other substance, especially as to its hardness, produced by some process of heating or cooling; as, the temper of iron or steel.
Middle state or course; mean; medium.
q: The perfect lawgiver is a just temper between the mere man of theory, who can see nothing but general principles, and the mere man of business, who can see nothing but particular circumstances.

senses.d: Milk of lime, or other substance, employed in the process formerly used to clarify sugar.

Temper.syn: Disposition; temperament; frame; humor; mood. See Disposition.

senses.d: To accord; to agree; to act and think in conformity.
To have or get a proper or desired state or quality; to grow soft and pliable.
q: I have him already tempering between my finger and my thumb, and shortly will I seal with him.

senses.d: Habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions; restrained or moderate indulgence; moderation; as, temperance in eating and drinking; temperance in the indulgence of joy or mirth; specifically, moderation, and sometimes abstinence, in respect to using intoxicating liquors.
Moderation of passion; patience; calmness; sedateness.
q: He calmed his wrath with goodly temperance.

senses.d: State with regard to heat or cold; temperature.

Temperance.etym: [L. temperantia: cf. F. tempérance. See Temper, v. t.]

senses.d: Moderate; not excessive; as, temperate heat; a temperate climate.
Not marked with passion; not violent; cool; calm; as, temperate language.
q: She is not hot, but temperate as the morn.
That sober freedom out of which there springs Our loyal passion for our temperate kings.

senses.d: Moderate in the indulgence of the natural appetites or passions; as, temperate in eating and drinking.
q: Be sober and temperate, and you will be healthy.

senses.d: Proceeding from temperance.
q: The temperate sleeps, and spirits light as air.

Temperate.etym: [L. temperatus, p. p. of temperare. See Temper, v. t.]

senses.d: To render temperate; to moderate; to soften; to temper.
q: It inflames temperance, and temperates wrath.

senses.d: Brought to a proper temper; as, tempered steel; having (such) a temper; — chiefly used in composition; as, a good-tempered or bad-tempered man; a well-tempered sword.
An extensive current of wind, rushing with great velocity and violence, and commonly attended with rain, hail, or snow; a furious storm.
q: caught in a fiery tempest, shall be hurled, Each on his rock transfixed.

senses.d: Fig.: Any violent tumult or commotion; as, a political tempest; a tempest of war, or of the passions.
A fashionable assembly; a drum. See the Note under Drum, n., 4.

Tempest.etym: [OF. tempeste, F. tempête, (assumed) LL. tempesta, fr. L. tempestas a portion of time, a season, weather, storm, akin to tempus time. See Temporal of time.]

senses.d: To disturb as by a tempest.
q: Part huge of bulk Wallowing unwieldy, enormous in their gait, Tempest the ocean.

Tempest.etym: [Cf. OF. tempester, F. tempêter to rage.]

senses.d: To storm.
Of or pertaining to a tempest; involving or resembling a tempest; turbulent; violent; stormy; as, tempestuous weather; a tempestuous night; a tempestuous debate.
q: They saw the Hebrew leader, Waiting, and clutching his tempestuous beard.

Tempestuous.etym: [L. tempestuous: cf. OF. tempestueux, F. tempêtueux.]

senses.d: A contrivence used in a loom for keeping the web stretched transversely.
The space, on either side of the head, back of the eye and forehead, above the zygomatic arch and in front of the ear.
One of the side bars of a pair of spectacles, jointed to the bows, and passing one on either side of the head to hold the spectacles in place.

Temple.etym: [OF. temple, F. tempe, from L. tempora, tempus; perhaps originally, the right place, the fatal spot, supposed to be the same word as tempus, temporis, the fitting or appointed time. See Temporal of time, and cf. Tempo, Tense, n.]

senses.d: A place or edifice dedicated to the worship of some deity; as, the temple of Jupiter at Athens, or of Juggernaut in India.
The edifice erected at Jerusalem for the worship of Jehovah.
q: Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch.

senses.d: Hence, among Christians, an edifice erected as a place of public worship; a church.
q: Can he whose life is a perpetual insult to the authority of God enter with any pleasure a temple consecrated to devotion and sanctified by prayer?

senses.d: Fig.: Any place in which the divine presence specially resides.
q: Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the spirit of God dwelleth in you?
The groves were God's first temples.

Temple.etym: [AS. tempel, from L. templum a space marked out, sanctuary, temple; cf. Gr. � a piece of land marked off, land dedicated to a god: cf. F. témple, from the Latin. Cf. Contemplate.]

senses.d: To build a temple for; to appropriate a temple to; as, to temple a god.
A building dedicated to the administration of ordinances.
A local organization of Odd Fellows.
Of or pertaining to the temple or temples; as, the temporal bone; a temporal artery.

Temporal.etym: [L. temporalis, fr. tempora the temples: cf. F. temporal. See Temple a part of the head.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to time, that is, to the present life, or this world; secular, as distinguished from sacred or eternal.
q: The things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Is this an hour for temporal affairs?

senses.d: Civil or political, as distinguished from ecclesiastical; as, temporal power; temporal courts.

Temporal.etym: [L. temporalis, fr. tempus, temporis, time, portion of time, the fitting or appointed time: cf. F. temporel. Cf. Contemporaneous, Extempore, Temper, v. t., Tempest, Temple a part of the head, Tense, n., Thing.]

senses.d: Anything temporal or secular; a temporality; — used chiefly in the plural.
q: He assigns supremacy to the pope in spirituals, and to the emperor or temporals.

senses.d: To put to trial; to prove; to test; to try.
q: God did tempt Abraham.
Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God.

senses.d: To lead, or endeavor to lead, into evil; to entice to what is wrong; to seduce.
q: Every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.

senses.d: To endeavor to persuade; to induce; to invite; to incite; to provoke; to instigate.
q: Tempt not the brave and needy to despair.
Nor tempt the wrath of heaven's avenging Sire.

senses.d: To endeavor to accomplish or reach; to attempt.
q: Ere leave be given to tempt the nether skies.

Tempt.syn: To entice; allure; attract; decoy; seduce.
Tempt.etym: [OE. tempten, tenten, from OF. tempter, tenter, F. tenter, fr. L. tentare, temptare, to handle, feel, attack, to try, put to the test, urge, freq. from tendere, tentum, and tensum, to stretch. See Thin, and cf. Attempt, Tend, Taunt, Tent a pavilion, Tent to probe.]

senses.d: The act of tempting, or enticing to evil; seduction.
q: When the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season.

senses.d: The state of being tempted, or enticed to evil.
q: Lead us not into temptation.

senses.d: That which tempts; an inducement; an allurement, especially to something evil.
q: Dare to be great, without a guilty crown; View it, and lay the bright temptation down.

Temptation.etym: [OF. temptation, tentation, F. tentation, L. tentatio.]

senses.d: One who tempts or entices; especially, Satan, or the Devil, regarded as the great enticer to evil.
q: So glozed the Tempter, and his proem tuned.

senses.d: Adapted to entice or allure; attractive; alluring; seductive; enticing; as, tempting pleasures.
One more than nine; twice five.
q: With twice ten sail I crossed the Phrygian Sea.
There 's proud modesty in merit, Averse from begging, and resolved to pay Ten times the gift it asks.

Ten.etym: [AS. tēn, tién, t�n, tēne; akin to OFries. tian, OS. tehan, D. tien, G. zehn, OHG. zehan, Icel. tīu, Sw. tio, Dan. ti, Goth. taíhun, Lith. deszimt, Russ. desiate, W. deg, Ir. & Gael. deich, L. decem, Gr. �, Skr. daçan. √308. Cf. Dean, Decade, Decimal, December, Eighteen, Eighty, Teens, Tithe.]

senses.d: The number greater by one than nine; the sum of five and five; ten units of objects.
q: I will not destroy it for ten's sake.

senses.d: A symbol representing ten units, as 10, x, or X.
To make a tender of; to offer or tender.
To accompany as an assistant or protector; to care for the wants of; to look after; to watch; to guard; as, shepherds tend their flocks.
q: And flaming ministers to watch and tend Their earthly charge.
There 's not a sparrow or a wren, There 's not a blade of autumn grain, Which the four seasons do not tend And tides of life and increase lend.

senses.d: To be attentive to; to note carefully; to attend to.
q: Being to descend A ladder much in height, I did not tend My way well down.

Tend.etym: [Aphetic form of attend. See Attend, Tend to move, and cf. Tender one that tends or attends.]

senses.d: To wait, as attendants or servants; to serve; to attend; — with on or upon.
q: Was he not companion with the riotous knights That tend upon my father?

senses.d: To await; to expect.
To move in a certain direction; — usually with to or towards.
q: Two gentlemen tending towards that sight.
Thus will this latter, as the former world, Still tend from bad to worse.
The clouds above me to the white Alps tend.

senses.d: To be directed, as to any end, object, or purpose; to aim; to have or give a leaning; to exert activity or influence; to serve as a means; to contribute; as, our petitions, if granted, might tend to our destruction.
q: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
The laws of our religion tend to the universal happiness of mankind.

Tend.etym: [F. tendre, L. tendere, tensum and tentum, to stretch, extend, direct one's course, tend; akin to Gr. � to stretch, Skr. tan. See Thin, and cf. Tend to attend, Contend, Intense, Ostensible, Portent, Tempt, Tender to offer, Tense, a.]

senses.d: One who tends; one who takes care of any person or thing; a nurse.
A vessel employed to attend other vessels, to supply them with provisions and other stores, to convey intelligence, or the like.
A car attached to a locomotive, for carrying a supply of fuel and water.
To offer in payment or satisfaction of a demand, in order to save a penalty or forfeiture; as, to tender the amount of rent or debt.
To offer in words; to present for acceptance.
q: You see how all conditions, how all minds, . . . tender down Their services to Lord Timon.

Tender.etym: [F. tendre to stretch, stretch out, reach, L. tendere. See Tend to move.]

senses.d: An offer, either of money to pay a debt, or of service to be performed, in order to save a penalty or forfeiture, which would be incurred by nonpayment or nonperformance; as, the tender of rent due, or of the amount of a note, with interest.
Any offer or proposal made for acceptance; as, a tender of a loan, of service, or of friendship; a tender of a bid for a contract.
q: A free, unlimited tender of the gospel.

senses.d: The thing offered; especially, money offered in payment of an obligation.
Easily impressed, broken, bruised, or injured; not firm or hard; delicate; as, tender plants; tender flesh; tender fruit.
Sensible to impression and pain; easily pained.
q: Our bodies are not naturally more tender than our faces.

senses.d: Physically weak; not hardly or able to endure hardship; immature; effeminate.
q: The tender and delicate woman among you.

senses.d: Susceptible of the softer passions, as love, compassion, kindness; compassionate; pitiful; anxious for another's good; easily excited to pity, forgiveness, or favor; sympathetic.
q: The Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
I am choleric by my nature, and tender by my temper.

senses.d: Exciting kind concern; dear; precious.
q: I love Valentine, Whose life's as tender to me as my soul!

senses.d: Careful to save inviolate, or not to injure; — with of.
q: The civil authority should be tender of the honor of God and religion.

senses.d: Unwilling to cause pain; gentle; mild.
q: You, that are thus so tender o'er his follies, Will never do him good.

senses.d: Adapted to excite feeling or sympathy; expressive of the softer passions; pathetic; as, tender expressions; tender expostulations; a tender strain.
Apt to give pain; causing grief or pain; delicate; as, a tender subject.
Heeling over too easily when under sail; — said of a vessel.

Tender.syn: Delicate; effeminate; soft; sensitive; compassionate; kind; humane; merciful; pitiful.
Tender.etym: [F. tendre, L. tener; probably akin to tenuis thin. See Thin.]

senses.d: Regard; care; kind concern.
To have a care of; to be tender toward; hence, to regard; to esteem; to value.
q: For first, next after life, he tendered her good.
Tender yourself more dearly.
To see a prince in want would move a miser's charity. Our western princes tendered his case, which they counted might be their own.

senses.d: The quality or state of being tender (in any sense of the adjective).

Tenderness.syn: Benignity; humanity; sensibility; benevolence; kindness; pity; clemency; mildness; mercy.

senses.d: A projecting member left by cutting away the wood around it, and made to insert into a mortise, and in this way secure together the parts of a frame; especially, such a member when it passes entirely through the thickness of the piece in which the mortise is cut, and shows on the other side. Cf. Tooth, Tusk.

Tenon.etym: [F., fr. tenir to hold. See Tenable.]

senses.d: To cut or fit for insertion into a mortise, as the end of a piece of timber.
A state of holding on in a continuous course; manner of continuity; constant mode; general tendency; course; career.
q: Along the cool sequestered vale of life They kept the noiseless tenor of their away.

senses.d: That course of thought which holds on through a discourse; the general drift or course of thought; purport; intent; meaning; understanding.
q: When it is paid according to the tenor.
Does not the whole tenor of the divine law positively require humility and meekness to all men?

senses.d: Stamp; character; nature.
q: This success would look like chance, if it were perpetual, and always of the same tenor.

senses.d: An exact copy of a writing, set forth in the words and figures of it. It differs from purport, which is only the substance or general import of the instrument.

The higher of the two kinds of voices usually belonging to adult males; hence, the part in the harmony adapted to this voice; the second of the four parts in the scale of sounds, reckoning from the base, and originally the air, to which the other parts were auxillary.

Tenor.etym: [L., from tenere to hold; hence, properly, a holding on in a continued course: cf. F. teneur. See Tenable, and cf. Tenor a kind of voice.]

senses.d: A kind of wine of a deep red color, chiefly from Galicia or Malaga in Spain; — called also tent wine, and tinta.

Tent.etym: [Sp. tinto, properly, deep-colored, fr. L. tinctus, p. p. of tingere to dye. See Tinge, and cf. Tint, Tinto.]

senses.d: Attention; regard, care.
Intention; design.
To attend to; to heed; hence, to guard; to hinder.
To probe or to search with a tent; to keep open with a tent; as, to tent a wound. Used also figuratively.
q: I'll tent him to the quick.

senses.d: A roll of lint or linen, or a conical or cylindrical piece of sponge or other absorbent, used chiefly to dilate a natural canal, to keep open the orifice of a wound, or to absorb discharges.
A probe for searching a wound.
q: The tent that searches To the bottom of the worst.

senses.d: A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of skins, canvas, or some strong cloth, stretched and sustained by poles, — used for sheltering persons from the weather, especially soldiers in camp.
q: Within his tent, large as is a barn.

senses.d: The representation of a tent used as a bearing.

Tent.etym: [OE. tente, F. tente, LL. tenta, fr. L. tendere, tentum, to stretch. See Tend to move, and cf. Tent a roll of lint.]

senses.d: To lodge as a tent; to tabernacle.
q: We 're tenting to-night on the old camp ground.

senses.d: Next in order after the ninth; coming after nine others.
Constituting or being one of ten equal parts into which anything is divided.

Tenth.etym: [From Ten: cf. OE. tethe, AS. teó�a. See Ten, and cf. Tithe.]

senses.d: The next in order after the ninth; one coming after nine others.
The quotient of a unit divided by ten; one of ten equal parts into which anything is divided.
The tenth part of annual produce, income, increase, or the like; a tithe.
The interval between any tone and the tone represented on the tenth degree of the staff above it, as between one of the scale and three of the octave above; the octave of the third.
A temporary aid issuing out of personal property, and granted to the king by Parliament; formerly, the real tenth part of all the movables belonging to the subject.
One whose occupation it is to make tents.
Images connected with the magical rites used by those Israelites who added corrupt practices to the patriarchal religion. Teraphim were consulted by the Israelites for oracular answers.
That which limits the extent of anything; limit; extremity; bound; boundary.
q: Corruption is a reciprocal to generation, and they two are as nature's two terms, or boundaries.

senses.d: The time for which anything lasts; any limited time; as, a term of five years; the term of life.
In universities, schools, etc., a definite continuous period during which instruction is regularly given to students; as, the school year is divided into three terms.
A point, line, or superficies, that limits; as, a line is the term of a superficies, and a superficies is the term of a solid.
A fixed period of time; a prescribed duration
The subject or the predicate of a proposition; one of the three component parts of a syllogism, each one of which is used twice.
q: The subject and predicate of a proposition are, after Aristotle, together called its terms or extremes.

senses.d: A word or expression; specifically, one that has a precisely limited meaning in certain relations and uses, or is peculiar to a science, art, profession, or the like; as, a technical term.
q: In painting, the greatest beauties can not always be expressed for want of terms.

senses.d: A quadrangular pillar, adorned on the top with the figure of a head, as of a man, woman, or satyr; — called also terminal figure. See Terminus, n., 2 and 3.
A member of a compound quantity; as, a or b in a + b; ab or cd in ab - cd.
The menses.
Propositions or promises, as in contracts, which, when assented to or accepted by another, settle the contract and bind the parties; conditions.
In Scotland, the time fixed for the payment of rents.

Term.syn: Limit; bound; boundary; condition; stipulation; word; expression.
Term.etym: [F. terme, L. termen, -inis, terminus, a boundary limit, end; akin to Gr. �, �. See Thrum a tuft, and cf. Terminus, Determine, Exterminate.]

senses.d: To apply a term to; to name; to call; to denominate.
q: Men term what is beyond the limits of the universe “imaginary space.”

senses.d: A raised level space, shelf, or platform of earth, supported on one or more sides by a wall, a bank of tuft, or the like, whether designed for use or pleasure.
A balcony, especially a large and uncovered one.
A flat roof to a house; as, the buildings of the Oriental nations are covered with terraces.
A street, or a row of houses, on a bank or the side of a hill; hence, any street, or row of houses.
A level plain, usually with a steep front, bordering a river, a lake, or sometimes the sea.

Terrace.etym: [F. terrasse (cf. Sp. terraza, It. terrazza), fr. L. terra the earth, probably for tersa, originally meaning, dry land, and akin to torrere to parch, E. torrid, and thirst. See Thirst, and cf. Fumitory, Inter, v., Patterre, Terrier, Trass, Tureen, Turmeric.]

senses.d: To form into a terrace or terraces; to furnish with a terrace or terraces, as, to terrace a garden, or a building.
q: Clermont's terraced height, and Esher's groves.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the earth; existing on the earth; earthly; as, terrestrial animals.
Representing, or consisting of, the earth; as, a terrestrial globe.
Of or pertaining to the world, or to the present state; sublunary; mundane.
q: Vain labors of terrestrial wit.
A genius bright and base, Of towering talents, and terrestrial aims.

senses.d: Consisting of land, in distinction from water; belonging to, or inhabiting, the land or ground, in distinction from trees, water, or the like; as, terrestrial serpents.
q: The terrestrial parts of the globe.

senses.d: Adapted for the observation of objects on land and on the earth; as, a terrestrial telescope, in distinction from an astronomical telescope.

Terrestrial.etym: [L. terrestris, from terra the earth. See Terrace.]

senses.d: An inhabitant of the earth.
Adapted or likely to excite terror, awe, or dread; dreadful; formidable.
q: Prudent in peace, and terrible in war.
Thou shalt not be affrighted at them; for the Lord thy God is among you, a mighty God and terrible.

senses.d: Excessive; extreme; severe.
q: The terrible coldness of the season.

Terrible.syn: Terrific; fearful; frightful; formidable; dreadful; horrible; shocking; awful.
Terrible.etym: [F., fr. L. terribilis, fr. terrere to frighten. See Terror.]

senses.d: To make terrible.
q: If the law, instead of aggravating and terrifying sin, shall give out license, it foils itself.

senses.d: To alarm or shock with fear; to frighten.
q: When ye shall hear of wars . . . be not terrified.

Terrify.etym: [L. terrere to frighten + -fy: cf. F. terrifier, L. terrificare. See Terrific, and -fy.]

senses.d: Extreme fear; fear that agitates body and mind; violent dread; fright.
q: Terror seized the rebel host.

senses.d: That which excites dread; a cause of extreme fear.
q: Those enormous terrors of the Nile.
Rulers are not a terror to good works.
There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats.

Terror.syn: Alarm; fright; consternation; dread; dismay. See Alarm.
Terror.etym: [L. terror, akin to terrere to frighten, for tersere; akin to Gr. � to flee away, dread, Skr. tras to tremble, to be afraid, Russ. triasti to shake: cf. F. terreur. Cf. Deter.]

senses.d: A solemn, authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his will as to disposal of his estate and effects after his death.

One of the two distinct revelations of God's purposes toward man; a covenant; also, one of the two general divisions of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures, in which the covenants are respectively revealed; as, the Old Testament; the New Testament; — often limited, in colloquial language, to the latter.
q: He is the mediator of the new testament . . . for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament.

Testament.etym: [F., fr. L. testamentum, fr. testari to be a witness, to make one's last will, akin to testis a witness. Cf. Intestate, Testify.]

senses.d: A man who makes and leaves a will, or testament, at death.
To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to give testimony for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of something not known to them.
q: Jesus . . . needed not that any should testify of man, for he knew what was in man.

senses.d: To make a solemn declaration under oath or affirmation, for the purpose of establishing, or making proof of, some fact to a court; to give testimony in a cause depending before a tribunal.
q: One witness shall not testify against any person to cause him to die.

senses.d: To declare a charge; to protest; to give information; to bear witness; — with against.
q: O Israel, . . . I will testify against thee.
I testified against them in the day wherein they sold victuals.

Testify.etym: [OF. testifier, L. testificari; testis a witness + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy, and cf. Attest, Contest, Detest, Protest, Testament.]

senses.d: To bear witness to; to support the truth of by testimony; to affirm or declare solemny.
q: We speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen; and ye receive not our witness.

senses.d: To affirm or declare under oath or affirmation before a tribunal, in order to prove some fact.
In a testy manner; fretfully; peevishly; with petulance.
A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.

Affirmation; declaration; as, these doctrines are supported by the uniform testimony of the fathers; the belief of past facts must depend on the evidence of human testimony, or the testimony of historians.
Open attestation; profession.
q: for the testimony of truth, hast borne Universal reproach.

senses.d: Witness; evidence; proof of some fact.
q: When ye depart thence, shake off the dust under your feet for a testimony against them.

senses.d: The two tables of the law.
q: Thou shalt put into the ark the testimony which I shall give thee.

senses.d: Hence, the whole divine revelation; the sacre� Scriptures.
q: The testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple.

Testimony.syn: Proof; evidence; attestation; witness; affirmation; confirmation; averment.
Testimony.etym: [L. testimonium, from testis a witness: cf. OF. testimoine, testemoine, testimonie. See Testify.]

senses.d: To witness; to attest; to prove by testimony.
A Roman governor of the fourth part of a province; hence, any subordinate or dependent prince; also, a petty king or sovereign.

Tetrarch.etym: [L. tetrarches, Gr. �, �; τέτρα- (see Tetra-) + � a ruler, � to lead; rule: cf. F. tétrarque. See Arch, a.]

senses.d: Four.

In Old English, the article the, when the following word began with a vowel, was often written with elision as if a part of the word. Thus in Chaucer, the forms thabsence, tharray, thegle, thend, thingot, etc., are found for the absence, the array, the eagle, the end, etc.

A particle expressing comparison, used after certain adjectives and adverbs which express comparison or diversity, as more, better, other, otherwise, and the like. It is usually followed by the object compared in the nominative case. Sometimes, however, the object compared is placed in the objective case, and than is then considered by some grammarians as a preposition. Sometimes the object is expressed in a sentence, usually introduced by that; as, I would rather suffer than that you should want.
q: Behold, a greater than Solomon is here.
Which when Beelzebub perceived, than whom, Satan except, none higher sat.
It's wiser being good than bad; It's safer being meek than fierce; It's fitter being sane than mad.

Than.etym: [OE. than, thon, then, thanne, thonne, thenne, than, then, AS. ðanne, ðonne, ðænne; akin to D. dan, OHG. danne, G. dann then, denn than, for, Goth. þan then, and to E. the, there, that. See That, and cf. Then.]

senses.d: Then. See Then.
q: Thanne longen folk to gon on pilgrimages.

senses.d: A expression of gratitude; an acknowledgment expressive of a sense of favor or kindness received; obligation, claim, or desert, or gratitude; — now generally used in the plural.
q: If ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.
What great thank, then, if any man, reputed wise and constant, will neither do, nor permit others under his charge to do, that which he approves not, especially in matter of sin?
Thanks, thanks to thee, most worthy friend, For the lesson thou hast taught.

Thank.etym: [AS. þanc, þonc, thanks, favor, thought; akin to OS. thank favor, pleasure, thanks, D. & G. dank thanks, Icel. þökk, Dan. tak, Sw. tack, Goth. þagks thanks; — originally, a thought, a thinking. See Think.]

senses.d: To express gratitude to (anyone) for a favor; to make acknowledgments to (anyone) for kindness bestowed; — used also ironically for blame.
q: “Graunt mercy, lord, that thank I you,” quod she.
I thank thee for thine honest care.
Weigh the danger with the doubtful bliss, And thank yourself if aught should fall amiss.

senses.d: Obtaining or deserving thanks; thankworthy.
q: Ladies, look here; this is the thankful glass That mends the looker's eyes; this is the well That washes what it shows.

senses.d: Impressed with a sense of kindness received, and ready to acknowledge it; grateful.
q: Be thankful unto him, and bless his name.

senses.d: To give or dedicate in token of thanks.
The act of rending thanks, or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
q: Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving.
In the thanksgiving before meat.
And taught by thee the Church prolongs Her hymns of high thanksgiving still.

senses.d: A public acknowledgment or celebration of divine goodness; also, a day set apart for religious services, specially to acknowledge the goodness of God, either in any remarkable deliverance from calamities or danger, or in the ordinary dispensation of his bounties.
Deserving thanks; worthy of gratitude; mreitorious.
q: For this thankworthy, if a man, for conscience toward God, endure grief, suffering wrongfully.

senses.d: As a demonstrative pronoun (pl. Those), that usually points out, or refers to, a person or thing previously mentioned, or supposed to be understood. That, as a demonstrative, may precede the noun to which it refers; as, that which he has said is true; those in the basket are good apples.
q: The early fame of Gratian was equal to that of the most celebrated princes.
That be far from thee, to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked.
And when Moses heard that, he was content.
I will know your business, Harry, that I will.
Two principles in human nature reign; Self-love, to urge, and Reason, to restrain; Nor this a good, nor that a bad we call.
If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this or that.

senses.d: As an adjective, that has the same demonstrative force as the pronoun, but is followed by a noun.
q: It shall be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment, than for that city.
The woman was made whole from that hour.
Upon a day out riden knightes two . . . That one of them came home, that other not.

senses.d: As a relative pronoun, that is equivalent to who or which, serving to point out, and make definite, a person or thing spoken of, or alluded to, before, and may be either singular or plural.
q: He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame.
A judgment that is equal and impartial must incline to the greater probabilities.

senses.d: As a conjunction, that retains much of its force as a demonstrative pronoun.
To introduce a clause employed as the object of the preceding verb, or as the subject or predicate nominative of a verb.
q: She tells them 't is a causeless fantasy, And childish error, that they are afraid.
I have shewed before, that a mere possibility to the contrary, can by no means hinder a thing from being highly credible.

senses.d: To introduce, a reason or cause; — equivalent to for that, in that, for the reason that, because.
q: He does hear me; And that he does, I weep.

senses.d: To introduce a purpose; — usually followed by may, or might, and frequently preceded by so, in order, to the end, etc.
q: These things I say, that ye might be saved.
To the end that he may prolong his days.

senses.d: To introduce a consequence, result, or effect; — usually preceded by so or such, sometimes by that.
q: The birds their notes renew, and bleating herds Attest their joy, that hill and valley rings.
He gazed so long That both his eyes were dazzled.
So wept Duessa until eventide, That shining lamps in Jove's high course were lit.
Is not this the day That Hermia should give answer of her choice?

senses.d: In an elliptical sentence to introduce a dependent sentence expressing a wish, or a cause of surprise, indignation, or the like.
q: Ha, cousin Silence, that thou hadst seen that that this knight and I have seen!
O God, that right should thus overcome might!

senses.d: As adverb: To such a degree; so; as, he was that frightened he could say nothing.

That.etym: [AS. ðæt, neuter nom. & acc. sing. of the article (originally a demonstrative pronoun). The nom. masc. sē, and the nom. fem. seó are from a different root. AS. ðæt is akin to D. dat, G. das, OHG. daz, Sw. & Dan. det, Icel. þat (masc. sā, fem. sō), Goth. þata (masc. sa, fem. sō), Gr. � (masc. �, fem.

senses.d: A word placed before nouns to limit or individualize their meaning.

The.etym: [AS. ðe, a later form for earlier nom. sing. masc. sē, formed under the influence of the oblique cases. See That, pron.]

senses.d: By that; by how much; by so much; on that account; — used before comparatives; as, the longer we continue in sin, the more difficult it is to reform.
q: So much the rather thou, Celestial Light, Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers Irradiate.

The.etym: [AS. ðē, ðȳ, instrumental case of sē, seó, ðæt, the definite article. See 2d The.]

senses.d: To thrive; to prosper.
q: Well mote thee, as well can wish your thought.

Thee.etym: [AS. �eón; akin to OS. thīhan, D. gedijen, G. gedeihen, OHG. gidihan, Goth. �eihan, Lith. tekti to fall to the lot of. Cf. Tight, a.]

senses.d: The objective case of thou. See Thou.
q: This sword hath ended him; so shall it thee, Unless thou yield thee as my prisoner.

Thee.etym: [AS. ðē, acc. & dat. of ðū thou. See Thou.]

senses.d: The act of stealing; specifically, the felonious taking and removing of personal property, with an intent to deprive the rightful owner of the same; larceny.
The thing stolen.
q: If the theft be certainly found in his hand alive, . . . he shall restore double.

Theft.etym: [OE. thefte, AS. þiéfðe, þȳfðe, þeófðe. See Thief.]

senses.d: The possessive case of the personal pronoun they; as, their houses; their country.
q: Nothing but the name of zeal appears 'Twixt our best actions and the worst of theirs.

Their.etym: [OE. thair, fr. Icel. þeirra, þeira, of them, but properly gen. pl. of the definite article; akin to AS. ðāra, ðǣra, gen. pl. of the definite article, or fr. AS. ðǣra, influenced by the Scandinavian use. See That.]

senses.d: The objective case of they. See They.
q: Go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.
Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father.
Little stars may hide them when they list.

Them.etym: [AS. ðǣm, dat. pl. of the article, but influenced by the Scand. use of the corresponding form þeim as a personal pronoun. See They.]

senses.d: The plural of himself, herself, and itself. See Himself, Herself, Itself.
At that time (referring to a time specified, either past or future).
q: And the Canaanite was then in the land.
Now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.

senses.d: Soon afterward, or immediately; next; afterward.
q: First be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

senses.d: At another time; later; again.
q: One while the master is not aware of what is done, and then in other cases it may fall out to be own act.
But that opinion, I trust, by then this following argument hath been well read, will be left for one of the mysteries of an indulgent Antichrist.

Then.etym: [Originally the same word as than. See Than.]

senses.d: Than.
In that case; in consequence; as a consequence; therefore; for this reason.
q: If all this be so, then man has a natural freedom.
Now, then, be all thy weighty cares away.

senses.d: From that place.
q: When ye depart thence, shake off the dust under your feet for a testimony against them.
Then I will send, and fetch thee from thence.

senses.d: From that time; thenceforth; thereafter.
q: There shall be no more thence an infant of days.

senses.d: For that reason; therefore.
q: Not to sit idle with so great a gift Useless, and thence ridiculous, about him.

senses.d: Not there; elsewhere; absent.

Thence.etym: [OE. thenne, thanne, and (with the adverbal -s; see -wards) thennes, thannes (hence thens, now written thence), AS. ðanon, ðanan, ðonan; akin to OHG. dannana, dannān, danān, and G. von dannen, E. that, there. See That.]

senses.d: From that time; thereafter.
