q: If the salt have lost his savor, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing.

senses.d: In or at that place.
q: The Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.

senses.d: In that matter, relation, etc.; at that point, stage, etc., regarded as a distinct place; as, he did not stop there, but continued his speech.
q: The law that theaten'd death becomes thy friend And turns it to exile; there art thou happy.

senses.d: To or into that place; thither.
q: The rarest that e'er came there.
A knight there was, and that a worthy man.
There is a path which no fowl knoweth.
Wherever there is a sense or perception, there some idea is actually produced.
There have been that have delivered themselves from their ills by their good fortune or virtue.
Spend their good there it is reasonable.

There.etym: [OE. ther, AS. ðǣr; akin to D. daar, G. da, OHG. dār, Sw. & Dan. der, Icel. & Goth. þar, Skr. tarhi then, and E. that. √184. See That, pron.]

senses.d: Near that place.
Near that number, degree, or quantity; nearly; as, ten men, or thereabouts.
q: Five or six thousand horse . . . or thereabouts.
Some three months since, or thereabout.

senses.d: Concerning that; about that.
q: What will ye dine? I will go thereabout.
They were much perplexed thereabout.

senses.d: At that place; there.
q: Wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat.

senses.d: At that occurrence or event; on that account.
q: Every error is a stain to the beauty of nature; for which cause it blusheth thereat.

senses.d: By that; by that means; in consequence of that.
q: Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace; thereby good shall come unto thee.

senses.d: Annexed to that.
Thereabout; — said of place, number, etc.
For that or this reason, referring to something previously stated; for that.
q: I have married a wife, and therefore I can not come.
Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?

senses.d: Consequently; by consequence.
q: He blushes; therefore he is guilty.

Therefore.etym: [OE. therfore. See There, and Fore, adv., For, and cf. Therefor.]

senses.d: From this or that.
q: Turn not aside therefrom to the right hand or to the left.

senses.d: In that or this place, time, or thing; in that particular or respect.
q: He pricketh through a fair forest, Therein is many a wild beast.
Bring forth abundantly in the earth, and multiply therein.
Therein our letters do not well agree.

senses.d: Into that or this, or into that place.
q: Let not them . . . enter thereinto.

senses.d: Of that or this.
q: In the day that thou eatest thereof, thou shalt surely die.

senses.d: On that or this.
q: Then the king said, Hang him thereon.

senses.d: Out of that or this.
q: He shall take thereout his handful of the flour.

senses.d: On the outside; out of doors.
To that or this.
Besides; moreover.
q: Her mouth full small, and thereto soft and red.

senses.d: Unto that or this; thereto; besides.
Upon that or this; thereon.
On account, or in consequence, of that; therefore.
q: hopes to find you forward, . . . And thereupon he sends you this good news.

senses.d: Immediately; at once; without delay.
With that or this.
In addition; besides; moreover.
q: To speak of strength and therewith hardiness.

senses.d: At the same time; forthwith.
The plural of this. See This.

These.etym: [OE. �es, �æs, a variant of �as, pl. of �es, thes, this. See This, and cf. Those.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Thessalonica, a city of Macedonia.
A native or inhabitant of Thessalonica.
The plural of he, she, or it. They is never used adjectively, but always as a pronoun proper, and sometimes refers to persons without an antecedent expressed.
q: Jolif and glad they went unto here rest And casten hem full early for to sail.
They of Italy salute you.
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness.

They.etym: [Icel. þeir they, properly nom. pl. masc. of sā, sū, þat, a demonstrative pronoun, akin to the English definite article, AS. sē, seó, ðæt, nom. pl. ðā. See That.]

senses.d: Measuring in the third dimension other than length and breadth, or in general dimension other than length; — said of a solid body; as, a timber seven inches thick.
q: Were it as thick as is a branched oak.
My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins.

senses.d: Having more depth or extent from one surface to its opposite than usual; not thin or slender; as, a thick plank; thick cloth; thick paper; thick neck.
Dense; not thin; inspissated; as, thick vapors. Also used figuratively; as, thick darkness.
q: Make the gruel thick and slab.

senses.d: Not transparent or clear; hence, turbid, muddy, or misty; as, the water of a river is apt to be thick after a rain.
Abundant, close, or crowded in space; closely set; following in quick succession; frequently recurring.
q: The people were gathered thick together.
Black was the forest; thick with beech it stood.

senses.d: Not having due distinction of syllables, or good articulation; indistinct; as, a thick utterance.
Deep; profound; as, thick sleep.
Dull; not quick; as, thick of fearing.
q: His dimensions to any thick sight were invincible.

senses.d: Intimate; very friendly; familiar.
q: We have been thick ever since.

Thick.syn: Dense; close; compact; solid; gross; coarse.
Thick.etym: [OE. thicke, AS. þicce; akin to D. dik, OS. thikki, OHG. dicchi thick, dense, G. dick thick, Icel. þykkr, þjökkr, and probably to Gael. & Ir. tiugh. Cf. Tight.]

senses.d: The thickest part, or the time when anything is thickest.
q: In the thick of the dust and smoke.

senses.d: A thicket; as, gloomy thicks.
q: Through the thick they heard one rudely rush.
He through a little window cast his sight Through thick of bars, that gave a scanty light.
Through thick and thin she followed him.
He became the panegyrist, through thick and thin, of a military frenzy.

senses.d: Frequently; fast; quick.
Closely; as, a plat of ground thick sown.
To a great depth, or to a greater depth than usual; as, land covered thick with manure.
To thicken.
q: The nightmare Life-in-death was she, Who thicks man's blood with cold.

senses.d: A wood or a collection of trees, shrubs, etc., closely set; as, a ram caught in a thicket.
The quality or state of being thick (in any of the senses of the adjective).
One who steals; one who commits theft or larceny. See Theft.
q: There came a privy thief, men clepeth death.
Where thieves break through and steal.

senses.d: A waster in the snuff of a candle.
q: Take heed, have open eye, for thieves do foot by night.
Some roving robber calling to his fellows.

Thief.etym: [OE. thef, theef, AS. �eóf; akin to OFries. thiaf, OS. theof, thiof, D. dief, G. dieb, OHG. diob, Icel. �jōfr, Sw. tjuf, Dan. tyv, Goth. �iufs, �iubs, and perhaps to Lith. tupeti to squat or crouch down. Cf. Theft.]

senses.d: To practice theft; to steal.
The proximal segment of the hind limb between the knee and the trunk. See Femur.
The coxa, or femur, of an insect.

Thigh.etym: [OE. thi, �ih, �eh, AS. �eóh; akin to OFries. thiach, D. dij, dije, OHG. dioh, thioh, Icel. �jō thigh, rump, and probably to Lith. taukas fat of animals, tuk�i to become fat, Russ. tuke fat of animals. √56.]

senses.d: Having little thickness or extent from one surface to its opposite; as, a thin plate of metal; thin paper; a thin board; a thin covering.
Rare; not dense or thick; — applied to fluids or soft mixtures; as, thin blood; thin broth; thin air.
q: In the day, when the air is more thin.
Satan, bowing low His gray dissimulation, disappeared, Into thin air diffused.

senses.d: Not close; not crowded; not filling the space; not having the individuals of which the thing is composed in a close or compact state; hence, not abundant; as, the trees of a forest are thin; the corn or grass is thin.
q: Ferrara is very large, but extremely thin of people.

senses.d: Not full or well grown; wanting in plumpness.
q: Seven thin ears . . . blasted with the east wind.

senses.d: Not stout; slim; slender; lean; gaunt; as, a person becomes thin by disease.
Wanting in body or volume; small; feeble; not full.
q: Thin, hollow sounds, and lamentable screams.

senses.d: Slight; small; slender; flimsy; wanting substance or depth or force; superficial; inadequate; not sufficient for a covering; as, a thin disguise.
q: My tale is done, for my wit is but thin.

Thin.etym: [OE. thinne, thenne, thunne, AS. þynne; akin to D. dun, G. dünn, OHG. dunni, Icel. þunnr, Sw. tunn, Dan. tynd, Gael. & Ir. tana, W. teneu, L. tenuis, Gr. � (in comp.) stretched out, � stretched, stretched out, long, Skr. tanu thin, slender; also to AS. �enian to extend, G. dehnen, Icel. �enja, Goth.

senses.d: Not thickly or closely; in a seattered state; as, seed sown thin.
q: Spain is thin sown of people.

senses.d: To make thin (in any of the senses of the adjective).
To grow or become thin; — used with some adverbs, as out, away, etc.; as, geological strata thin out, i.e., gradually diminish in thickness until they disappear.

A form of the possessive case of the pronoun thou, now superseded in common discourse by your, the possessive of you, but maintaining a place in solemn discourse, in poetry, and in the usual language of the Friends, or Quakers.

Thine.etym: [OE. thin, AS. ðīn, originally gen. of ðu, ðū, thou; akin to G. dein thine, Icel. þinn, possessive pron., þīn, gen. of þū thou, Goth. þeins, possessive pron., þeina, gen. of þu thou. See Thou, and cf. Thy.]

senses.d: Whatever exists, or is conceived to exist, as a separate entity, whether animate or inanimate; any separable or distinguishable object of thought.
q: God made . . . every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind.
He sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt.
A thing of beauty is a joy forever.

senses.d: An inanimate object, in distinction from a living being; any lifeless material.
q: Ye meads and groves, unsonscious things!

senses.d: A transaction or occurrence; an event; a deed.
q: All these things are against me.
Which if ye tell me, I in like wise will tell you by what authority I do these things.

senses.d: A portion or part; something.
q: Wieked men who understand any thing of wisdom.

senses.d: A diminutive or slighted object; any object viewed as merely existing; — often used in pity or contempt.
q: See, sons, what things you are!
The poor thing sighed, and . . . turned from me.
I'll be this abject thing no more.
I have a thing in prose.

senses.d: Clothes; furniture; appurtenances; luggage; as, to pack or store one's things.
q: And them she gave her moebles and her thing.
In the garden walketh to and fro, And hath his things [i.e., prayers, devotions] said full courteously.
Hearkening his minstrels their things play.

senses.d: Whatever may be possessed or owned; a property; — distinguished from person.
In Scandinavian countries, a legislative or judicial assembly.

Thing.etym: [AS. þing a thing, cause, assembly, judicial assembly; akin to þingan to negotiate, þingian to reconcile, conciliate, D. ding a thing, OS. thing thing, assembly, judicial assembly, G. ding a thing, formerly also, an assembly, court, Icel. þing a thing, assembly, court, Sw. & Dan. ting; perhaps origi

senses.d: In Scandinavian countries, a legislative or judicial assembly; — used, esp. in composition, in titles of such bodies. See Legislature, Norway.

Thing.etym: [Dan. thing, ting, Norw. ting, or Sw. ting.]

senses.d: To seem or appear; — used chiefly in the expressions methinketh or methinks, and methought.
To employ any of the intellectual powers except that of simple perception through the senses; to exercise the higher intellectual faculties.
q: For that I am I know, because I think.

senses.d: To call anything to mind; to remember; as, I would have sent the books, but I did not think of it.
q: Well thought upon; I have it here.

senses.d: To reflect upon any subject; to muse; to meditate; to ponder; to consider; to deliberate.
q: And when he thought thereon, he wept.
He thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?

senses.d: To form an opinion by reasoning; to judge; to conclude; to believe; as, I think it will rain to-morrow.
q: Let them marry to whom they think best.

senses.d: To purpose; to intend; to design; to mean.
q: I thought to promote thee unto great honor.
Thou thought'st to help me.

senses.d: To presume; to venture.
q: Think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.

Think.syn: To expect; guess; cogitate; reflect; ponder; contemplate; meditate; muse; imagine; suppose; believe. See Expect, Guess.
Think.etym: [OE. thinken, properly, to seem, from AS. þyncean (cf. Methinks), but confounded with OE. thenken to think, fr. AS. þencean (imp. þōhte); akin to D. denken, dunken, OS. thenkian, thunkian, G. denken, dünken, Icel. þekkja to perceive, to know, þykkja to seem, Goth. þagkjan, þaggkjan, to think, þygkja

senses.d: To conceive; to imagine.
q: Charity . . . thinketh no evil.

senses.d: To plan or design; to plot; to compass.
q: So little womanhood And natural goodness, as to think the death Of her own son.

senses.d: To believe; to consider; to esteem.
q: Nor think superfluous other's aid.

senses.d: Act of thinking; a thought.
Having the faculty of thought; cogitative; capable of a regular train of ideas; as, man is a thinking being.
The act of thinking; mode of thinking; imagination; cogitation; judgment.
q: I heard a bird so sing, Whose music, to my thinking, pleased the king.

senses.d: Next after the second; coming after two others; — the ordinal of three; as, the thirdhour in the day.
Constituting or being one of three equal parts into which anything is divided; as, the third part of a day.

Third.etym: [OE. thirde, AS. �ridda, fr. �rī, �reó, three; akin to D. derde third, G. dritte, Icel. �ri�i, Goth. �ridja, L. tertius, Gr. �, Skr. t�tīya. See Three, and cf. Riding a jurisdiction, Tierce.]

senses.d: The quotient of a unit divided by three; one of three equal parts into which anything is divided.
The sixtieth part of a second of time.
The third tone of the scale; the mediant.
The third part of the estate of a deseased husband, which, by some local laws, the widow is entitled to enjoy during her life.
In the third place.

A sensation of dryness in the throat associated with a craving for liquids, produced by deprivation of drink, or by some other cause (as fear, excitement, etc.) which arrests the secretion of the pharyngeal mucous membrane; hence, the condition producing this sensation.
q: Wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us, and our children . . . with thirst?
With thirst, with cold, with hunger so confounded.

senses.d: Fig.: A want and eager desire after anything; a craving or longing; — usually with for, of, or after; as, the thirst for gold.

Thirst.etym: [OE. thirst, þurst, AS. þurst, þyrst; akin to D. dorst, OS. thurst, G. durst, Icel. þorsti, Sw. & Dan. törst, Goth. þaúrstei thirst, þaúrsus dry, withered, þaúrsieþ mik I thirst, gaþaírsan to wither, L. torrere to parch, Gr. τέρσεσθαι to become dry, τεσαίνειν to dry up, Skr. tṛsh to thirst. √54. Cf.

senses.d: To feel thirst; to experience a painful or uneasy sensation of the throat or fauces, as for want of drink.
q: The people thirsted there for water.

senses.d: To have a vehement desire.
q: My soul thirsteth for . . . the living God.

senses.d: To have a thirst for.
q: He seeks his keeper's flesh, and thirsts his blood.

senses.d: Feeling thirst; having a painful or distressing sensation from want of drink; hence, having an eager desire.
q: Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.

senses.d: Deficient in moisture; dry; parched.
q: A dry and thirsty land, where no water is.
When in the sultry glebe I faint, Or on the thirsty mountain pant.

senses.d: One more than twelve; ten and three; as, thirteen ounces or pounds.

Thirteen.etym: [OE. threttene, AS. �reótēne, �reótyne. See Three, and Ten, and cf. Thirty.]

senses.d: The number greater by one than twelve; the sum of ten and three; thirteen units or objects.
A symbol representing thirteen units, as 13 or xiii.
Next in order after the twelfth; the third after the tenth; — the ordinal of thirteen; as, the thirteenth day of the month.
Constituting or being one of thirteen equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of a unit divided by thirteen; one of thirteen equal parts into which anything is divided.
The next in order after the twelfth.
The interval comprising an octave and a sixth.
Next in order after the twenty-ninth; the tenth after the twentieth; — the ordinal of thirty; as, the thirtieth day of the month.
Constituting or being one of thirty equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of a unit divided by thirty; one of thirty equal parts.
Being three times ten; consisting of one more than twenty-nine; twenty and ten; as, the month of June consists of thirty days.

Thirty.etym: [OE. thritty, AS. þrītig, þrittig; akin to D. dertig, G. dreissig, Icel. þrjātīu, þrjātigi, þrir teger, Goth. þreis tigjus, i.e., three tens. See Three, and Ten, and cf. Thirteen.]

senses.d: The sum of three tens, or twenty and ten; thirty units or objects.
A symbol expressing thirty, as 30, or XXX.
As a demonstrative pronoun, this denotes something that is present or near in place or time, or something just mentioned, or that is just about to be mentioned.
q: When they heard this, they were pricked in their heart.
But know this, that if the good man of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched.

senses.d: As an adjective, this has the same demonstrative force as the pronoun, but is followed by a noun; as, this book; this way to town.
q: This way and that wavering sails they bend.
A body of this or that denomination is produced.
Their judgment in this we may not, and in that we need not, follow.
Consider the arguments which the author had to write this, or to design the other, before you arraign him.
Thy crimes . . . soon by this or this will end.
This twenty years have I been with thee..
I have not wept this years; but now My mother comes afresh into my eyes.

This.etym: [OE. this, thes, AS. ðēs, masc., ðeós, fem., ðis, neut.; akin to OS. these, D. deze, G. dieser, OHG. diser, deser, Icel. þessi; originally from the definite article + a particle -se, -si; cf. Goth. sai behold. See The, That, and cf. These, Those.]

senses.d: Any one of several prickly composite plants, especially those of the genera Cnicus, Craduus, and Onopordon. The name is often also applied to other prickly plants.

Thistle.etym: [OE. thistil, AS. þistel; akin to D. & G. distel, OHG. distila, distil, Icel. þistill, Sw. tistel, Dan. tidsel; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To that place; — opposed to hither.
q: This city is near; . . . O, let me escape thither.
Where I am, thither ye can not come.

senses.d: To that point, end, or result; as, the argument tended thither.

Thither.etym: [OE. thider, AS. ðider; akin to E. that; cf. Icel. þaðra there, Goth. þaþrō thence. See That, and The.]

senses.d: Being on the farther side from the person speaking; farther; — a correlative of hither; as, on the thither side of the water.
Applied to time: On the thither side of, older than; of more years than. See Hither, a.
To ward that place; in that direction.
q: They shall ask the way to Zion, with their faces thitherward.

senses.d: A strap of leather; especially, one used for fastening anything.
q: And nails for loosened spears, and thongs for shields, provide.

Thong.etym: [OE. thong, þwong, thwang, AS. þwang; akin to Icel. þvengr a thong, latchet. √57. Cf. Twinge.]

senses.d: A hard and sharp-pointed projection from a woody stem; usually, a branch so transformed; a spine.
Any shrub or small tree which bears thorns; especially, any species of the genus Cratægus, as the hawthorn, whitethorn, cockspur thorn.
Fig.: That which pricks or annoys as a thorn; anything troublesome; trouble; care.
q: There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me.
The guilt of empire, all its thorns and cares, Be only mine.

senses.d: The name of the Anglo-Saxon letter �, capital form �. It was used to represent both of the sounds of English th, as in thin, then. So called because it was the initial letter of thorn, a spine.

Thorn.etym: [AS. þorn; akin to OS. & OFries. thorn, D. doorn, G. dorn, Dan. torn, Sw. törne, Icel. þorn, Goth. þaúrnus; cf. Pol. tarn, Russ. tern' the blackthorn, ternie thorns, Skr. tṛṇa grass, blade of grass. √53.]

senses.d: To prick, as with a thorn.
q: I am the only rose of all the stock That never thorn'd him.

senses.d: Through.
Passing through; as, thorough lights in a house.
Passing through or to the end; hence, complete; perfect; as, a thorough reformation; thorough work; a thorough translator; a thorough poet.
Thoroughly.
Through.
A furrow between two ridges, to drain off the surface water.
In a thorough manner; fully; entirely; completely.
The plural of that. See That.

Those.etym: [OE. þos, þas, AS. ðās, nom. and acc. pl. of ðēs this. See This, and cf. These.]

senses.d: The second personal pronoun, in the singular number, denoting the person addressed; thyself; the pronoun which is used in addressing persons in the solemn or poetical style.
q: Art thou he that should come?

Thou.etym: [OE. thou, þu, AS. ðū, ðu; akin to OS. & OFries. thu, G., Dan. & Sw. du, Icel. þū, Goth. þu, Russ. tui, Ir. & Gael. tu, W. ti, L. tu, Gr. σύ, Dor. τύ, Skr. tvam. √185. Cf. Thee, Thine, Te Deum.]

senses.d: To address as thou, esp. to do so in order to treat with insolent familiarity or contempt.
q: If thou thouest him some thrice, it shall not be amiss.

senses.d: To use the words thou and thee in discourse after the manner of the Friends.
Granting, admitting, or supposing that; notwithstanding that; if.
q: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
Not that I so affirm, though so it seem.
In the vine were three branches; and it was as though it budded.

Though.etym: [OE. thogh, þah, AS. ðeáh, ðǣh, ðēh; akin to OS. thōh, OFries. thach, D. & G. doch but, yet, OHG. doh but, yet though, Icel. þō yet, nevertheless, Sw. dock, Dan. dog, Goth. þáuh, þáu, than, or, yet; of uncertain origin. √184.]

senses.d: However; nevertheless; notwithstanding; — used in familiar language, and in the middle or at the end of a sentence.
q: I would not be as sick though for his place.
A good cause would do well, though.

senses.d: The act of thinking; the exercise of the mind in any of its higher forms; reflection; cogitation.
q: Thought can not be superadded to matter, so as in any sense to render it true that matter can become cogitative.

senses.d: Meditation; serious consideration.
q: Pride, of all others the most dangerous fault, Proceeds from want of sense or want of thought.

senses.d: That which is thought; an idea; a mental conception, whether an opinion, judgment, fancy, purpose, or intention.
q: Thus Bethel spoke, who always speaks his thought.
Why do you keep alone, . . . Using those thoughts which should indeed have died With them they think on?
Thoughts come crowding in so fast upon me, that my only difficulty is to choose or to reject.
All their thoughts are against me for evil.

senses.d: Solicitude; anxious care; concern.
q: Hawis was put in trouble, and died with thought and anguish before his business came to an end.
Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink.

senses.d: A small degree or quantity; a trifle; as, a thought longer; a thought better.
q: If the hair were a thought browner.
This , to which I gave the name of the “elaborative faculty,” — the faculty of relations or comparison, — constitutes what is properly denominated thought.

Thought.syn: Idea; conception; imagination; fancy; conceit; notion; supposition; reflection; consideration; meditation; contemplation; cogitation; deliberation.
Thought.etym: [OE. þoght, þouht, AS. þōht, geþōht, fr. þencean to think; akin to D. gedachte thought, MHG. dāht, gedāht, Icel. þōttr, þōtti. See Think.]

senses.d: The number of ten hundred; a collection or sum consisting of ten times one hundred units or objects.
Hence, indefinitely, a great number.
q: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand.

senses.d: A symbol representing one thousand units; as, 1,000, M or CIↃ.

Thousand.etym: [OE. þousend, þusend, AS. þūsend; akin to OS. thūsundig, thūsind, OFries. thusend, D. duizend, G. tausend, OHG. tūsunt, dūsunt, Icel. þūsund, þūshund, Sw. tusen, Dan. tusind, Goth. þūsundi, Lith. tukstantis, Russ. tuisiacha; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Consisting of ten hundred; being ten times one hundred.
Hence, consisting of a great number indefinitely.

A very small twist of flax, wool, cotton, silk, or other fibrous substance, drawn out to considerable length; a compound cord consisting of two or more single yarns doubled, or joined together, and twisted.
A filament, as of a flower, or of any fibrous substance, as of bark; also, a line of gold or silver.
The prominent part of the spiral of a screw or nut; the rib. See Screw, n., 1.
Fig.: Something continued in a long course or tenor; a,s the thread of life, or of a discourse.
Fig.: Composition; quality; fineness.
q: A neat courtier, Of a most elegant thread.

Thread.etym: [OE. threed, þred, AS. þrǣd; akin to D. draad, G. draht wire, thread, OHG. drāt, Icel. þrāðr a thread, Sw. tråd, Dan. traad, and AS. þrāwan to twist. See Throw, and cf. Third.]

senses.d: To pass a thread through the eye of; as, to thread a needle.
To pass or pierce through as a narrow way; also, to effect or make, as one's way, through or between obstacles; to thrid.
q: Heavy trading ships . . . threading the Bosphorus.
They would not thread the gates.

senses.d: To form a thread, or spiral rib, on or in; as, to thread a screw or nut.
To utter threats against; to menace; to inspire with apprehension; to alarm, or attempt to alarm, as with the promise of something evil or disagreeable; to warn.
q: Let us straitly threaten them, that they speak henceforth to no man in this name.

senses.d: To exhibit the appearance of (something evil or unpleasant) as approaching; to indicate as impending; to announce the conditional infliction of; as, to threaten war; to threaten death.
q: The skies look grimly And threaten present blusters.
By turns put on the suppliant and the lord: Threatened this moment, and the next implored.
Of the sharp ax Regardless, that o'er his devoted head Hangs menacing.

senses.d: To use threats, or menaces; also, to have a threatening appearance.
q: Though the seas threaten, they are merciful.

senses.d: One more than two; two and one.
q: Three solemn aisles approach the shrine.

Three.etym: [OE. þre, þreo, þri, AS. þrī, masc., þreó, fem. and neut.; akin to OFries. thre, OS. thria, threa, D. drie, G. drei, OHG. drī, Icel. þrīr, Dan. & Sw. tre, Goth. þreis, Lith. trys, Ir., Gael. & W. tri, Russ. tri, L. tres, Gr. τρει̑σ, Skr. tri. √301. Cf. 3d Drilling, Tern, a., Third, Thirteen, Thirty,

senses.d: The number greater by a unit than two; three units or objects.
A symbol representing three units, as 3 or iii.
Consisting of three, or thrice repeated; triple; as, threefold justice.
q: A threefold cord is not quickly broken.

senses.d: Same as Thrash.
q: He would thresh, and thereto dike and delve.

senses.d: The plank, stone, or piece of timber, which lies under a door, especially of a dwelling house, church, temple, or the like; the doorsill; hence, entrance; gate; door.
Fig.: The place or point of entering or beginning, entrance; outset; as, the threshold of life.

Threshold.etym: [OE. threswold, þreshwold, AS. þrescwald, þerscwald, þerscold, þrescold, fr. þrescan, þerscan, to thresh; akin to Icel. þreskjöde, þröskuldr, Sw. tröskel, Dan. tærskel. See Thrash.]

senses.d: Three times.
q: Verily I say unto thee. That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.

senses.d: In a threefold manner or degree; repeatedly; very.
q: Thrice noble lord, let me entreat of you To pardon me.
Thrice is he armed that hath his quarrel just.

Thrice.etym: [OE. thries; thrie thrice (AS. þriga, þriwa) + -s, the adverbal suffix. See Three, and -wards.]

senses.d: The part of the neck in front of, or ventral to, the vertebral column.
q: I can vent clamor from my throat.

senses.d: A contracted portion of a vessel, or of a passage way; as, the throat of a pitcher or vase.
The part of a chimney between the gathering, or portion of the funnel which contracts in ascending, and the flue.
The upper fore corner of a boom-and-gaff sail, or of a staysail.
The inside of a timber knee.
The orifice of a tubular organ; the outer end of the tube of a monopetalous corolla; the faux, or fauces.

Throat.etym: [OE. throte, AS. þrote, þrotu; akin to OHG. drozza, G. drossel; cf. OFries. & D. stort. Cf. Throttle.]

senses.d: To utter in the throat; to mutter; as, to throat threats.
To mow, as beans, in a direction against their bending.
A chair of state, commonly a royal seat, but sometimes the seat of a prince, bishop, or other high dignitary.
q: The noble king is set up in his throne.
High on a throne of royal state.

senses.d: Hence, sovereign power and dignity; also, the one who occupies a throne, or is invested with sovereign authority; an exalted or dignified personage.
q: Only in the throne will I be greater than thou.
To mold a mighty state's decrees, And shape the whisper of the throne.

senses.d: A high order of angels in the celestial hierarchy; — a meaning given by the schoolmen.
q: Great Sire! whom thrones celestial ceaseless sing.

Throne.etym: [OE. trone, F. trône, L. thronus, Gr. �; cf. � a bench, � a footstool, � to set one's self, to sit, Skr. dharaṇa supporting, dhṛ to hold fast, carry, and E. firm, a.]

senses.d: To place on a royal seat; to enthrone.
To place in an elevated position; to give sovereignty or dominion to; to exalt.
q: True image of the Father, whether throned In the bosom of bliss, and light of light.

senses.d: To be in, or sit upon, a throne; to be placed as if upon a throne.
A multitude of persons or of living beings pressing or pressed into a close body or assemblage; a crowd.
A great multitude; as, the heavenly throng.
q: So, with this bold opposer rushes on This many-headed monster, multitude.
Not to know me argues yourselves unknown, The lowest of your throng.
I come from empty noise, and tasteless pomp, From crowds that hide a monarch from himself.

Throng.etym: [OE. þrong, þrang, AS. geþrang, fr. þringan to crowd, to press; akin to OS. thringan, D. & G. dringen, OHG. dringan, Icel. þryngva, þröngva, Goth. þriehan, D. & G. drang a throng, press, Icel. þröng a throng, Lith. trenkti to jolt, tranksmas a tumult. Cf. Thring.]

senses.d: To crowd together; to press together into a close body, as a multitude of persons; to gather or move in multitudes.
q: I have seen the dumb men throng to see him.

senses.d: To crowd, or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of living beings.
q: Much people followed him, and thronged him.

senses.d: To crowd into; to fill closely by crowding or pressing into, as a hall or a street.
Thronged; crowded; also, much occupied; busy.
q: To the intent the sick . . . should not lie too throng.

senses.d: From end to end of, or from side to side of; from one surface or limit of, to the opposite; into and out of at the opposite, or at another, point; as, to bore through a piece of timber, or through a board; a ball passes through the side of a ship.
Between the sides or walls of; within; as, to pass through a door; to go through an avenue.
q: Through the gate of ivory he dismissed His valiant offspring.

senses.d: By means of; by the agency of.
q: Through these hands this science has passed with great applause.
Material things are presented only through their senses.

senses.d: Over the whole surface or extent of; as, to ride through the country; to look through an account.
Among or in the midst of; — used to denote passage; as, a fish swims through the water; the light glimmers through a thicket.
From the beginning to the end of; to the end or conclusion of; as, through life; through the year.

Through.etym: [OE. thurgh, þurh, þuruh, þoruh, AS. þurh; akin to OS. thurh, thuru, OFries. thruch, D. door, OHG. durh, duruh, G. durch, Goth. þaírh; cf. Ir. tri, tre, W. trwy. √53. Cf. Nostril, Thorough, Thrill.]

senses.d: From one end or side to the other; as, to pierce a thing through.
From beginning to end; as, to read a letter through.
To the end; to a conclusion; to the ultimate purpose; as, to carry a project through.

Going or extending through; going, extending, or serving from the beginning to the end; thorough; complete; as, a through line; a through ticket; a through train. Also, admitting of passage through; as, a through bridge.
Thoroughly.
q: Wash me throughly from mine iniquity.
To dare in fields is valor; but how few Dare to be throughly valiant to be true?

senses.d: Quite through; from one extremity to the other of; also, every part of; as, to search throughout the house.
q: Nor to their idle orbs doth sight appear Of sun, or moon, or star, throughout the year.

senses.d: In every part; as, the cloth was of a piece throughout.
Pain; especially, pain of travail; throe.
Time; while; space of time; moment; trice.
q: I will with Thomas speak a little throw.

senses.d: To fling, cast, or hurl with a certain whirling motion of the arm, to throw a ball; — distinguished from to toss, or to bowl.

To fling or cast in any manner; to drive to a distance from the hand or from an engine; to propel; to send; as, to throw stones or dust with the hand; a cannon throws a ball; a fire engine throws a stream of water to extinguish flames.
To drive by violence; as, a vessel or sailors may be thrown upon a rock.
To cause to take a strategic position; as, he threw a detachment of his army across the river.
To overturn; to prostrate in wrestling; as, a man throws his antagonist.
To cast, as dice; to venture at dice.
q: Set less than thou throwest.

senses.d: To put on hastily; to spread carelessly.
q: O'er his fair limbs a flowery vest he threw.

senses.d: To divest or strip one's self of; to put off.
q: There the snake throws her enameled skin.

senses.d: To form or shape roughly on a throwing engine, or potter's wheel, as earthen vessels.
To give forcible utterance to; to cast; to vent.
q: I have thrown A brave defiance in King Henry's teeth.

senses.d: To bring forth; to produce, as young; to bear; — said especially of rabbits.

To twist two or more filaments of, as silk, so as to form one thread; to twist together, as singles, in a direction contrary to the twist of the singles themselves; — sometimes applied to the whole class of operations by which silk is prepared for the weaver.

Throw.etym: [OE. þrowen, þrawen, to throw, to twist, AS. þrāwan to twist, to whirl; akin to D. draaijen, G. drehen, OHG. drājan, L. terebra an auger, gimlet, Gr. � to bore, to turn, � to pierce, � a hole. Cf. Thread, Trite, Turn, v. t.]

senses.d: To perform the act of throwing or casting; to cast; specifically, to cast dice.
The act of hurling or flinging; a driving or propelling from the hand or an engine; a cast.
q: He heaved a stone, and, rising to the throw, He sent it in a whirlwind at the foe.

senses.d: A stroke; a blow.
q: Nor shield defend the thunder of his throws.

senses.d: The distance which a missile is, or may be, thrown; as, a stone's throw.
A cast of dice; the manner in which dice fall when cast; as, a good throw.
An effort; a violent sally.
q: Your youth admires The throws and swellings of a Roman soul.

senses.d: The extreme movement given to a sliding or vibrating reciprocating piece by a cam, crank, eccentric, or the like; travel; stroke; as, the throw of a slide valve. Also, frequently, the length of the radius of a crank, or the eccentricity of an eccentric; as, the throw of the crank of a steam engine is equal to half the stroke of the piston.
A potter's wheel or table; a jigger. See 2d Jigger, 2 (a).
A turner's lathe; a throwe.
The amount of vertical displacement produced by a fault; — according to the direction it is designated as an upthrow, or a downthrow.
A turning lathe.
Through.
Thrist.
To push or drive with force; to drive, force, or impel; to shove; as, to thrust anything with the hand or foot, or with an instrument.
q: Into a dungeon thrust, to work with slaves.

senses.d: To stab; to pierce; — usually with through.

Thrust.etym: [OE. �rusten, �risten, �resten, Icel. �r�st� to thrust, press, force, compel; perhaps akin to E. threat.]

senses.d: To make a push; to attack with a pointed weapon; as, a fencer thrusts at his antagonist.
To enter by pushing; to squeeze in.
q: And thrust between my father and the god.

senses.d: To push forward; to come with force; to press on; to intrude.
q: As doth an eager hound Thrust to an hind within some covert glade.

senses.d: A violent push or driving, as with a pointed weapon moved in the direction of its length, or with the hand or foot, or with any instrument; a stab; — a word much used as a term of fencing.
q: Pyrrhus with his lance pursues, And often reaches, and his thrusts renews.

senses.d: An attack; an assault.
q: One thrust at your pure, pretended mechanism.

senses.d: The force or pressure of one part of a construction against other parts; especially (Arch.), a horizontal or diagonal outward pressure, as of an arch against its abutments, or of rafters against the wall which support them.
The breaking down of the roof of a gallery under its superincumbent weight.
The short, thick first digit of the human hand, differing from the other fingers in having but two phalanges; the pollex. See Pollex.
q: Upon his thumb he had of gold a ring.

Thumb.etym: [OE. thombe, thoumbe, þume, AS. þūma; akin to OFries. thūma, D. duim, G. daumen, OHG. dūmo, Icel. þumall, Dan. tommelfinger, Sw. tumme, and perhaps to L. tumere to swell. √56. Cf. Thimble, Tumid.]

senses.d: To handle awkwardly.
To play with the thumbs, or with the thumbs and fingers; as, to thumb over a tune.
To soil or wear with the thumb or the fingers; to soil, or wear out, by frequent handling; also, to cover with the thumb; as, to thumb the touch-hole of a cannon.
q: He gravely informed the enemy that all his cards had been thumbed to pieces, and begged them to let him have a few more packs.

senses.d: To play with the thumb or thumbs; to play clumsily; to thrum.
A mysterious part or decoration of the breastplate of the Jewish high priest. See the note under Urim.
The sound which follows a flash of lightning; the report of a discharge of atmospheric electricity.
The discharge of electricity; a thunderbolt.
q: The revenging gods 'Gainst parricides did all their thunders bend.

senses.d: Any loud noise; as, the thunder of cannon.
An alarming or statrling threat or denunciation.
q: The thunders of the Vatican could no longer strike into the heart of princes.

Thunder.etym: [OE. þunder, þonder, þoner, AS. þunor; akin to þunian to stretch, to thunder, D. donder thunder, G. donner, OHG. donar, Icel. þōrr Thor, L. tonare to thunder, tonitrus thunder, Gr. τόνοσ a stretching, straining, Skr. tan to stretch. √52. See Thin, and cf. Astonish, Detonate, Intone, Thursday, Tone.]

senses.d: To produce thunder; to sound, rattle, or roar, as a discharge of atmospheric electricity; — often used impersonally; as, it thundered continuously.
q: Canst thou thunder with a voice like him?

senses.d: Fig.: To make a loud noise; esp. a heavy sound, of some continuance.
q: His dreadful voice no more Would thunder in my ears.

senses.d: To utter violent denunciation.
To emit with noise and terror; to utter vehemently; to publish, as a threat or denunciation.
q: Oracles severe Were daily thundered in our general's ear.
An archdeacon, as being a prelate, may thunder out an ecclesiastical censure.

senses.d: A shaft of lightning; a brilliant stream of electricity passing from one part of the heavens to another, or from the clouds to the earth.
Something resembling lightning in suddenness and effectiveness.
q: The Scipios' worth, those thunderbolts of war.

senses.d: Vehement threatening or censure; especially, ecclesiastical denunciation; fulmination.
q: He severely threatens such with the thunderbolt of excommunication.

senses.d: A belemnite, or thunderstone.
Emitting thunder.
q: Roll the thundering chariot o'er the ground.

senses.d: Very great; — often adverbially.
Thunder.
The commoner kind of frankincense, or that obtained from the Norway spruce, the long-leaved pine, and other conifers.

Thus.etym: [L. thus, better tus, frankincense. See Thurible.]

senses.d: In this or that manner; on this wise.
q: Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.
Thus God the heaven created, thus the earth.

senses.d: To this degree or extent; so far; so; as, thus wise; thus peaceble; thus bold.
q: Thus far extend, thus far thy bounds.

Thus.etym: [OE. thus, AS. ðus; akin to OFries. & OS. thus, D. dus, and E. that; cf. OHG. sus. See That.]

senses.d: Of thee, or belonging to thee; the more common form of thine, possessive case of thou; — used always attributively, and chiefly in the solemn or grave style, and in poetry. Thine is used in the predicate; as, the knife is thine. See Thine.
q: Our father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done.
These are thy glorious works, Parent of good.

Thy.etym: [OE. thi, shortened from thin. See Thine, Thou.]

senses.d: An emphasized form of the personal pronoun of the second person; — used as a subject commonly with thou; as, thou thyself shalt go; that is, thou shalt go, and no other. It is sometimes used, especially in the predicate, without thou, and in the nominative as well as in the objective case.
q: Thyself shalt see the act.
Ere I do thee, thou to thyself wast cruel.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to tides; caused by tides; having tides; periodically rising and falling, or following and ebbing; as, tidal waters.
q: The tidal wave of deeper souls Into our inmost being rolls, And lifts us unawares Out of all meaner cares.

senses.d: Tidings.
Account of what has taken place, and was not before known; news.
q: I shall make my master glad with these tidings.
Full well the busy whisper, circling round, Conveyed the dismal tidings when he frowned.
Now near the tidings of our comfort is.
Tidings to the contrary Are brought your eyes.
Evil news rides post, while good news baits.
What tidings dost thou bring?

Tidings.etym: [OE. tidinge, ti�inge, tidinde, from or influenced by Icel. tī�indi; akin to Dan. tidende, Sw. tidning, G. zeung, AS. tīdan to happen, E. betide, tide. See Tide, v. i. & n.]

senses.d: A knot; a fastening.
A bond; an obligation, moral or legal; as, the sacred ties of friendship or of duty; the ties of allegiance.
q: No distance breaks the tie of blood.

senses.d: A knot of hair, as at the back of a wig.
An equality in numbers, as of votes, scores, etc., which prevents either party from being victorious; equality in any contest, as a race.
A beam or rod for holding two parts together; in railways, one of the transverse timbers which support the track and keep it in place.

A line, usually straight, drawn across the stems of notes, or a curved line written over or under the notes, signifying that they are to be slurred, or closely united in the performance, or that two notes of the same pitch are to be sounded as one; a bind; a ligature.
Low shoes fastened with lacings.

Tie.etym: [AS. tēge, t�ge, tīge. √64. See Tie, v. t.]

senses.d: To fasten with a band or cord and knot; to bind.
q: My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother: bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck.

senses.d: To form, as a knot, by interlacing or complicating a cord; also, to interlace, or form a knot in; as, to tie a cord to a tree; to knit; to knot.
To unite firmly; to fasten; to hold.
q: In bond of virtuous love together tied.

senses.d: To hold or constrain by authority or moral influence, as by knotted cords; to oblige; to constrain; to restrain; to confine.
q: Not tied to rules of policy, you find Revenge less sweet than a forgiving mind.

senses.d: To unite, as notes, by a cross line, or by a curved line, or slur, drawn over or under them.
To make an equal score with, in a contest; to be even with.

Tie.etym: [OE. ti�en, teyen, AS. tīgan, tiégan, fr. teág, teáh, a rope; akin to Icel. taug, and AS. teón to draw, to pull. See Tug, v. t., and cf. Tow to drag.]

senses.d: To make a tie; to make an equal score.
To protect from the intrusion of the uninitiated; as, to tile a Masonic lodge.
A plate, or thin piece, of baked clay, used for covering the roofs of buildings, for floors, for drains, and often for ornamental mantel works.
A small slab of marble or other material used for flooring.
A small, flat piece of dried earth or earthenware, used to cover vessels in which metals are fused.
A draintile.
A stiff hat.

Tile.etym: [OE. tile, tigel, AS. tigel, tigol, fr. L. tegula, from tegere to cover. See Thatch, and cf. Tegular.]

senses.d: To cover with tiles; as, to tile a house.
Fig.: To cover, as if with tiles.
q: The muscle, sinew, and vein, Which tile this house, will come again.

senses.d: A surface covered with tiles, or composed of tiles.
q: They . . . let him down through the tiling.

senses.d: Tiles, collectively.
A vetch; a tare.
A drawer.
A tray or drawer in a chest.
A money drawer in a shop or store.

Till.etym: [Properly, a drawer, from OE. tillen to draw. See Tiller the lever of a rudder.]

senses.d: A deposit of clay, sand, and gravel, without lamination, formed in a glacier valley by means of the waters derived from the melting glaciers; — sometimes applied to alluvium of an upper river terrace, when not laminated, and appearing as if formed in the same manner.
A kind of coarse, obdurate land.

To; unto; up to; as far as; until; — now used only in respect to time, but formerly, also, of place, degree, etc., and still so used in Scotland and in parts of England and Ireland; as, I worked till four o'clock; I will wait till next week.
q: He . . . came till an house.
Women, up till this Cramped under worse than South-sea-isle taboo.
Similar sentiments will recur to every one familiar with his writings — all through them till the very end.

Till.etym: [OE. til, Icel. til; akin to Dan. til, Sw. till, OFries. til, also to AS. til good, excellent, G. ziel end, limit, object, OHG. zil, Goth. tils, gatils, fit, convenient, and E. till to cultivate. See Till, v. t.]

senses.d: As far as; up to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; that is, to the time specified in the sentence or clause following; until.
q: And said unto them, Occupy till I come.
Mediate so long till you make some act of prayer to God.
There was no outbreak till the regiment arrived.

senses.d: To plow and prepare for seed, and to sow, dress, raise crops from, etc., to cultivate; as, to till the earth, a field, a farm.
q: No field nolde tilye.
the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

senses.d: To prepare; to get.

Till.etym: [OE. tilen, tilien, AS. tilian, teolian, to aim, strive for, till; akin to OS. tilian to get, D. telen to propagate, G. zielen to aim, ziel an end, object, and perhaps also to E. tide, time, from the idea of something fixed or definite. Cf. Teal, Till, prep..]

senses.d: To cultivate land.
The operation, practice, or art of tilling or preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground in a proper state for the growth of crops.
A place tilled or cultivated; cultivated land.
One who tills; a husbandman; a cultivator; a plowman.
A shoot of a plant, springing from the root or bottom of the original stalk; a sucker.
A young timber tree.

Tiller.etym: [AS. telgor a small branch. Cf. Till to cultivate.]

senses.d: To put forth new shoots from the root, or round the bottom of the original stalk; as, wheat or rye tillers; some spread plants by tillering.

A lever of wood or metal fitted to the rudder head and used for turning side to side in steering. In small boats hand power is used; in large vessels, the tiller is moved by means of mechanical appliances. See Illust. of Rudder. Cf. 2d Helm, 1.
The stalk, or handle, of a crossbow; also, sometimes, the bow itself.
q: You can shoot in a tiller.

senses.d: The handle of anything.
A small drawer; a till.

Tiller.etym: [From OE. tillen, tullen, to draw, pull; probably fr. AS. tyllan in fortyllan to lead astray; or cf. D. tillen to lift up. Cf. Till a drawer.]

senses.d: A certain quantity of fur skins, as of martens, ermines, sables, etc., packed between boards; being in some cases forty skins, in others one hundred and twenty; — called also timmer.

Timber.etym: [Probably the same word as timber sort of wood; cf. Sw. timber, LG. timmer, MHG. zimber, G. zimmer, F. timbre, LL. timbrium. Cf. Timmer.]

senses.d: The crest on a coat of arms.
To surmount as a timber does.

That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture, carriages, fences, ships, and the like; — usually said of felled trees, but sometimes of those standing. Cf. Lumber, 3.
q: And ta'en my fiddle to the gate, . . . And fiddled in the timber!

senses.d: The body, stem, or trunk of a tree.
Fig.: Material for any structure.
q: Such dispositions are the very errors of human nature; and yet they are the fittest timber to make politics of.

senses.d: A single piece or squared stick of wood intended for building, or already framed; collectively, the larger pieces or sticks of wood, forming the framework of a house, ship, or other structure, in distinction from the covering or boarding.
q: So they prepared timber . . . to build the house.
Many of the timbers were decayed.

senses.d: Woods or forest; wooden land.
A rib, or a curving piece of wood, branching outward from the keel and bending upward in a vertical direction. One timber is composed of several pieces united.

Timber.etym: [AS. timbor, timber, wood, building; akin to OFries. timber, D. timmer a room, G. zimmer, OHG. zimbar timber, a dwelling, room, Icel. timbr timber, Sw. timmer, Dan. tömmer, Goth. timrjan to build, timrja a builder, L. domus a house, Gr. � house, � to build, Skr. dama a house. √62. Cf. Dome, Domestic

senses.d: To furnish with timber; — chiefly used in the past participle.
q: His bark is stoutly timbered.

senses.d: To light on a tree.
To make a nest.
A kind of drum, tabor, or tabret, in use from the highest antiquity.
q: Miriam . . . took a timbrel in her hand, and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.

Timbrel.etym: [Dim. of OE. timbre, OF. timbre; probably fr. L. typmanum, Gr. � a kettledrum, but influenced perhaps by Ar. tabl a drum; cf. Per. tambal a drum. See Tympanum, and cf. 2d Timbre, Tymbal.]

senses.d: Duration, considered independently of any system of measurement or any employment of terms which designate limited portions thereof.
q: The time wasteth [i.e. passes away] night and day.
I know of no ideas . . . that have a better claim to be accounted simple and original than those of space and time.

senses.d: A particular period or part of duration, whether past, present, or future; a point or portion of duration; as, the time was, or has been; the time is, or will be.
q: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets.

senses.d: The period at which any definite event occurred, or person lived; age; period; era; as, the Spanish Armada was destroyed in the time of Queen Elizabeth; — often in the plural; as, ancient times; modern times.
The duration of one's life; the hours and days which a person has at his disposal.
q: Believe me, your time is not your own; it belongs to God, to religion, to mankind.

senses.d: A proper time; a season; an opportunity.
q: There is . . . a time to every purpose.
The time of figs was not yet.

senses.d: Hour of travail, delivery, or parturition.
q: She was within one month of her time.

senses.d: Performance or occurrence of an action or event, considered with reference to repetition; addition of a number to itself; repetition; as, to double cloth four times; four times four, or sixteen.
q: Summers three times eight save one.

senses.d: The present life; existence in this world as contrasted with immortal life; definite, as contrasted with infinite, duration.
q: Till time and sin together cease.

senses.d: Tense.
The measured duration of sounds; measure; tempo; rate of movement; rhythmical division; as, common or triple time; the musician keeps good time.
q: Some few lines set unto a solemn time.

Time.etym: [OE. time, AS. tīma, akin to tīd time, and to Icel. tīmi, Dan. time an hour, Sw. timme. √58. See Tide, n.]

senses.d: To appoint the time for; to bring, begin, or perform at the proper season or time; as, he timed his appearance rightly.
q: There is no greater wisdom than well to time the beginnings and onsets of things.

senses.d: To regulate as to time; to accompany, or agree with, in time of movement.
q: Who overlooked the oars, and timed the stroke.
He was a thing of blood, whose every motion Was timed with dying cries.

senses.d: To ascertain or record the time, duration, or rate of; as, to time the speed of horses, or hours for workmen.
To measure, as in music or harmony.
To keep or beat time; to proceed or move in time.
q: With oar strokes timing to their song.

senses.d: To pass time; to delay.

A kind of grass (Phleum pratense) with long cylindrical spikes; — called also herd's grass, in England, cat's-tail grass, and meadow cat's-tail grass. It is much prized for fodder. See Illustration in Appendix.

Timothy.etym: [From Timothy Hanson, who carried the seed from New England to Maryland about 1720.]

senses.d: An elementary substance found as an oxide in the mineral cassiterite, and reduced as a soft white crystalline metal, malleable at ordinary temperatures, but brittle when heated. It is not easily oxidized in the air, and is used chiefly to coat iron to protect it from rusting, in the form of tin foil with mercury to form the reflective surface of mirrors, and in solder, bronze, speculum metal, and other alloys. Its compounds are designated as stannous, or stannic. Symbol Sn (Stannum). Atomic weight 117.4.
Thin plates of iron covered with tin; tin plate.
Money.

Tin.etym: [As. tin; akin to D. tin, G. zinn, OHG. zin, Icel. & Dan. tin, Sw. tenn; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To cover with tin or tinned iron, or to overlay with tin foil.
To feel a kind of thrilling sensation, as in hearing a shrill sound.
q: At which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle.

senses.d: To feel a sharp, thrilling pain.
q: The pale boy senator yet tingling stands.

senses.d: To have, or to cause, a sharp, thrilling sensation, or a slight pricking sensation.
q: They suck pollution through their tingling vein.

senses.d: To make, or give forth, small, quick, sharp sounds, as a piece of metal does when struck; to clink.
q: As sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
The sprightly horse Moves to the music of his tinkling bells.

senses.d: To hear, or resound with, a small, sharp sound.

senses.d: To cause to clonk, or make small, sharp, quick sounds.
A small, sharp, quick sound, as that made by striking metal.
A tinkle, or succession of tinkles.
q: Drowsy tinklings lull the distant folds.

senses.d: A grackle (Quiscalus crassirostris) native of Jamaica. It often associates with domestic cattle, and rids them of insects.
The point or extremity of anything; a pointed or somewhat sharply rounded end; the end; as, the tip of the finger; the tip of a spear.

senses.d: An end piece or part; a piece, as a cap, nozzle, ferrule, or point, applied to the extreme end of anything; as, a tip for an umbrella, a shoe, a gas burner, etc.
A piece of stiffened lining pasted on the inside of a hat crown.
A thin, boarded brush made of camel's hair, used by gilders in lifting gold leaf.
Rubbish thrown from a quarry.

Tip.etym: [Akin to D. & Dan. tip, LG. & Sw. tipp, G. zipfel, and probably to E. tap a plug, a pipe.]

senses.d: To form a point upon; to cover the tip, top, or end of; as, to tip anything with gold or silver.
q: With truncheon tipped with iron head.
Tipped with jet, Fair ermines spotless as the snows they press.

senses.d: To strike slightly; to tap.

senses.d: To bestow a gift, or douceur, upon; to give a present to; as, to tip a servant.
To lower one end of, or to throw upon the end; to tilt; as, to tip a cask; to tip a cart.

Tip.etym: [Cf. LG. tippen to tap, Sw. tippa, and E. tap to strike gently.]

senses.d: To fall on, or incline to, one side.
A light touch or blow; a tap.
A gift; a douceur; a fee.
A hint, or secret intimation, as to the chances in a horse race, or the like.

Tip.etym: [See Tip to strike slightly, and cf. Tap a slight blow.]

senses.d: A tier, row, or rank. See Tier.
q: In posture to displode their second tire Of thunder.

senses.d: Attire; apparel.
A covering for the head; a headdress.

senses.d: A child's apron, covering the breast and having no sleeves; a pinafore; a tier.
Furniture; apparatus; equipment.
A hoop or band, as of metal, on the circumference of the wheel of a vehicle, to impart strength and receive the wear.

Tire.etym: [Aphetic form of attire; OE. tir, a tir. See Attire.]

senses.d: To adorn; to attire; to dress.
q: painted her face, and tired her head.

senses.d: To seize, pull, and tear prey, as a hawk does.
q: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast, Tires with her beak on feathers, flesh, and bone.
Ye dregs of baseness, vultures among men, That tire upon the hearts of generous spirits.

senses.d: To seize, rend, or tear something as prey; to be fixed upon, or engaged with, anything.
q: Thus made she her remove, And left wrath tiring on her son.
Upon that were my thoughts tiring.

Tire.etym: [F. tirer to draw or pull; of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. tear to rend. See Tirade.]

senses.d: To become weary; to be fatigued; to have the strength fail; to have the patience exhausted; as, a feeble person soon tires.

Tire.etym: [OE. teorien to become weary, to fail, AS. teorian to be tired, be weary, to tire, exhaust; perhaps akin to E. tear to rend, the intermediate sense being, perhaps, to wear out; or cf. E. tarry.]

senses.d: To exhaust the strength of, as by toil or labor; to exhaust the patience of; to wear out (one's interest, attention, or the like); to weary; to fatigue; to jade.
q: Tired with toil, all hopes of safety past.

Tire.syn: To jade; weary; exhaust; harass. See Jade.

senses.d: Weary; fatigued; exhausted.
Tight; nimble.
q: Of a good stirring strain too, she goes tith.

senses.d: A tenth; the tenth part of anything; specifically, the tenthpart of the increase arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support, as in England, or devoted to religious or charitable uses. Almost all the tithes of England and Wales are commuted by law into rent charges.
q: The tithes of the corn, the new wine, and the oil.

senses.d: Hence, a small part or proportion.

Tithe.etym: [OE. tithe, tethe, properly an adj., tenth, AS. teó�a the tenth; akin to tién, t�n, tēn, ten, G. zehnte, adj., tenth, n., a tithe, Icel. tīund the tenth; tithe, Goth. taíhunda tenth. See Ten, and cf. Tenth, Teind.]

senses.d: Tenth.
q: Every tithe soul, 'mongst many thousand.

senses.d: To levy a tenth part on; to tax to the amount of a tenth; to pay tithes on.

senses.d: Tp pay tithes.
The act of levying or taking tithes; that which is taken as tithe; a tithe.
q: To take tithing of their blood and sweat.

senses.d: A number or company of ten householders who, dwelling near each other, were sureties or frankpledges to the king for the good behavior of each other; a decennary.
An inscription put over or upon anything as a name by which it is known.
The inscription in the beginning of a book, usually containing the subject of the work, the author's and publisher's names, the date, etc.
The panel for the name, between the bands of the back of a book.
A section or division of a subject, as of a law, a book, specif. (Roman & Canon Laws), a chapter or division of a law book.
An appellation of dignity, distinction, or preëminence (hereditary or acquired), given to persons, as duke marquis, honorable, esquire, etc.
q: With his former title greet Macbeth.

senses.d: A name; an appellation; a designation.
That which constitutes a just cause of exclusive possession; that which is the foundation of ownership of property, real or personal; a right; as, a good title to an estate, or an imperfect title.
A church to which a priest was ordained, and where he was to reside.

Title.syn: Epithet; name; appellation; denomination. See epithet, and Name.
Title.etym: [OF. title, F. titre, L. titulus an inscription, label, title, sign, token. Cf. Tilde, Titrate, Titular.]

senses.d: To call by a title; to name; to entitle.
q: Hadrian, having quieted the island, took it for honor to be titled on his coin, “The Restorer of Britain.”

Title.etym: [Cf. L. titulare, F. titrer. See Title, n.]

senses.d: A particle; a minute part; a jot; an iota.
q: It is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail.
Every tittle of this prophecy is most exactly verified.

Tittle.etym: [OE. titel, titil, apparently a dim. of tit, in the sense of small; cf. G. tüttel a tittle, dim. of OHG. tutta teat. Perhaps, however, the same word as title, n.]

senses.d: The preposition to primarily indicates approach and arrival, motion made in the direction of a place or thing and attaining it, access; and also, motion or tendency without arrival; movement toward; — opposed to from.
q: Stay with us, go not to Wittenberg.
So to the sylvan lodge They came, that like Pomona's arbor smiled.
I'll to him again, . . . He'll tell me all his purpose. She stretched her arms to heaven.

senses.d: Hence, it indicates motion, course, or tendency toward a time, a state or condition, an aim, or anything capable of being regarded as a limit to a tendency, movement, or action; as, he is going to a trade; he is rising to wealth and honor.

In a very general way, and with innumerable varieties of application, to connects transitive verbs with their remoter or indirect object, and adjectives, nouns, and neuter or passive verbs with a following noun which limits their action. Its sphere verges upon that of for, but it contains less the idea of design or appropriation; as, these remarks were addressed to a large audience; let us keep this seat to ourselves; a substance sweet to the taste; an event painful to the mind; duty to God and to our parents; a dislike to spirituous liquor.
q: Marks and points out each man of us to slaughter.
Whilst they, distilled Almost to jelly with the act of fear, Stand dumb and speak not to him.

Add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; and to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; and to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.
I have a king's oath to the contrary.
Numbers were crowded to death.
Fate and the dooming gods are deaf to tears.
Go, buckle to the law.

senses.d: As sign of the infinitive, to had originally the use of last defined, governing the infinitive as a verbal noun, and connecting it as indirect object with a preceding verb or adjective; thus, ready to go, i.e., ready unto going; good to eat, i.e., good for eating; I do my utmost to lead my life pleasantly. But it has come to be the almost constant prefix to the infinitive, even in situations where it has no prepositional meaning, as where the infinitive is direct object or subject; thus, I love to learn, i.e., I love learning; to die for one's country is noble, i.e., the dying for one's country. Where the infinitive denotes the design or purpose, good usage formerly allowed the prefixing of for to the to; as, what went ye out for see? (Matt. xi. 8).
q: Then longen folk to go on pilgrimages, And palmers for to seeken strange stranders.

senses.d: In many phrases, and in connection with many other words, to has a pregnant meaning, or is used elliptically.

Few of the Esquimaux can count to ten.

senses.d: Effect; end; consequence; as, the prince was flattered to his ruin; he engaged in a war to his cost; violent factions exist to the prejudice of the state.
Apposition; connection; antithesis; opposition; as, they engaged hand to hand.
q: Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.

senses.d: Accord; adaptation; as, an occupation to his taste; she has a husband to her mind.
q: He to God's image, she to his was made.

senses.d: Comparison; as, three is to nine as nine is to twenty-seven; it is ten to one that you will offend him.
q: All that they did was piety to this.

senses.d: Addition; union; accumulation.
q: Wisdom he has, and to his wisdom, courage.

senses.d: Accompaniment; as, she sang to his guitar; they danced to the music of a piano.
q: Anon they move In perfect phalanx to the Dorian mood Of flutes and soft recorders.

senses.d: Character; condition of being; purpose subserved or office filled.
q: Made his masters and others . . . to consider him to a little wonder.

To.etym: [AS. tō; akin to OS. & OFries. tō, D. toe, G. zu, OHG. zuo, zua, zō, Russ. do, Ir. & Gael. do, OL. -do, -du, as in endo, indu, in, Gr. �, as in � homeward. √200. Cf. Too, Tatoo a beat of drums.]

The fore part of the hoof or foot of an animal.
Anything, or any part, corresponding to the toe of the foot; as, the toe of a boot; the toe of a skate.
The journal, or pivot, at the lower end of a revolving shaft or spindle, which rests in a step.

Toe.etym: [OE. too, taa, AS. tā; akin to D. teen, G. zehe, OHG. zēha, Icel. tā, Sw. tå, Dan. taa; of uncertain origin. √60.]

In company or association with respect to place or time; as, to live together in one house; to live together in the same age; they walked together to the town.

senses.d: In concert; with mutual coöperation; as, the allies made war upon France together.

To labor; to work; — often with out.

toiled out my uncouth passage.

A weight of British India. The standard tola is equal to 180 grains.
Capable of being borne or endured; supportable, either physically or mentally.

senses.d: Moderately good or agreeable; not contemptible; not very excellent or pleasing, but such as can be borne or received without disgust, resentment, or opposition; passable; as, a tolerable administration; a tolerable entertainment; a tolerable translation.

A liberty to buy and sell within the bounds of a manor.
A portion of grain taken by a miller as a compensation for grinding.

Toll.etym: [OE. tol, AS. toll; akin to OS. & D. tol, G. zoll, OHG. zol, Icel. tollr, Sw. tull, Dan. told, and also to E. tale; — originally, that which is counted out in payment. See Tale number.]

To take toll; to raise a tax.

A pit in which the dead body of a human being is deposited; a grave; a sepulcher.

A monument erected to inclose the body and preserve the name and memory of the dead.

senses.d: Tongue.
In China, an association, secret society, or organization of any kind; in the United States, usually, a secret association of Chinese such as that of the highbinders.

Over; more than enough; — noting excess; as, a thing is too long, too short, or too wide; too high; too many; too much.

A stroke on the top of the ball.
A forward spin given to the ball by hitting it on or near the top.
To cover with another dye; as, to top aniline black with methyl violet to prevent greening and crocking.
To put a stiffening piece or back on (a saw blade).
To arrange, as fruit, with the best on top.
To strike the top of, as a wall, with the hind feet, in jumping, so as to gain new impetus; — said of a horse.
To improve (domestic animals, esp. sheep) by crossing certain individuals or breeds with other superior.
To raise one end of, as a yard, so that that end becomes higher than the other.
To cut, break, or otherwise take off the top of (a steel ingot) to remove unsound metal.
To strike (the ball) above the center; also, to make (as a stroke) by hitting the ball in this way.
To strike a ball above the center.
To rise at one end, as a yard; — usually with up.

A mineral occurring in rhombic prisms, generally yellowish and pellucid, also colorless, and of greenesh, bluish, or brownish shades. It sometimes occurs massive and opaque. It is a fluosilicate of alumina, and is used as a gem.
Either one of two species of large, brilliantly colored humming birds of the Topaza, of South America and the West Indies.

Topaz.etym: [OE. topas, F. topaze, L. topazos, or topazion, a kind of precious stone, Gr. τόπαζοσ, τοπάζιον; possibly akin to Skr. tap to glow (cf. Tepid). According to some, the name is from Topazos, a small island in the Red Sea, where the Romans obtained a stone which they called by this name, but which is t

senses.d: kind of sandstone.

Toph.etym: [L. tophus, tofus, tufa, or tuft. Cf. Tufa, Tofus, Tophus.]

senses.d: A place lying east or southeast of Jerusalem, in the valley of Hinnom.
q: And he defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom.
The pleasant valley of Hinnom, Tophet thence And black Gehenna called, the type of hell.

Tophet.etym: [Heb. tōphet, literally, a place to be spit upon, an abominable place, fr. tūph to spit out.]

senses.d: A light or luminary formed of some combustible substance, as of resinous wood; a large candle or flambeau, or a lamp giving a large, flaring flame.
q: They light the nuptial torch.

Torch.etym: [OE. torche, F. torche a torch, rag, wisp, pad; probably from a derivative of L. torquere, tortum, to twist, because twisted like a rope; cf. F. torcher to rub, wipe, It. topcia a torch, torciare to wrap, twist, OF. torse a torse. Cf. Torture.]

senses.d: An engine for casting stones.
Extreme pain; anguish; torture; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind.
q: The more I see Pleasures about me, so much more I feel Torment within me.

senses.d: That which gives pain, vexation, or misery.
q: They brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments.

Torment.etym: [OF. torment, F. tourment, fr. L. tormentum an engine for hurling missiles, an instrument of torture, a rack, torture, fr. torquere to turn, to twist, hurl. See Turture.]

senses.d: To put to extreme pain or anguish; to inflict excruciating misery upon, either of body or mind; to torture.
To pain; to distress; to afflict.
q: Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented.

senses.d: To tease; to vex; to harass; as, to be tormented with importunities, or with petty annoyances.
To put into great agitation.
One who, or that which, torments; one who inflicts penal anguish or tortures.
q: Thoughts, my tormentors, armed with deadly stings.

senses.d: An implement for reducing a stiff soil, resembling a harrow, but running upon wheels.
Any one of numerous species of reptiles of the order Testudinata.
Same as Testudo, 2.

Tortoise.etym: [OE. tortuce, fr. OF. tortis crooked, fr. L. tortus isted, crooked, contorted, p. p. of torquere, tortum, to wind; cf. F. tortue tortoise, LL. tortuca, tartuca, Pr. tortesa crookedness, tortis crooked. so called in allusion to its crooked feet. See Torture.]

senses.d: Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; pang; agony; torment; as, torture of mind.
q: Ghastly spasm or racking torture.

senses.d: Especially, severe pain inflicted judicially, either as punishment for a crime, or for the purpose of extorting a confession from an accused person, as by water or fire, by the boot or thumbkin, or by the rack or wheel.
The act or process of torturing.
q: Torture, whitch had always been deciared illegal, and which had recently been declared illegal even by the servile judges of that age, was inflicted for the last time in England in the month of May, 1640.

Torture.etym: [F.,fr.L. tortura, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist, rack, torture; probably akin to Gr. τρέπειν to turn, G. drechsein to turn on a lathe, and perhaps to E. queer. Cf. Contort, Distort, Extort, Retort, Tart, n., Torch, Torment, Tortion, Tort, Trope.]

senses.d: To put to torture; to pain extremely; to harass; to vex.
To punish with torture; to put to the rack; as, to torture an accused person.
To wrest from the proper meaning; to distort.
To keep on the stretch, as a bow.
q: The bow tortureth the string.

senses.d: To throw with the hand; especially, to throw with the palm of the hand upward, or to throw upward; as, to toss a ball.
To lift or throw up with a sudden or violent motion; as, to toss the head.
q: He tossed his arm aloft, and proudly told me, He would not stay.

senses.d: To cause to rise and fall; as, a ship tossed on the waves in a storm.
q: We being exceedingly tossed with a tempeat.

senses.d: To agitate; to make restless.
q: Calm region once, And full of peace, now tossed and turbulent.

senses.d: Hence, to try; to harass.
q: Whom devils fly, thus is he tossed of men.

senses.d: To keep in play; to tumble over; as, to spend four years in tossing the rules of grammar.

Toss.etym: [ W. tosiaw, tosio, to jerk, toss, snatch, tosa quick jerk, a toss, a snatch. ]

senses.d: To roll and tumble; to be in violent commotion; to write; to fling.
q: To toss and fling, and to be restless, only frets and enreges our pain.

senses.d: To be tossed, as a fleet on the ocean.
A throwing upward, or with a jerk; the act of tossing; as, the toss of a ball.
A throwing up of the head; a particular manner of raising the head with a jerk.
The act of throwing upward; a rising and falling suddenly; a rolling and tumbling.
A process which consists in washing ores by violent agitation in water, in order to separate the lighter or earhy particles; — called also tozing, and treloobing, in Cornwall.
To shake so as to threaten a fall; to vacillate; to be unsteady; to stagger; as,an old man totters with age.
To shake; to reel; to lean; to waver.
q: Troy nods from high, and totters to her fall.

Totter.etym: [Probably for older tolter; cf. AS. tealtrian to totter, vacillate. Cf.Tilt to incline, Toddle, Tottle, Totty.]

senses.d: To come in contact with; to hit or strike lightly against; to extend the hand, foot, or the like, so as to reach or rest on.
q: Him thus intent Ithuriel with his spear Touched lightly.

senses.d: To perceive by the sense of feeling.
q: Nothing but body can be touched or touch.

senses.d: To come to; to reach; to attain to.
q: The god, vindictive, doomed them never more- Ah, men unblessed! — to touch their natal shore.

senses.d: To try; to prove, as with a touchstone.
q: Wherein I mean to touch your love indeed.

senses.d: To relate to; to concern; to affect.
q: The quarrel toucheth none but us alone.

senses.d: To handle, speak of, or deal with; to treat of.
q: Storial thing that toucheth gentilesse.

senses.d: To meddle or interfere with; as, I have not touched the books.
To affect the senses or the sensibility of; to move; to melt; to soften.
q: What of sweet before Hath touched my sense, flat seems to this and harsh.
The tender sire was touched with what he said.

senses.d: To mark or delineate with touches; to add a slight stroke to with the pencil or brush.
q: The lines, though touched but faintly, are drawn right.

senses.d: To infect; to affect slightly.
To make an impression on; to have effect upon.
q: Its face . . . so hard that a file will not touch it.

senses.d: To strike; to manipulate; to play on; as, to touch an instrument of music.
q: touched their golden harps.

Touch.etym: [F. toucher, OF. touchier, tuchier; of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. zucchen, zukken, to twitch, pluck, draw, G. zukken, zukken, v. intens. fr. OHG. ziohan to draw, G. ziehen, akin to E. tug. See Tuck, v. t., Tug, and cf. Tocsin, Toccata.]

senses.d: To be in contact; to be in a state of junction, so that no space is between; as, two spheres touch only at points.
To fasten; to take effect; to make impression.
q: Strong waters pierce metals, and will touch upon gold, that will not touch upon silver.

senses.d: To treat anything in discourse, especially in a slight or casual manner; — often with on or upon.
q: If the antiquaries have touched upon it, they immediately quitted it.

senses.d: To be brought, as a sail, so close to the wind that its weather leech shakes.
q: I made a little voyage round the lake, and touched on the several towns that lie on its coasts.

senses.d: The act of touching, or the state of being touched; contact.
q: Their touch affrights me as a serpent's sting.

senses.d: The sense by which pressure or traction exerted on the skin is recognized; the sense by which the properties of bodies are determined by contact; the tactile sense. See Tactile sense, under Tactile.
q: The spider's touch, how exquisitely fine.

senses.d: Act or power of exciting emotion.
q: Not alone The death of Fulvia, with more urgent touches, Do strongly speak to us.

senses.d: An emotion or affection.
q: A true, natural, and a sensible touch of mercy.

senses.d: Personal reference or application.
q: Speech of touch toward others should be sparingly used.

senses.d: A stroke; as, a touch of raillery; a satiric touch; hence, animadversion; censure; reproof.
q: I never bare any touch of conscience with greater regret.

senses.d: A single stroke on a drawing or a picture.
q: Never give the least touch with your pencil till you have well examined your design.

senses.d: Feature; lineament; trait.
q: Of many faces, eyes, and hearts, To have the touches dearest prized.

senses.d: The act of the hand on a musical instrument; bence, in the plural, musical notes.
q: Soft stillness and the night Become the touches of sweet harmony.

senses.d: A small quantity intermixed; a little; a dash.
q: Eyes La touch of Sir Peter Lely in them.
Madam, I have a touch of your condition.

senses.d: A hint; a suggestion; slight notice.
q: A small touch will put him in mind of them.

senses.d: A slight and brief essay.
q: Print my preface in such form as, in the booksellers' phrase, will make a sixpenny touch.

senses.d: To compare with; of be equal to; — usually with a negative; as, he held that for good cheer nothing could touch an open fire.
To induce to give or lend; to borrow from; as, to touch one for a loan; hence, to steal from.
A set of changes less than the total possible on seven bells, that is, less than 5,040.
An act of borrowing or stealing.
Tallow; — a plumber's term.
Affecting; moving; pathetic; as, a touching tale.
Concerning; with respect to.
q: Now, as touching things offered unto idols.

senses.d: The sense or act of feeling; touch.
The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel or swingle.

Tow.etym: [OE. tow, AS. tow, akin to OD. touw, Icel. � a tuft of wool for spinning; cf. E. taw, v.t.]

senses.d: To draw or pull through the water, as a vessel of any kind, by means of a rope.

Tow.etym: [OE. towen, to�en; akin to OFries. toga to pull about, OHG. zogōn, Icel. toga, AS. tohline a towline, and AS.teón to draw, p. p. getogen. See Tug]

senses.d: A rope by which anything is towed; a towline, or towrope.
The act of towing, or the state of being towed;-chiefly used in the phrase, to take in tow, that is to tow.
That which is towed, or drawn by a towline, as a barge, raft, collection of boats, ect.

Tow.etym: [Cf. Icel. taug a rope, from the same root as E. tow, v. t.]

senses.d: In the direction of; to.
q: He set his face toward the wilderness.
The waves make towards″ the pebbled shore.

senses.d: With direction to, in a moral sense; with respect or reference to; regarding; concerning.
