q: His eye shall be evil toward his brother.
Herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offense toward God, and toward men.

senses.d: Tending to; in the direction of; in behalf of.
q: This was the first alarm England received towards any trouble.

senses.d: Near; about; approaching to.
q: I am toward nine years older since I left you.

Toward.etym: [AS. � impending, imminent, future, toward, � towards. See To, and -ward, wards.]

senses.d: Near; at hand; in state of preparation.
q: Do you hear sught, sir, of a battle toward ?
We have a trifling foolish banquet Towards.

senses.d: Approaching; coming near.
Readly to do or learn; compliant with duty; not froward; apt; docile; tractable; as, a toward youth.
Ready to act; forward; bold; valiant.
q: Why, that is spoken like a toward prince.

senses.d: A cloth used for wiping, especially one used for drying anything wet, as the person after a bath.

Towel.etym: [OE. towaille, towail, F. touaille, LL. toacula, of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. dwahila, swahilla, G. zwehle, fr. OHG. dwahan to wash; akin to D. dwaal a towel, AS. þweán to wash, OS. thwahan, Icel. þvā, Sw. två, Dan. toe, Goth. þwahan. Cf. Doily.]

senses.d: To beat with a stick.
A mass of building standing alone and insulated, usually higher than its diameter, but when of great size not always of that proportion.
A citadel; a fortress; hence, a defense.
q: Thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy.

senses.d: A headdress of a high or towerlike form, fashionable about the end of the seventeenth century and until 1715; also, any high headdress.
q: Lay trains of amorous intrigues In towers, and curls, and periwigs.

senses.d: High flight; elevation.

Tower.etym: [OE. tour,tor,tur, F. tour, L. turris; akin to Gr. �; cf. W. twr a tower, Ir. tor a castle, Gael. torr a tower, castle. Cf. Tor, Turret.]

senses.d: To rise and overtop other objects; to be lofty or very high; hence, to soar.
q: On the other side an high rock towered still.
My lord protector's hawks do tower so well.

senses.d: To soar into.

Formerly: (a) An inclosure which surrounded the mere homestead or dwelling of the lord of the manor. (b) The whole of the land which constituted the domain. (c) A collection of houses inclosed by fences or walls.
Any number or collection of houses to which belongs a regular market, and which is not a city or the see of a bishop.

Any collection of houses larger than a village, and not incorporated as a city; also, loosely, any large, closely populated place, whether incorporated or not, in distinction from the country, or from rural communities.
q: God made the country, and man made the town.

senses.d: The body of inhabitants resident in a town; as, the town voted to send two representatives to the legislature; the town voted to lay a tax for repairing the highways.
A township; the whole territory within certain limits, less than those of a country.
The court end of London;-commonly with the.
The metropolis or its inhabitants; as, in winter the gentleman lives in town; in summer, in the country.
q: Always hankering after the diversions of the town.
Stunned with his giddy larum half the town.

senses.d: A farm or farmstead; also, a court or farmyard.

Town.etym: [OE. toun, tun, AS. tun inclosure, fence, village, town; akin to D. tuin a garden, G. zaun a hadge, fence, OHG. zun, Icel. tun an inclosure, homestead, house, Ir. & Gael. dun a fortress, W. din. Cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune, tine to inclose.]

senses.d: A track; a trail; a way; a path; also, passage; travel; resort.
q: A postern with a blind wicket there was, A common trade to pass through Priam's house.
Hath tracted forth some salvage beastes trade.
Or, I'll be buried in the king's highway, Some way of common trade, where subjects' feet May hourly trample on their sovereign's head.

senses.d: Course; custom; practice; occupation; employment.
q: There those five sisters had continual trade.
Long did I love this lady, Long was my travel, long my trade to win her.
Thy sin's not accidental but a trade.

senses.d: Business of any kind; matter of mutual consideration; affair; dealing.
q: Have you any further trade with us?

senses.d: Specifically: The act or business of exchanging commodities by barter, or by buying and selling for money; commerce; traffic; barter.

The business which a person has learned, and which he engages in, for procuring subsistence, or for profit; occupation; especially, mechanical employment as distinguished from the liberal arts, the learned professions, and agriculture; as, we speak of the trade of a smith, of a carpenter, or mason, but not now of the trade of a farmer, or a lawyer, or a physician.
q: Accursed usury was all his trade.
The homely, slighted, shepherd's trade.
I will instruct thee in my trade.

senses.d: Instruments of any occupation.
q: The house and household goods, his trade of war.

senses.d: A company of men engaged in the same occupation; thus, booksellers and publishers speak of the customs of the trade, and are collectively designated as the trade.
The trade winds.
Refuse or rubbish from a mine.

Trade.syn: Profession; occupation; office; calling; avocation; employment; commerce; dealing; traffic.
Trade.etym: [Formerly, a path, OE. tred a footmark. See Tread, n. & v.]

senses.d: To barter, or to buy and sell; to be engaged in the exchange, purchase, or sale of goods, wares, merchandise, or anything else; to traffic; to bargain; to carry on commerce as a business.
q: A free port, where nations . . . resorted with their goods and traded.

senses.d: To buy and sell or exchange property in a single instance.
To have dealings; to be concerned or associated; — usually followed by with.
q: How did you dare to trade and traffic with Macbeth?

senses.d: To sell or exchange in commerce; to barter.
q: They traded the persons of men.
To dicker and to swop, to trade rifles and watches.

senses.d: Professional; practiced.
Carrying on trade or commerce; engaged in trade; as, a trading company.
Frequented by traders.
Venal; corrupt; jobbing; as, a trading politician.
The act of delivering into the hands of another; delivery.

The unwritten or oral delivery of information, opinions, doctrines, practices, rites, and customs, from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; the transmission of any knowledge, opinions, or practice, from forefathers to descendants by oral communication, without written memorials.
Hence, that which is transmitted orally from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; knowledge or belief transmitted without the aid of written memorials; custom or practice long observed.
q: Will you mock at an ancient tradition begun upon an honorable respect?
Naught but tradition remains of the beautiful village of Grand-Pré.

senses.d: An unwritten code of law represented to have been given by God to Moses on Sinai.
q: Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered.

senses.d: That body of doctrine and discipline, or any article thereof, supposed to have been put forth by Christ or his apostles, and not committed to writing.
q: Stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word or our epistle.

Tradition.etym: [OE. tradicioun, L. traditio, from tradere to give up, transmit. See Treason, Traitor.]

senses.d: To transmit by way of tradition; to hand down.
q: The following story is . . . traditioned with very much credit amongst our English Catholics.

senses.d: One who traffics, or carries on commerce; a trader; a merchant.
To draw along; to trail; to drag.
q: In hollow cube Training his devilish enginery.

senses.d: To draw by persuasion, artifice, or the like; to attract by stratagem; to entice; to allure.
q: If but a dozen French Were there in arms, they would be as a call To train ten thousand English to their side.
O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note.
This feast, I'll gage my life, Is but a plot to train you to your ruin.

senses.d: To teach and form by practice; to educate; to exercise; to discipline; as, to train the militia to the manual exercise; to train soldiers to the use of arms.
q: Our trained bands, which are the trustiest and most proper strength of a free nation.
The warrior horse here bred he's taught to train.

senses.d: To break, tame, and accustom to draw, as oxen.
To lead or direct, and form to a wall or espalier; to form to a proper shape, by bending, lopping, or pruning; as, to train young trees.
q: He trained the young branches to the right hand or to the left.

senses.d: To trace, as a lode or any mineral appearance, to its head.
q: Train up a child in the way he should go; and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
The first Christians were, by great hardships, trained up for glory.

Train.etym: [OF. trahiner, traïner,F. traîner, LL. trahinare, trainare, fr. L. trahere to draw. See Trail.]

senses.d: To be drilled in military exercises; to do duty in a military company.
To prepare by exercise, diet, instruction, etc., for any physical contest; as, to train for a boat race.
That which draws along; especially, persuasion, artifice, or enticement; allurement.
Hence, something tied to a lure to entice a hawk; also, a trap for an animal; a snare.
q: With cunning trains him to entrap un wares.

senses.d: That which is drawn along in the rear of, or after, something; that which is in the hinder part or rear.
That part of a gown which trails behind the wearer.
The after part of a gun carriage; the trail.
The tail of a bird.
A number of followers; a body of attendants; a retinue; a suite.
q: The king's daughter with a lovely train.
My train are men of choice and rarest parts.

senses.d: A consecution or succession of connected things; a series.
q: The train of ills our love would draw behind it.
Rivers now Stream and perpetual draw their humid train.
Other truths require a train of ideas placed in order.

senses.d: Regular method; process; course; order; as, things now in a train for settlement.
q: If things were once in this train, . . . our duty would take root in our nature.

senses.d: The number of beats of a watch in any certain time.
A line of gunpowder laid to lead fire to a charge, mine, or the like.
A connected line of cars or carriages on a railroad.

Train.etym: [F. train, OF. traïn, trahin; cf. (for some of the senses) F. traine. See Train, v.]

senses.d: A heavy long sleigh used in Canada for the transportation of merchandise, wood, and the like.
The aggregation of men, animals, and vehicles which accompany an army or one of its subdivisions, and transport its baggage, ammunition, supplies, and reserve materials of all kinds.

One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one guilty of treason; one who, in breach of trust, delivers his country to an enemy, or yields up any fort or place intrusted to his defense, or surrenders an army or body of troops to the enemy, unless when vanquished; also, one who takes arms and levies war against his country; or one who aids an enemy in conquering his country. See Treason.
q: O passing traitor, perjured and unjust!

senses.d: Hence, one who betrays any confidence or trust; a betrayer.

Traitor.etym: [OE. traitour, OF. traïtor, traïteur, F. treître, L. traditor, fr. tradere, traditum, to deliver, to give up or surrender treacherously, to betray; trans across, over + dare to give. See Date time, and cf. Betray,Tradition, Traditor, Treason.]

senses.d: Traitorous.
To act the traitor toward; to betray; to deceive.
To tread under foot; to tread down; to prostrate by treading; as, to trample grass or flowers.
q: Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet.

senses.d: Fig.: To treat with contempt and insult.

Trample.etym: [OE. trampelen, freq. of trampen. See Tramp, v. t.]

senses.d: To tread with force and rapidity; to stamp.
To tread in contempt; — with on or upon.
q: Diogenes trampled on Plato's pride with greater of his own.

senses.d: The act of treading under foot; also, the sound produced by trampling.
q: The huddling trample of a drove of sheep.

senses.d: A tedious journey.
A state in which the soul seems to have passed out of the body into another state of being, or to be rapt into visions; an ecstasy.
q: And he became very hungry, and would have eaten; but while they made ready, he fell into a trance.
My soul was ravished quite as in a trance.

senses.d: A condition, often simulating death, in which there is a total suspension of the power of voluntary movement, with abolition of all evidences of mental activity and the reduction to a minimum of all the vital functions so that the patient lies still and apparently unconscious of surrounding objects, while the pulsation of the heart and the breathing, although still present, are almost or altogether imperceptible.
q: He fell down in a trance.

Trance.etym: [F. transe fright, in OF. also, trance or swoon, fr. transir to chill, benumb, to be chilled, to shiver, OF. also, to die, L. transire to pass over, go over, pass away, cease; trans across, over + ire to go; cf. L. transitus a passing over. See Issue, and cf. Transit.]

senses.d: To entrance.
q: And three I left him tranced.

senses.d: To pass over or across; to traverse.
q: Trance the world over.
When thickest dark did trance the sky.

senses.d: To pass; to travel.
The quality or state of being tranquil; calmness; composure.
To convey from one place or person another; to transport, remove, or cause to pass, to another place or person; as, to transfer the laws of one country to another; to transfer suspicion.
To make over the possession or control of; to pass; to convey, as a right, from one person to another; to give; as, the title to land is transferred by deed.
To remove from one substance or surface to another; as, to transfer drawings or engravings to a lithographic stone.

Transfer.syn: To sell; give; alienate; estrange; sequester.
Transfer.etym: [L. transferre; trans across, over + ferre to bear: cf. F. transférer. See Bear to carry.]

senses.d: The act of transferring, or the state of being transferred; the removal or conveyance of a thing from one place or person to another.
The conveyance of right, title, or property, either real or personal, from one person to another, whether by sale, by gift, or otherwise.
q: I shall here only consider it as a transfer of property.

senses.d: That which is transferred.
A picture, or the like, removed from one body or ground to another, as from wood to canvas, or from one piece of canvas to another.
A drawing or writing printed off from one surface on another, as in ceramics and in many decorative arts.
A soldier removed from one troop, or body of troops, and placed in another.
A pathological process by virtue of which a unilateral morbid condition on being abolished on one side of the body makes its appearance in the corresponding region upon the other side.
To change the outward form or appearance of; to metamorphose; to transform.
Especially, to change to something exalted and glorious; to give an ideal form to.
q: was transfigured before them; and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.

Transfigure.etym: [F. transfigurer, L. transfigurare, transfiguratum; trans across, over + figurare to form, shape. See Figure, v. t.]

senses.d: To change the form of; to change in shape or appearance; to metamorphose; as, a caterpillar is ultimately transformed into a butterfly.
q: Love may transform me to an oyster.

senses.d: To change into another substance; to transmute; as, the alchemists sought to transform lead into gold.
To change in nature, disposition, heart, character, or the like; to convert.
q: Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.

senses.d: To change, as an algebraic expression or geometrical figure, into another from without altering its value.

Transform.etym: [L. transformare, transformatum; trans across, over + formare to from: cf. F. transformer. See Form, v. t.]

senses.d: To be changed in form; to be metamorphosed.
q: His hair transforms to down.

senses.d: To pass over or beyond; to surpass.
q: Surpassing common faith, transgressing nature's law.

senses.d: Hence, to overpass, as any prescribed as the �imit of duty; to break or violate, as a law, civil or moral.
q: For man will hearken to his glozing lies, And easily transgress the sole command.

senses.d: To offend against; to vex.
q: Why give you peace to this imperate beast That hath so long transgressed you ?

senses.d: To offend against the law; to sin.
q: Who transgressed in the thing accursed.

senses.d: The act of transgressing, or of passing over or beyond any law, civil or moral; the violation of a law or known principle of rectitude; breach of command; fault; offense; crime; sin.
q: Forgive thy people . . . all their transgressions wherein they have transgressed against thee.
What rests, but that the mortal sentence pass On his transgression, death denounced that day ?
The transgression is in the stealer.

Transgression.syn: Fault; offense; crime; infringement; misdemeanor; misdeed; affront; sin.
Transgression.etym: [L. transgressio a going across, going over, transgression of the law, from transgredi, transgressus, to step across, go over; trans over, across + gradi to step, walk: cf. F. transgression. See Grade.]

senses.d: One who transgresses; one who breaks a law, or violates a command; one who violates any known rule or principle of rectitude; a sinner.
q: The way of transgressors is hard.

senses.d: To bear, carry, or remove, from one place to another; to transfer; as, to translate a tree.
q: In the chapel of St. Catharine of Sienna, they show her head- the rest of her body being translated to Rome.

senses.d: To change to another condition, position, place, or office; to transfer; hence, to remove as by death.
To remove to heaven without a natural death.
q: By faith Enoch was translated, that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translatedhim.

senses.d: To remove, as a bishop, from one see to another.
To render into another language; to express the sense of in the words of another language; to interpret; hence, to explain or recapitulate in other words.
q: Translating into his own clear, pure, and flowing language, what he found in books well known to the world, but too bulky or too dry for boys and girls.

senses.d: To change into another form; to transform.
q: Happy is your grace, That can translatethe stubbornness of fortune Into so quiet and so sweet a style.

senses.d: To cause to remove from one part of the body to another; as, to translate a disease.
To cause to lose senses or recollection; to entrance.

Translate.etym: [f. translatus, used as p. p. of transferre to transfer, but from a different root. See Trans-, and Tolerate, and cf. Translation.]

senses.d: To make a translation; to be engaged in translation.
The act of translating, removing, or transferring; removal; also, the state of being translated or removed; as, the translation of Enoch; the translation of a bishop.
The act of rendering into another language; interpretation; as, the translation of idioms is difficult.
That which is obtained by translating something a version; as, a translation of the Scriptures.
A transfer of meaning in a word or phrase, a metaphor; a tralation.
Transfer of meaning by association; association of ideas.
Motion in which all the points of the moving body have at any instant the same velocity and direction of motion; — opposed to rotation.

Translation.etym: [F. translation, L. translatio a transferring, translation, version. See Translate, and cf. Tralation.]

senses.d: Having the property of transmitting rays of light, so that bodies can be distinctly seen through; pervious to light; diaphanous; pellucid; as, transparent glass; a transparent diamond; — opposed to opaque.
Admitting the passage of light; open; porous; as, a transparent veil.

Transparent.syn: Translucent; pellucid; clear; bright; limpid; lucid; diaphanous. See Translucent.
Transparent.etym: [F., from LL. transparens, -entis, p. pr. of transparere to be transparent; L. trans across, through + parere to appear. See Appear.]

senses.d: To dress with ornaments; to adorn; — said especially of horses.
q: Steeds . . . that trapped were in steel all glittering.
To deck his hearse, and trap his tomb-black steed.
There she found her palfrey trapped In purple blazoned with armorial gold.

Trap.etym: [Akin to OE. trappe trappings, and perhaps from an Old French word of the same origin as E. drab a kind of cloth.]

senses.d: An old term rather loosely used to designate various dark-colored, heavy igneous rocks, including especially the feldspathic-augitic rocks, basalt, dolerite, amygdaloid, etc., but including also some kinds of diorite. Called also trap rock.

Trap.etym: [Sw. trapp; akin to trappa stairs, Dan. trappe, G. treppe, D. trap; — so called because the rocks of this class often occur in large, tabular masses, rising above one another, like steps. See Tramp.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to trap rock; as, a trap dike.
A machine or contrivance that shuts suddenly, as with a spring, used for taking game or other animals; as, a trap for foxes.
q: She would weep if that she saw a mouse Caught in a trap.

senses.d: Fig.: A snare; an ambush; a stratagem; any device by which one may be caught unawares.
q: Let their table be made a snare and a trap.
God and your majesty Protect mine innocence, or I fall into The trap is laid for me!

senses.d: A wooden instrument shaped somewhat like a shoe, used in the game of trapball. It consists of a pivoted arm on one end of which is placed the ball to be thrown into the air by striking the other end. Also, a machine for throwing into the air glass balls, clay pigeons, etc., to be shot at.
The game of trapball.
A bend, sag, or partitioned chamber, in a drain, soil pipe, sewer, etc., arranged so that the liquid contents form a seal which prevents passage of air or gas, but permits the flow of liquids.
A place in a water pipe, pump, etc., where air accumulates for want of an outlet.
A wagon, or other vehicle.
A kind of movable stepladder.

Trap.etym: [OE. trappe, AS. treppe; akin to OD. trappe, OHG. trapo; probably fr. the root of E. tramp, as that which is trod upon: cf. F. trappe, which is trod upon: cf. F. trappe, which perhaps influenced the English word.]

senses.d: To catch in a trap or traps; as, to trap foxes.
Fig.: To insnare; to take by stratagem; to entrap.
To provide with a trap; as, to trap a drain; to trap a sewer pipe. See 4th Trap, 5.
To set traps for game; to make a business of trapping game; as, to trap for beaver.
Small or portable articles for dress, furniture, or use; goods; luggage; things.
Labor with pain; severe toil or exertion.
q: As everything of price, so this doth require travail.

senses.d: Parturition; labor; as, an easy travail.

Travail.etym: [F. travail; cf. Pr. trabalh, trebalh, toil, torment, torture; probably from LL. trepalium a place where criminals are tortured, instrument of torture. But the French word may be akin to L. trabs a beam, or have been influenced by a derivative from trabs (cf. Trave). Cf. Travel.]

senses.d: To labor with pain; to toil.
To suffer the pangs of childbirth; to be in labor.

Travail.etym: [F. travailler, OF. traveillier, travaillier, to labor, toil, torment; cf. Pr. trebalhar to torment, agitate. See Travail, n.]

senses.d: To harass; to tire.
q: As if all these troubles had not been sufficient to travail the realm, a great division fell among the nobility.

senses.d: Same as Travois.

Travail.etym: [Cf. F. travail, a frame for confining a horse, or OF. travail beam, and E. trave, n. Cf. Travail, v. i.]

senses.d: To labor; to travail.
To go or march on foot; to walk; as, to travel over the city, or through the streets.
To pass by riding, or in any manner, to a distant place, or to many places; to journey; as, a man travels for his health; he is traveling in California.
To pass; to go; to move.
q: Time travels in divers paces with divers persons.

Travel.etym: [Properly, to labor, and the same word as travail.]

senses.d: To journey over; to traverse; as, to travel the continent.
To force to journey.
q: They shall not be traveled forth of their own franchises.

senses.d: The act of traveling, or journeying from place to place; a journey.
q: With long travel I am stiff and weary.
His travels ended at his country seat.

senses.d: An account, by a traveler, of occurrences and observations during a journey; as, a book of travels; — often used as the title of a book; as, Travels in Italy.
The length of stroke of a reciprocating piece; as, the travel of a slide valve.
Labor; parturition; travail.
Across; athwart.
q: The earl . . . caused . . . high trees to be hewn down, and laid travers one over another.

Travers.etym: [F. travers, breadth, extent from side, à travers, en travers, de travers, across, athwart. See Traverse, a.]

senses.d: Lying across; being in a direction across something else; as, paths cut with traverse trenches.
q: Oak . . . being strong in all positions, may be better trusted in cross and traverse work.
The ridges of the fallow field traverse.

Traverse.etym: [OF. travers, L. transversus, p. p. of transvertere to turn or direct across. See Transverse, and cf. Travers.]

senses.d: Athwart; across; crosswise.
Anything that traverses, or crosses.
Something that thwarts, crosses, or obstructs; a cross accident; as, he would have succeeded, had it not been for unlucky traverses not under his control.
A barrier, sliding door, movable screen, curtain, or the like.
q: Men drinken and the travers draw anon.
And the entrance of the king, The first traverse was drawn.

senses.d: A gallery or loft of communication from side to side of a church or other large building.
A work thrown up to intercept an enfilade, or reverse fire, along exposed passage, or line of work.

A formal denial of some matter of fact alleged by the opposite party in any stage of the pleadings. The technical words introducing a traverse are absque hoc, without this; that is, without this which follows.
The zigzag course or courses made by a ship in passing from one place to another; a compound course.
A line lying across a figure or other lines; a transversal.
A line surveyed across a plot of ground.
The turning of a gun so as to make it point in any desired direction.
A turning; a trick; a subterfuge.
To lay in a cross direction; to cross.
q: The parts should be often traversed, or crossed, by the flowing of the folds.

senses.d: To cross by way of opposition; to thwart with obstacles; to obstruct; to bring to naught.
q: I can not but . . . admit the force of this reasoning, which I yet hope to traverse.

senses.d: To wander over; to cross in traveling; as, to traverse the habitable globe.
q: What seas you traversed, and what fields you fought.

senses.d: To pass over and view; to survey carefully.
q: My purpose is to traverse the nature, principles, and properties of this detestable vice — ingratitude.

senses.d: To turn to the one side or the other, in order to point in any direction; as, to traverse a cannon.
To plane in a direction across the grain of the wood; as, to traverse a board.

To deny formally, as what the opposite party has alleged. When the plaintiff or defendant advances new matter, he avers it to be true, and traverses what the other party has affirmed. To traverse an indictment or an office is to deny it.
q: And save the expense of long litigious laws, Where suits are traversed, and so little won That he who conquers is but last undone.

senses.d: To use the posture or motions of opposition or counteraction, as in fencing.
q: To see thee fight, to see thee foin, to see thee traverse.

senses.d: To turn, as on a pivot; to move round; to swivel; as, the needle of a compass traverses; if it does not traverse well, it is an unsafe guide.
To tread or move crosswise, as a horse that throws his croup to one side and his head to the other.
Adjustable laterally; having a lateral motion, or a swinging motion; adapted for giving lateral motion.
Like a traitor; involving treachery; violating allegiance or faith pledged; traitorous to the state or sovereign; perfidious in private life; betraying a trust; faithless.
q: Loyal father of a treacherous son.
The treacherous smile, a mask for secret hate.

Treacherous.syn: Faithless; perfidious; traitorous; false; insidious; plotting.

senses.d: Violation of allegiance or of faith and confidence; treasonable or perfidious conduct; perfidy; treason.
q: Be ware, ye lords, of their treachery.
In the council chamber at Edinburgh, he had contracted a deep taint of treachery and corruption.

Treachery.etym: [OE. trecherïe, trichere, OF. trecherie, tricherie, F. tricherie trickery, from tricher to cheat, to trick, OF. trichier, trechier; probably of Teutonic origin. See Trickery, Trick.]

senses.d: To set the foot; to step.
q: Where'er you tread, the blushing flowers shall rise.
Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
The hard stone Under our feet, on which we tread and go.

senses.d: To walk or go; especially, to walk with a stately or a cautious step.
q: Ye that . . . stately tread, or lowly creep.

senses.d: To copulate; said of birds, esp. the males.
q: One woe doth tread upon another's heel.

Tread.etym: [OE. treden, AS. tredan; akin to OFries. treda, OS. tredan, D. & LG. treden, G. treten, OHG. tretan, Icel. tro�a, Sw. tråda, träda, Dan. træde, Goth. trudan, and perhaps ultimately to F. tramp; cf. Gr. � a running, Skr. dram to run. Cf. Trade, Tramp, Trot.]

senses.d: To step or walk on.
q: Forbid to tread the promised land he saw.
Methought she trod the ground with greater grace.

senses.d: To beat or press with the feet; as, to tread a path; to tread land when too light; a well-trodden path.
To go through or accomplish by walking, dancing, or the like.
q: They have measured many a mile, To tread a measure with you on this grass.

senses.d: To crush under the foot; to trample in contempt or hatred; to subdue.
q: Through thy name will we tread them under that rise up against us.

senses.d: To copulate with; to feather; to cover; — said of the male bird.
A step or stepping; pressure with the foot; a footstep; as, a nimble tread; a cautious tread.
q: She is coming, my own, my sweet; Were it ever so airy a tread, My heart would hear her and beat.

senses.d: Manner or style of stepping; action; gait; as, the horse has a good tread.
Way; track; path.
The act of copulation in birds.
The upper horizontal part of a step, on which the foot is placed.
The top of the banquette, on which soldiers stand to fire over the parapet.
The part of a wheel that bears upon the road or rail.
The chalaza of a bird's egg; the treadle.
A bruise or abrasion produced on the foot or ankle of a horse that interferes. See Interfere, 3.
One who treads.
The offense of attempting to overthrow the government of the state to which the offender owes allegiance, or of betraying the state into the hands of a foreign power; disloyalty; treachery.
q: The treason of the murthering in the bed.

senses.d: Loosely, the betrayal of any trust or confidence; treachery; perfidy.
q: If he be false, she shall his treason see.

Treason.etym: [OE. tresun, treisun, traisoun, OF. traïson, F. trahison, L. traditio a giving up, a delivering up, fr. tradere to give up, betray. See Traitor, and cf. Tradition.]

senses.d: Wealth accumulated; especially, a stock, or store of money in reserve.
q: This treasure hath fortune unto us given.

senses.d: A great quantity of anything collected for future use; abundance; plenty.
q: We have treasures in the field, of wheat and of barley, and of oil and of honey.

senses.d: That which is very much valued.
q: Ye shall be peculiar treasure unto me.
From thy wardrobe bring thy chiefest treasure.

Treasure.etym: [OE. tresor, tresour, F. trésor, L. thesaurus, Gr. � a stone laid up, treasure, probably from the root of � to put, place. See Thesis, and cf. Thesaurus.]

senses.d: To collect and deposit, as money or other valuable things, for future use; to lay up; to hoard; usually with up; as, to treasure up gold.

One who has the care of a treasure or treasure or treasury; an officer who receives the public money arising from taxes and duties, or other sources of revenue, takes charge of the same, and disburses it upon orders made by the proper authority; one who has charge of collected funds; as, the treasurer of a society or corporation.

A place or building in which stores of wealth are deposited; especially, a place where public revenues are deposited and kept, and where money is disbursed to defray the expenses of government; hence, also, the place of deposit and disbursement of any collected funds.
That department of a government which has charge of the finances.
A repository of abundance; a storehouse.
Hence, a book or work containing much valuable knowledge, wisdom, wit, or the like; a thesaurus; as, “ Maunder's Treasury of Botany.”
A treasure.
A written composition on a particular subject, in which its principles are discussed or explained; a tract.
q: He published a treatise in which he maintained that a marriage between a member of the Church of England and a dissenter was a nullity.

senses.d: Story; discourse.

Treatise.etym: [OE. tretis, OF. treitis, traitis, well made. See Treat.]

senses.d: Any perennial woody plant of considerable size (usually over twenty feet high) and growing with a single trunk.
Something constructed in the form of, or considered as resembling, a tree, consisting of a stem, or stock, and branches; as, a genealogical tree.
A piece of timber, or something commonly made of timber; — used in composition, as in axletree, boottree, chesstree, crosstree, whiffletree, and the like.
A cross or gallows; as Tyburn tree.
q: whom they slew and hanged on a tree.

senses.d: Wood; timber.
q: In a great house ben not only vessels of gold and of silver but also of tree and of earth.

senses.d: A mass of crystals, aggregated in arborescent forms, obtained by precipitation of a metal from solution. See Lead tree, under Lead.

Tree.etym: [OE. tree, tre, treo, AS. treó, treów, tree, wood; akin to OFries. tr�, OS. treo, trio, Icel. tr�, Dan. træ, Sw. trä, träd, Goth. triu, Russ. drevo, W. derw an oak, Ir. darag, darog, Gr. � a tree, oak, � a beam, spear shaft, spear, Skr. dru tree, wood, dāru wood. ���, ���. Cf. Dryad, Germander, Tar,

senses.d: To drive to a tree; to cause to ascend a tree; as, a dog trees a squirrel.
To place upon a tree; to fit with a tree; to stretch upon a tree; as, to tree a boot. See Tree, n., 3.
To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness; to quake; to quiver; to shiver; to shudder; — said of a person or an animal.
q: I tremble still with fear.
Frighted Turnus trembled as he spoke.

senses.d: To totter; to shake; — said of a thing.
q: The Mount of Sinai, whose gray top Shall tremble.

senses.d: To quaver or shake, as sound; to be tremulous; as the voice trembles.

Tremble.etym: [F. trembler, fr. L. tremulus trembling, tremulous, fr. tremere to shake, tremble; akin to Gr. �, Lith. trimti. Cf. Tremulous, Tremor.]

senses.d: An involuntary shaking or quivering.
q: I am all of a tremble when I think of it.

senses.d: Shaking; tottering; quivering.
To cut; to form or shape by cutting; to make by incision, hewing, or the like.
q: The wide wound that the boar had trenched In his soft flank.
This weak impress of love is as a figure Trenched in ice, which with an hour's heat Dissolves to water, and doth lose its form.

senses.d: To fortify by cutting a ditch, and raising a rampart or breastwork with the earth thrown out of the ditch; to intrench.
q: No more shall trenching war channel her fields.

senses.d: To cut furrows or ditches in; as, to trench land for the purpose of draining it.
To dig or cultivate very deeply, usually by digging parallel contiguous trenches in succession, filling each from the next; as, to trench a garden for certain crops.

Trench.etym: [OF. trenchier to cut, F. trancher; akin to Pr. trencar, trenchar, Sp. trinchar, It. trinciare; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To encroach; to intrench.
q: Does it not seem as if for a creature to challenge to itself a boundless attribute, were to trench upon the prerogative of the divine nature?

senses.d: To have direction; to aim or tend.
q: Like powerful armies, trenching at a town By slow and silent, but resistless, sap.

senses.d: A long, narrow cut in the earth; a ditch; as, a trench for draining land.
An alley; a narrow path or walk cut through woods, shrubbery, or the like.
q: In a trench, forth in the park, goeth she.

senses.d: An excavation made during a siege, for the purpose of covering the troops as they advance toward the besieged place. The term includes the parallels and the approaches.

Trench.etym: [OE. trenche, F. tranchée. See Trench, v. t.]

senses.d: To pass beyond a limit or boundary; hence, to depart; to go.
q: Soon after this, noble Robert de Bruce . . . trespassed out of this uncertain world.

senses.d: To commit a trespass; esp., to enter unlawfully upon the land of another.
To go too far; to put any one to inconvenience by demand or importunity; to intrude; as, to trespass upon the time or patience of another.

To commit any offense, or to do any act that injures or annoys another; to violate any rule of rectitude, to the injury of another; hence, in a moral sense, to transgress voluntarily any divine law or command; to violate any known rule of duty; to sin; — often followed by against.
q: In the time of his distress did he trespass yet more against the Lord.

Trespass.etym: [OF. trespasser to go across or over, transgress, F. trépasser to die; pref. tres- (L. trans across, over) + passer to pass. See Pass, v. i., and cf. Transpass.]

senses.d: Any injury or offence done to another.
q: I you forgive all wholly this trespass.
If ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

senses.d: Any voluntary transgression of the moral law; any violation of a known rule of duty; sin.
q: The fatal trespass done by Eve.
You . . . who were dead in trespasses and sins.

senses.d: An unlawful act committed with force and violence (vi et armis) on the person, property, or relative rights of another.

Trespass.syn: Offense; breach; infringement; transgression; misdemeanor; misdeed.
Trespass.etym: [OF. tr�spas, F. trépas death. See Trespass, v.]

senses.d: The act of trying or testing in any manner.
Any effort or exertion of strength for the purpose of ascertaining what can be done or effected.
q: defy thee to the trial of mortal fight.

senses.d: The act of testing by experience; proof; test.
q: Repeated trials of the issues and events of actions.

senses.d: Examination by a test; experiment, as in chemistry, metallurgy, etc.
The state of being tried or tempted; exposure to suffering that tests strength, patience, faith, or the like; affliction or temptation that exercises and proves the graces or virtues of men.
q: Others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings.

senses.d: That which tries or afflicts; that which harasses; that which tries the character or principles; that which tempts to evil; as, his child's conduct was a sore trial.
q: Every station is exposed to some trials.

senses.d: The formal examination of the matter in issue in a cause before a competent tribunal; the mode of determining a question of fact in a court of law; the examination, in legal form, of the facts in issue in a cause pending before a competent tribunal, for the purpose of determining such issue.

Trial.syn: Test; attempt; endeavor; effort; experiment; proof; essay. See Test, and Attempt.

senses.d: A family, race, or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor, and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob.
q: A wealthy Hebrew of my tribe.

senses.d: A number of species or genera having certain structural characteristics in common; as, a tribe of plants; a tribe of animals.
A nation of savages or uncivilized people; a body of rude people united under one leader or government; as, the tribes of the Six Nations; the Seneca tribe.
A division, class, or distinct portion of a people, from whatever cause that distinction may have originated; as, the city of Athens was divided into ten tribes.
A family of animals descended from some particular female progenitor, through the female line; as, the Duchess tribe of shorthorns.

Tribe.etym: [L. tribus, originally, a third part of the Roman people, afterwards, a division of the people, a tribe; of uncertain origin: cf. F. tribu.]

senses.d: To distribute into tribes or classes.
q: Our fowl, fish, and quadruped are well tribed.

senses.d: That which occasions distress, trouble, or vexation; severe affliction.
q: When tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
In the world ye shall have tribulation.

Tribulation.etym: [OE. tribulacium, F. tribulation, L. tribulatio, from tribulare to press, afflict, fr. tribulum a thrashing sledge, akin to terere, tritum, to rub. See Trite.]

senses.d: Paying tribute to another, either from compulsion, as an acknowledgment of submission, or to secure protection, or for the purpose of purchasing peace.
q: unto Rome made them tributary.

senses.d: Hence, subject; subordinate; inferior.
q: He to grace his tributary gods.

senses.d: Paid in tribute.

Yielding supplies of any kind; serving to form or make up, a greater object of the same kind, as a part, branch, etc.; contributing; as, the Ohio has many tributary streams, and is itself tributary to the Mississippi.

Tributary.etym: [OE. tributaire, F. tributaire, L. tributarius. See Tribute.]

senses.d: A ruler or state that pays tribute, or a stated sum, to a conquering power, for the purpose of securing peace and protection, or as an acknowledgment of submission, or for the purchase of security.
A stream or river flowing into a larger river or into a lake; an affluent.

An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one ruler or nation to another, either as an acknowledgment of submission, or as the price of peace and protection, or by virtue of some treaty; as, the Romans made their conquered countries pay tribute.
q: Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute.

senses.d: A personal contribution, as of money, praise, service, etc., made in token of services rendered, or as that which is due or deserved; as, a tribute of affection.
q: Implores the passing tribute of a sigh.

senses.d: A certain proportion of the ore raised, or of its value, given to the miner as his recompense.

Tribute.etym: [OE. tribut, L. tributum, fr. tribuere, tributum, to bestow, grant, pay, allot, assign, originally, to a tribe, from tribus tribe; cf. F. tribut. See Tribe, and cf. Attribute, Contribute.]

senses.d: To pay as tribute.
To flow in a small, gentle stream; to run in drops.
q: His salt tears trickled down as rain.
Fast beside there trickled softly down A gentle stream.

Trickle.etym: [OE. triklen, probably for striklen, freq. of striken to flow, AS. str�can. See Strike, v. t.]

senses.d: The act or state of trickling; also, that which trickles; a small stream; drip.
q: Streams that . . . are short and rapid torrents after a storm, but at other times dwindle to feeble trickles of mud.

senses.d: Proved; tested; faithful; trustworthy; as, a tried friend.
To make trim; to put in due order for any purpose; to make right, neat, or pleasing; to adjust.
q: The hermit trimmed his little fire.

senses.d: To dress; to decorate; to adorn; to invest; to embellish; as, to trim a hat.
q: A rotten building newly trimmed over.
I was trimmed in Julia's gown.

senses.d: To make ready or right by cutting or shortening; to clip or lop; to curtail; as, to trim the hair; to trim a tree.
To dress, as timber; to make smooth.

To adjust, as a ship, by arranging the cargo, or disposing the weight of persons or goods, so equally on each side of the center and at each end, that she shall sit well on the water and sail well; as, to trim a ship, or a boat.
To rebuke; to reprove; also, to beat.
q: I found her trimming up the diadem On her dead mistress.

Trim.etym: [OE. trimen, trumen, AS. trymian, trymman, to prepare, dispose, make strong, fr. trum firm, strong; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To balance; to fluctuate between parties, so as to appear to favor each.
Dress; gear; ornaments.
q: Seeing him just pass the window in his woodland trim.

senses.d: Order; disposition; condition; as, to be in good trim.
The state of a ship or her cargo, ballast, masts, etc., by which she is well prepared for sailing.
The lighter woodwork in the interior of a building; especially, that used around openings, generally in the form of a molded architrave, to protect the plastering at those points.

Fitly adjusted; being in good order., or made ready for service or use; firm; compact; snug; neat; fair; as, the ship is trim, or trim built; everything about the man is trim; a person is trim when his body is well shaped and firm; his dress is trim when it fits closely to his body, and appears tight and snug; a man or a soldier is trim when he stands erect.
q: With comely carriage of her countenance trim.
So deemed I till I viewed their trim array Of boats last night.

senses.d: A magnificent and imposing ceremonial performed in honor of a general who had gained a decisive victory over a foreign enemy.
Hence, any triumphal procession; a pompous exhibition; a stately show or pageant.
q: Our daughter, In honor of whose birth these triumphs are, Sits here, like beauty's child.

senses.d: A state of joy or exultation for success.
q: Great triumph and rejoicing was in heaven.
Hercules from Spain Arrived in triumph, from Geryon slain.

senses.d: Success causing exultation; victory; conquest; as, the triumph of knowledge.
A trump card; also, an old game at cards.

Triumph.etym: [L. triumphus, OL. triumpus; of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. � a procession in honor of Bacchus: cf. F. triomphe. Cf. Trump at cards.]

senses.d: To celebrate victory with pomp; to rejoice over success; to exult in an advantage gained; to exhibit exultation.
q: How long shall the wicked triumph?
Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you That triumph thus upon my misery!

senses.d: To obtain victory; to be successful; to prevail.
q: Triumphing over death, and chance, and thee, O Time.
On this occasion, however, genius triumphed.

senses.d: To be prosperous; to flourish.
q: Where commerce triumphed on the favoring gales.

senses.d: To play a trump card.

Triumph.etym: [L. triumphare: cf. F. triompher. See Triumph, n.]

senses.d: To obtain a victory over; to prevail over; to conquer. Also, to cause to triumph.
q: Two and thirty legions that awe All nations of the triumphed word.

senses.d: Having or celebrating a triumph; victorious; triumphant.
Tread; footing.

Trode.etym: [AS. trod, fr. tredan to tread. See Tread.]

senses.d: A collection of people; a company; a number; a multitude.
q: That which should accompany old age — As honor, love, obedience, troops of friends — I must not look to have.

senses.d: Soldiers, collectively; an army; — now generally used in the plural.
q: Farewell the plumed troop, and the big wars.
His troops moved to victory with the precision of machines.

senses.d: Specifically, a small body of cavalry, light horse, or dragoons, consisting usually of about sixty men, commanded by a captain; the unit of formation of cavalry, corresponding to the company in infantry. Formerly, also, a company of horse artillery; a battery.
A company of stageplayers; a troupe.
A particular roll of the drum; a quick march.

Troop.etym: [F. troupe, OF. trope, trupe, LL. troppus; of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. þorp a hamlet, village, G. dorf a village, dial. G. dorf a meeting. Norw. torp a little farm, a crowd, E. thorp. Cf. Troupe.]

senses.d: To move in numbers; to come or gather in crowds or troops.
To march on; to go forward in haste.
q: Nor do I, as an enemy to peace, Troop in the throngs of military men.

senses.d: To put into confused motion; to disturb; to agitate.
q: An angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water.
God looking forth will trouble all his host.

senses.d: To disturb; to perplex; to afflict; to distress; to grieve; to fret; to annoy; to vex.
q: Now is my soul troubled.
Take the boy to you; he so troubles me 'T is past enduring.
Never trouble yourself about those faults which age will cure.

senses.d: To give occasion for labor to; — used in polite phraseology; as, I will not trouble you to deliver the letter.

Trouble.syn: To disturb; perplex; afflict; distress; grieve; harass; annoy; tease; vex; molest.
Trouble.etym: [F. troubler, OF. trobler, trubler, tourbler,fr. (assumed) LL. turbulare, L. turbare to disorderly group, a little crowd; both from turba a disorder, tumult, crowd; akin to Gr. �, and perhaps to E. thorp; cf. Skr. tvar, tur,o hasten. Cf. Turbid.]

senses.d: Troubled; dark; gloomy.
The state of being troubled; disturbance; agitation; uneasiness; vexation; calamity.
q: Lest the fiend . . . some new trouble raise.
Foul whisperings are abroad; unnatural deeds Do breed unnatural troubles.

senses.d: That which gives disturbance, annoyance, or vexation; that which afflicts.
A fault or interruption in a stratum.

Trouble.syn: Affliction; disturbance; perplexity; annoyance; molestation; vexation; inconvenience; calamity; misfortune; adversity; embarrassment; anxiety; sorrow; misery.
Trouble.etym: [F. trouble, OF. troble, truble. See Trouble, v. t.]

senses.d: One who troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber; as, a troubler of the peace.
q: The rich troublers of the world's repose.

senses.d: Full of trouble; causing trouble.
q: A tall ship tossed in troublous seas.

senses.d: A long, hollow vessel, generally for holding water or other liquid, especially one formed by excavating a log longitudinally on one side; a long tray; also, a wooden channel for conveying water, as to a mill wheel.
Any channel, receptacle, or depression, of a long and narrow shape; as, trough between two ridges, etc.

Trough.etym: [OE. trough, trogh, AS. trog, troh; akin to D., G., & Icel. trog, Sw. tråg, Dan. trug; probably originally meaning, made of wood, and akin to E. tree. � & 241. See Tree, and cf. Trug.]

senses.d: The transverse section of a cyclonic area where the barometric pressure, neither rising nor falling, has reached its lowest point.
A boat with an open well amidships. It is used in spearing fish.
To believe; to trust; to think or suppose.
q: So that ye trow in Christ, and you baptize.
A better priest, I trow, there nowhere none is.
It never yet was worn, I trow.
What tempest, I trow, threw this whale . . . ashore?
What is the matter, trow?

Trow.etym: [OE. trowen, AS. treówan to trust, believe, fr. treów trust, treówe true, faithful. See True.]

senses.d: One who violates a truce, covenant, or engagement.

Conformable to fact; in accordance with the actual state of things; correct; not false, erroneous, inaccurate, or the like; as, a true relation or narration; a true history; a declaration is true when it states the facts.
Right to precision; conformable to a rule or pattern; exact; accurate; as, a true copy; a true likeness of the original.
q: Making his eye, foot, and hand keep true time.

senses.d: Steady in adhering to friends, to promises, to a prince, or the like; unwavering; faithful; loyal; not false, fickle, or perfidious; as, a true friend; a wife true to her husband; an officer true to his charge.
q: Thy so true, So faithful, love unequaled.
Dare to be true: nothing can need a lie.

senses.d: Actual; not counterfeit, adulterated, or pretended; genuine; pure; real; as, true balsam; true love of country; a true Christian.
q: The true light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
True ease in writing comes from art, not chance.

True.etym: [OE. trewe, AS. treówe faithful, true, from treów fidelity, faith, troth; akin to OFries. triuwe, adj., treuwa, n., OS. triuwi, adj., trewa, n., D. trouw, adj. & n., G. treu, adj., treue, n., OHG. gitriuwi, adj., triuwa, n., Icel. tryggr, adj., Dan. tro, adj. & n., Sw. trogen, adj., tro, n., Goth. t

senses.d: In accordance with truth; truly.
Genuine; real; not deviating from the essential characters of a class; as, a lizard is a true reptile; a whale is a true, but not a typical, mammal.
In a true manner; according to truth; in agreement with fact; as, to state things truly; the facts are truly represented.
q: I can not truly say how I came here.

senses.d: Exactly; justly; precisely; accurately; as, to estimate truly the weight of evidence.
Sincerely; honestly; really; faithfully; as, to be truly attached to a lover; the citizens are truly loyal to their prince or their country.
Conformably to law; legally; legitimately.
q: His innocent babe truly begotten.

senses.d: In fact; in deed; in reality; in truth.
q: Beauty is excelled by manly grace And wisdom, which alone is truly fair.

senses.d: A wind instrument of music; a trumpet, or sound of a trumpet; — used chiefly in Scripture and poetry.
q: We shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump.
The wakeful trump of doom.

Trump.etym: [OE. trumpe, trompe, F. trompe; probably fr. L. triumphare to triumph, to exult, hence, probably, to make a joyous sound or noise. See Triumph, v. i. & n., and cf. Trombone, Tromp, Trump at cards, Trumpery, Trumpet, Trunk a proboscis.]

senses.d: To blow a trumpet.

Trump.etym: [Cf. OF. tromper. See Trump a trumpet.]

senses.d: A winning card; one of a particular suit (usually determined by chance for each deal) any card of which takes any card of the other suits.
An old game with cards, nearly the same as whist; — called also ruff.
A good fellow; an excellent person.
q: Alfred is a trump, I think you say.
But when kings come so low as to fawn upon philosophy, which before they neither valued nor understood, it is a sign that fails not, they are then put to their last trump.
Put the housekeeper to her trumps to accommodate them.

Trump.etym: [A corruption of triumph, F. triomphe. See Triumph, and cf. Trump a trumpet.]

senses.d: To play a trump card when one of another suit has been led.
To play a trump card upon; to take with a trump card; as, she trumped the first trick.
To trick, or impose on; to deceive.
To impose unfairly; to palm off.
q: Authors have been trumped upon us.

Trump.etym: [F. tromper to deceive, in OF., to blow a trumpet, se tromper de to mock. See Trump a trumpet.]

senses.d: A wind instrument of great antiquity, much used in war and military exercises, and of great value in the orchestra. In consists of a long metallic tube, curved (once or twice) into a convenient shape, and ending in a bell. Its scale in the lower octaves is limited to the first natural harmonics; but there are modern trumpets capable, by means of valves or pistons, of producing every tone within their compass, although at the expense of the true ringing quality of tone.
q: The trumpet's loud clangor Excites us to arms.

senses.d: A trumpeter.
One who praises, or propagates praise, or is the instrument of propagating it.
q: That great politician was pleased to have the greatest wit of those times . . . to be the trumpet of his praises.

senses.d: A funnel, or short, fiaring pipe, used as a guide or conductor, as for yarn in a knitting machine.

Trumpet.etym: [F. trompette, dim. of trompe. See Trump a trumpet.]

senses.d: To publish by, or as by, sound of trumpet; to noise abroad; to proclaim; as, to trumpet good tidings.
q: They did nothing but publish and trumpet all the reproaches they could devise against the Irish.

senses.d: To sound loudly, or with a tone like a trumpet; to utter a trumplike cry.
One who sounds a trumpet.
One who proclaims, publishes, or denounces.
q: These men are good trumpeters.

senses.d: Any one of several species of long-legged South American birds of the genus Psophia, especially P. crepitans, which is abundant, and often domesticated and kept with other poultry by the natives. They are allied to the cranes. So called from their loud cry. Called also agami, and yakamik.
A large edible fish (Latris hecateia) of the family Cirrhitidæ, native of Tasmania and New Zealand. It sometimes weighs as much as fifty or sixty pounds, and is highly esteemed as a food fish.
A plant (Sarracenia flava) with long, hollow leaves.
Assured resting of the mind on the integrity, veracity, justice, friendship, or other sound principle, of another person; confidence; reliance; reliance.
q: Most take things upon trust.

senses.d: Credit given; especially, delivery of property or merchandise in reliance upon future payment; exchange without immediate receipt of an equivalent; as, to sell or buy goods on trust.
Assured anticipation; dependence upon something future or contingent, as if present or actual; hope; belief.
q: His trust was with the Eternal to be deemed Equal in strength.

senses.d: That which is committed or intrusted to one; something received in confidence; charge; deposit.
The condition or obligation of one to whom anything is confided; responsible charge or office.
q: serve him truly that will put me in trust.
Reward them well, if they observe their trust.

senses.d: That upon which confidence is reposed; ground of reliance; hope.
q: O Lord God, thou art my trust from my youth.

senses.d: An estate devised or granted in confidence that the devisee or grantee shall convey it, or dispose of the profits, at the will, or for the benefit, of another; an estate held for the use of another; a confidence respecting property reposed in one person, who is termed the trustee, for the benefit of another, who is called the cestui que trust.
An organization formed mainly for the purpose of regulating the supply and price of commodities, etc.; as, a sugar trust.

Trust.etym: [OE. trust, trost, Icel. traust confidence, security; akin to Dan. & Sw. tröst comfort, consolation, G. trost, Goth. trausti a convention, covenant, and E. true. See True, and cf. Tryst.]

senses.d: Held in trust; as, trust property; trustmoney.
To place confidence in; to rely on, to confide, or repose faith, in; as, we can not trust those who have deceived us.
q: I will never trust his word after.
He that trusts every one without reserve will at last be deceived.

senses.d: To give credence to; to believe; to credit.
q: Trust me, you look well.

senses.d: To hope confidently; to believe; — usually with a phrase or infinitive clause as the object.
q: I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face.
We trustwe have a good conscience.

senses.d: to show confidence in a person by intrusting (him) with something.
q: Whom, with your power and fortune, sir, you trust, Now to suspect is vain.

senses.d: To commit, as to one's care; to intrust.
q: Merchants were not willing to trust precious cargoes to any custody but that of a man-of-war.

senses.d: To give credit to; to sell to upon credit, or in confidence of future payment; as, merchants and manufacturers trust their customers annually with goods.
To risk; to venture confidently.
q: by thee to trust thee from my side.

senses.d: To have trust; to be credulous; to be won to confidence; to confide.
q: More to know could not be more to trust.

senses.d: To be confident, as of something future; to hope.
q: I will trust and not be afraid.

senses.d: To sell or deliver anything in reliance upon a promise of payment; to give credit.
q: It is happier sometimes to be cheated than not to trust.

senses.d: An equitable right or interest in property distinct from the legal ownership thereof; a use (as it existed before the Statute of Uses); also, a property interest held by one person for the benefit of another. Trusts are active, or special, express, implied, constructive, etc. In a passive trust the trustee simply has title to the trust property, while its control and management are in the beneficiary.

A business organization or combination consisting of a number of firms or corporations operating, and often united, under an agreement creating a trust (in sense 1), esp. one formed mainly for the purpose of regulating the supply and price of commodities, etc.; often, opprobriously, a combination formed for the purpose of controlling or monopolizing a trade, industry, or business, by doing acts in restraint or trade; as, a sugar trust. A trust may take the form of a corporation or of a body of persons or corporations acting together by mutual arrangement, as under a contract or a so-called gentlemen's agreement. When it consists of corporations it may be effected by putting a majority of their stock either in the hands of a board of trustees (whence the name trust for the combination) or by transferring a majority to a holding company. The advantages of a trust are partly due to the economies made possible in carrying on a large business, as well as the doing away with competition. In the United States severe statutes against trusts have been passed by the Federal government and in many States, with elaborate statutory definitions.
Having or exercising trust; confiding; unsuspecting; trustful.
Admitting of being safely trusted; justly deserving confidence; fit to be confided in; trustworthy; reliable.
q: Your trusty and most valiant servitor.

senses.d: Hence, not liable to fail; strong; firm.
q: His trusty sword he called to his aid.

senses.d: Involving trust; as, a trusty business.
The quality or being true; as: — (a) Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been; or shall be.
Conformity to rule; exactness; close correspondence with an example, mood, object of imitation, or the like.
q: Plows, to go true, depend much on the truth of the ironwork.

senses.d: Fidelity; constancy; steadfastness; faithfulness.
q: Alas! they had been friends in youth, But whispering tongues can poison truth.

senses.d: The practice of speaking what is true; freedom from falsehood; veracity.
q: If this will not suffice, it must appear That malice bears down truth.

senses.d: That which is true or certain concerning any matter or subject, or generally on all subjects; real state of things; fact; verity; reality.
q: Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbor.
I long to know the truth here of at large.
The truth depends on, or is only arrived at by, a legitimate deduction from all the facts which are truly material.

senses.d: A true thing; a verified fact; a true statement or proposition; an established principle, fixed law, or the like; as, the great truths of morals.
q: Even so our boasting . . . is found a truth.

senses.d: Righteousness; true religion.
q: Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.
Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth.
He that doeth truth cometh to the light.

Truth.etym: [OE. treuthe, trouthe, treowpe, AS. treów�. See True; cf. Troth, Betroth.]

senses.d: To assert as true; to declare.
q: Had they dreamt this, they would have truthed it heaven.

senses.d: To divide or separate, as one sort from another; to winnow; to sift; to pick out; — frequently followed by out; as, to try out the wild corn from the good.
To purify or refine, as metals; to melt out, and procure in a pure state, as oil, tallow, lard, etc.
q: The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried.

senses.d: To prove by experiment; to apply a test to, for the purpose of determining the quality; to examine; to prove; to test; as, to try weights or measures by a standard; to try a man's opinions.
q: Let the end try the man.

senses.d: To subject to severe trial; to put to the test; to cause suffering or trouble to.
q: Thus far to try thee, Adam, I was pleased.

senses.d: To experiment with; to test by use; as, to try a remedy for disease; to try a horse.
q: Come, try upon yourselves what you have seen me.
To ease her cares the force of sleep she tries.

senses.d: To strain; to subject to excessive tests; as, the light tries his eyes; repeated disappointments try one's patience.
To examine or investigate judicially; to examine by witnesses or other judicial evidence and the principles of law; as, to try a cause, or a criminal.
To settle; to decide; to determine; specifically, to decide by an appeal to arms; as, to try rival claims by a duel; to try conclusions.
q: Left I the court, to see this quarrel tried.

senses.d: To experience; to have or gain knowledge of by experience.
q: Or try the Libyan heat or Scythian cold.

senses.d: To essay; to attempt; to endeavor.
q: Let us try . . . to found a path.
He first deceased: she for a little tried To live without him; liked it not, and died.
Alack, I am afraid they have a waked, And 't is not done. The attempt, and not the deed, Confounds us.

Try.syn: To attempt; endeavor; strive; aim; examine.
Try.etym: [OE. trien to select, pick out, F. trier to cull, to out, LL. tritare to triturate (hence the sense of, to thresh, to separate the grain from the straw, to select), L. terere, tritum, to rub, bruise, grind, thresh. See Trite.]

senses.d: To exert strength; to endeavor; to make an effort or an attempt; as, you must try hard if you wish to learn.
To do; to fare; as, how do you try!
A screen, or sieve, for grain.
Act of trying; attempt; experiment; trial.
q: This breaking of his has been but a try for his friends.

senses.d: Refined; select; excellent; choice.

In Rugby and Northern Union football, a score (counting three points) made by grounding the ball on or behind the opponent's goal line; — so called because it entitles the side making it to a place kick for a goal (counting two points more if successful).
Adapted to try, or put to severe trial; severe; afflictive; as, a trying occasion or position.
Of or pertaining to a tube; specifically, of or pertaining to one of the Fallopian tubes; as, tubal pregnancy.
To roll over, or to and fro; to throw one's self about; as, a person on pain tumbles and tosses.
To roll down; to fall suddenly and violently; to be precipitated; as, to tumble from a scaffold.
q: He who tumbles from a tower surely has a greater blow than he who slides from a molehill.

senses.d: To play tricks by various movements and contortions of the body; to perform the feats of an acrobat.

Tumble.etym: [OE. tumblen, AS. tumbian to turn heels over head, to dance violently; akin to D. tuimelen to fall, Sw. tumla, Dan. tumle, Icel. tumba; and cf. G. taumeln to reel, to stagger.]

senses.d: To turn over; to turn or throw about, as for examination or search; to roll or move in a rough, coarse, or unceremonious manner; to throw down or headlong; to precipitate; — sometimes with over, about, etc.; as, to tumble books or papers.
To disturb; to rumple; as, to tumble a bed.
Act of tumbling, or rolling over; a fall.
The commotion or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar, and confusion of voices; hurly-burly; noisy confusion.
q: What meaneth the noise of this tumult ?
Till in loud tumult all the Greeks arose.

senses.d: Violent commotion or agitation, with confusion of sounds; as, the tumult of the elements.
Irregular or confused motion; agitation; high excitement; as, the tumult of the spirits or passions.

Tumult.syn: Uproar; ferment; disturbance; turbulence; disorder; confusion; noise; bluster; hubbub; bustle; stir; brawl; riot.
Tumult.etym: [L. tumultus; probably akin to Skr. tumula noise, noisy, and perhaps to L. tumere to swell, E. tumid: cf. F. tumulte.]

senses.d: To make a tumult; to be in great commotion.
q: Importuning and tumulting even to the fear of a revolt.

senses.d: Full of tumult; characterized by tumult; disorderly; turbulent.
q: The flight became wild and tumultuous.

senses.d: Conducted with disorder; noisy; confused; boisterous; disorderly; as, a tumultuous assembly or meeting.
Agitated, as with conflicting passions; disturbed.
q: His dire attempt, which, nigh the birth Now rolling, boils in his tumultuous breast.

senses.d: Turbulent; violent; as, a tumultuous speech.

Tumultuous.syn: Disorderly; irregular; noisy; confused; turbulent; violent; agitated; disturbed; boisterous; lawless; riotous; seditious.

senses.d: To cause to move upon a center, or as if upon a center; to give circular motion to; to cause to revolve; to cause to move round, either partially, wholly, or repeatedly; to make to change position so as to present other sides in given directions; to make to face otherwise; as, to turn a wheel or a spindle; to turn the body or the head.
q: Turn the adamantine spindle round.
The monarch turns him to his royal guest.

senses.d: To cause to present a different side uppermost or outmost; to make the upper side the lower, or the inside to be the outside of; to reverse the position of; as, to turn a box or a board; to turn a coat.

To give another direction, tendency, or inclination to; to direct otherwise; to deflect; to incline differently; — used both literally and figuratively; as, to turn the eyes to the heavens; to turn a horse from the road, or a ship from her course; to turn the attention to or from something.
q: Thrice I deluded her, and turned to sport Her importunity.
My thoughts are turned on peace.

senses.d: To change from a given use or office; to divert, as to another purpose or end; to transfer; to use or employ; to apply; to devote.
q: Therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David.
God will make these evils the occasion of a greater good, by turning them to advantage in this world.
When the passage is open, land will be turned most to cattle; when shut, to sheep.

senses.d: To change the form, quality, aspect, or effect of; to alter; to metamorphose; to convert; to transform; — often with to or into before the word denoting the effect or product of the change; as, to turn a worm into a winged insect; to turn green to blue; to turn prose into verse; to turn a Whig to a Tory, or a Hindoo to a Christian; to turn good to evil, and the like.
q: The Lord thy God will turn thy captivity, and have compassion upon thee.
And David said, O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.
Impatience turns an ague into a fever.

senses.d: To form in a lathe; to shape or fashion (anything) by applying a cutting tool to it while revolving; as, to turn the legs of stools or tables; to turn ivory or metal.
q: I had rather hear a brazen canstick turned.

senses.d: Hence, to give form to; to shape; to mold; to put in proper condition; to adapt.
q: His limbs how turned, how broad his shoulders spread !
He was perfectly well turned for trade.

senses.d: To translate; to construe; as, to turn the Iliad.
q: Who turns a Persian tale for half a crown.

senses.d: To make acid or sour; to ferment; to curdle, etc.: as, to turn cider or wine; electricity turns milk quickly.
To sicken; to nauseate; as, an emetic turns one's stomach.

Turn.etym: [OE. turnen, tournen, OF. tourner, torner, turner, F. tourner, LL. tornare, fr. L. tornare to turn in a lathe, to rounds off, fr. tornus a lathe, Gr. � a turner's chisel, a carpenter's tool for drawing circles; probably akin to E. throw. See Throw, and cf. Attorney, Return, Tornado, Tour, Tournament

senses.d: To move round; to have a circular motion; to revolve entirely, repeatedly, or partially; to change position, so as to face differently; to whirl or wheel round; as, a wheel turns on its axis; a spindle turns on a pivot; a man turns on his heel.
q: The gate . . . on golden hinges turning.

senses.d: Hence, to revolve as if upon a point of support; to hinge; to depend; as, the decision turns on a single fact.
q: Conditions of peace certainly turn upon events of war.

senses.d: To result or terminate; to come about; to eventuate; to issue.
q: If we repent seriously, submit contentedly, and serve him faithfully, afflictions shall turn to our advantage.

senses.d: To be deflected; to take a different direction or tendency; to be directed otherwise; to be differently applied; to be transferred; as, to turn from the road.
q: Turn from thy fierce wrath.
Turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways.
The understanding turns inward on itself, and reflects on its own operations.

senses.d: To be changed, altered, or transformed; to become transmuted; also, to become by a change or changes; to grow; as, wood turns to stone; water turns to ice; one color turns to another; to turn Mohammedan.
q: I hope you have no intent to turn husband.
Cygnets from gray turn white.

senses.d: To undergo the process of turning on a lathe; as, ivory turns well.
To become acid; to sour; — said of milk, ale, etc.
To become giddy; — said of the head or brain.
q: I'll look no more; Lest my brain turn.

senses.d: To be nauseated; — said of the stomach.
To become inclined in the other direction; — said of scales.
To change from ebb to flow, or from flow to ebb; — said of the tide.
To bring down the feet of a child in the womb, in order to facilitate delivery.
The act of turning; movement or motion about, or as if about, a center or axis; revolution; as, the turn of a wheel.
Change of direction, course, or tendency; different order, position, or aspect of affairs; alteration; vicissitude; as, the turn of the tide.
q: At length his complaint took a favorable turn.
The turns and varieties of all passions.
Too well the turns of mortal chance I know.

senses.d: One of the successive portions of a course, or of a series of occurrences, reckoning from change to change; hence, a winding; a bend; a meander.
q: And all its thousand turns disclose. Some fresher beauty varying round.

senses.d: A circuitous walk, or a walk to and fro, ending where it began; a short walk; a stroll.
q: Come, you and I must walk a turn together.
I will take a turn in your garden.

senses.d: Successive course; opportunity enjoyed by alternation with another or with others, or in due order; due chance; alternate or incidental occasion; appropriate time.
q: His turn will come to laugh at you again.
Every one has a fair turn to be as great as he pleases.

senses.d: Incidental or opportune deed or office; occasional act of kindness or malice; as, to do one an ill turn.
q: Had I not done a friendes turn to thee?
thanks are half lost when good turns are delayed.

senses.d: Convenience; occasion; purpose; exigence; as, this will not serve his turn.
q: I have enough to serve mine own turn.

senses.d: Form; cast; shape; manner; fashion; — used in a literal or figurative sense; hence, form of expression; mode of signifying; as, the turn of thought; a man of a sprightly turn in conversation.
q: The turn of both his expressions and thoughts is unharmonious.
The Roman poets, in their description of a beautiful man, often mention the turn of his neck and arms.

senses.d: A change of condition; especially, a sudden or recurring symptom of illness, as a nervous shock, or fainting spell; as, a bad turn.
A fall off the ladder at the gallows; a hanging; — so called from the practice of causing the criminal to stand on a ladder which was turned over, so throwing him off, when the signal was given.
A round of a rope or cord in order to secure it, as about a pin or a cleat.
A pit sunk in some part of a drift.
To make a turn about or around (something); to go or pass around by turning; as, to turn a corner.
q: The ranges are not high or steep, and one can turn a kopje instead of cutting or tunneling through it.

senses.d: The act of one who, or that which, turns; also, a winding; a bending course; a fiexure; a meander.
q: Through paths and turnings often trod by day.

senses.d: The place of a turn; an angle or corner, as of a road.
q: It is preached at every turning.

senses.d: Deviation from the way or proper course.
Turnery, or the shaping of solid substances into various by means of a lathe and cutting tools.
The pieces, or chips, detached in the process of turning from the material turned.
A maneuver by which an enemy or a position is turned.
The turtledove.

Turtle.etym: [AS. turtle, L. turtur; probably of imitative origin. Cf. Turtle the sea tortoise.]

senses.d: Any one of the numerous species of Testudinata, especially a sea turtle, or chelonian.
The curved plate in which the form is held in a type-revolving cylinder press.

Turtle.etym: [Probably the same word as the word preceding, and substituted (probably by sailors) for the Spanish or Portuguese name; cf. Sp. tortuga tortoise, turtle, Pg. tartaruga, also F. tortue, and E. tortoise.]

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of pigeons belonging to Turtur and allied genera, native of various parts of the Old World; especially, the common European species (Turtur vulgaris), which is noted for its plaintive note, affectionate disposition, and devotion to its mate.
Any one of several species of pigeons more or less resembling the true turtledoves, as the American mourning dove (see under Dove), and the Australian turtledove (Stictopelia cuneata).
One who guards, protects, watches over, or has the care of, some person or thing.
A treasurer; a keeper.
One who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate; a guardian.
A private or public teacher.
An officer or member of some hall, who instructs students, and is responsible for their discipline.
An instructor of a lower rank than a professor.

Tutor.etym: [OE. tutour, L. tutor, fr. tueri to watch, defend: cf. F. tuteur. Cf. Tuition.]

senses.d: To have the guardianship or care of; to teach; to instruct.
q: Their sons are well tutored by you.

senses.d: To play the tutor toward; to treat with authority or severity.
Two;- nearly obsolete in common discourse, but used in poetry and burlesque.
q: And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.

Twain.etym: [OE. twein, tweien, tweyne, AS. twēgen, masc. See Two.]

senses.d: Next in order after the eleventh; coming after eleven others; — the ordinal of twelve.
Consisting, or being one of, twelve equal parts into which anything is divided.

Twelfth.etym: [For twelft, OE. twelfte, AS. twelfta. See Twelve.]

senses.d: The quotient of a unit divided by twelve; one of twelve equal parts of one whole.
The next in order after the eleventh.
An interval comprising an octave and a fifth.
One more that eleven; two and ten; twice six; a dozen.

Twelve.etym: [OE. twelve, twelf, AS. twelf; akin to OFries. twelf, twelef, twilif, OS. twelif, D. twaalf, G. zwölf, OHG. zwelif, Icel. t�lf, Sw. tolf, Dan. tolv, Goth. twalif, from the root of E. two + the same element as in the second part of E. eleven. See Two, and Eleven.]

senses.d: The number next following eleven; the sum of ten and two, or of twice six; twelve units or objects; a dozen.
A symbol representing twelve units, as 12, or xii.
Next in order after the nineteenth; tenth after the tenth; coming after nineteen others; — the ordinal of twenty.
Consisting, or being, one of twenty equal parts into which anything is divided.

Twentieth.etym: [From Twenty; cf. AS. twentigo�a. See Twenty.]

senses.d: The next in order after the nineteen; one coming after nineteen others.
The quotient of a unit divided by twenty; one of twenty equal parts of one whole.
One more that nineteen; twice; as, twenty men.
An indefinite number more or less that twenty.
q: Maximilian, upon twenty respects, could not have been the man.

Twenty.etym: [OE. twenty, AS. tw�ntig, twentig; akin to OFris. twintich, OS. tw�ntig, D. & LG. twintig, OHG. zweinzug, G. zwanzig, Goth. twai tigjis; that is, two tens. See Twain, Two, and Ten.]

senses.d: The number next following nineteen; the sum of twelve and eight, or twice ten; twenty units or objects; a score.
A symbol representing twenty units, as 20, or xx.
Two times; once and again.
